scored.name: Large-load powered site on state trust land (data centre)
scored.one_line: Company applies for commercial or option leases on school-trust parcels next to transmission substations, in states that lease by application at appraised or schedule rents (MT DNRC, ND, SD, WY OSLI, OK CLO). It funds a utility large-load study to get a will-serve letter for 100-500 MW, then assigns the powered lease to a hyperscaler or data-centre developer.
scored.unproven_right: State trust land commercial or option lease at a fixed schedule or appraised agricultural-grade rent, assignable with board consent
scored.proving_step: Utility large-load interconnection or service study plus a water and fibre desktop review, about $100k-$500k and 6-18 months. With ML picking substations that have headroom, perhaps 30-50% come back with a will-serve on an acceptable timeline.
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers and data-centre developers (QTS, Vantage, Aligned, Tract), who pay $200k-$1M+ per acre for powered land
scored.public_data: State PUC dockets and IRPs, scanned utility transmission plans, FERC Form 715 and OATI postings, ISO large-load study reports and state trust land lease ledgers. Substation headroom for large loads sits in unstructured filings, not in a status field.
scored.rough_step_up: Trust land rented at grazing value of about $5-20 per acre per year (about $1-3k per acre capitalised) moves to $200k-1M per acre once powered, roughly 100-500x. Caveat: trusts may reappraise or require an auction at assignment, which is the key risk to check.
scored.frame: The rung is a powered data-centre site: land control plus a utility will-serve letter, sold to a hyperscaler or developer. Finding a substation with headroom is perhaps 50-60% of the work inside that rung. The rest is not trivial: utility politics, large-load tariff deposits, credibility with the utility, water, fibre and zoning, plus getting the state board to approve the lease and its assignment. Utilities increasingly refuse to study speculative loads without a named end customer, which makes the physical/administrative step a gate rather than an abstraction. Below the 80% bar.
scored.step_up: Powered land does sell for $200k-1M+/acre. Arizona sold 165 acres of trust land in Mesa to Novva for $62.7M (about $380k/acre), but that was the department's posted minimum, set by appraisal at data-centre value. The trust captured the uplift, not the applicant. The headline 100-500x (grazing rent to powered value) is not what the company keeps. Commercial leases are priced at fair market value for the proposed use, and boards can reprice at assignment. The realistic spread to the company is an option/assignment premium of perhaps 10-50x on its outlay.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $100k-500k and 6-18 months per site (utility large-load study, deposits, desktop diligence); that estimate is from the candidate and is plausible given large-load tariffs that require study deposits. Base will-serve rate is perhaps 30-50% (candidate's estimate, unverified). ML that ranks substations by headroom from IRPs and FERC 715 filings could plausibly lift the hit rate 1.3-2x. Under the relaxed C3 the lever is real, but the hit/miss outcome depends heavily on utility discretion and queue politics, not just on headroom data.
scored.data: Headroom signals do sit in unstructured PUC dockets, IRPs, FERC Form 715 and ISO study reports, so the data is partly illegible. But the field is crowded: hyperscaler site-selection teams, Tract, LandGate-style data vendors and utility economic-development offices already compile it. The edge is thin, not Terranox-like.
scored.right_bought: The right fails the fixed-price test. Montana: under 77-1-904 MCA, DNRC must run a competitive RFP for any commercial lease of trust land and must get fair market value whatever the use. Leasing by application at an agricultural rent is not possible. Wyoming OSLI: special-use leases go through an RFP with 30 days' public notice to the website, county paper, lessees and adjoining owners (2023 HB171). Arizona: auctions with a minimum appraised at data-centre value. Assignment needs board consent and can trigger reappraisal. So the public body does price in the hope value, or auctions it, and the notice process tips off competitors. The right is transferable only with consent, and the uplift is largely captured by the trust.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers and data-centre developers (QTS, Vantage, Aligned, Tract, Novva) are well capitalised and actively buying powered land. This leg is strong.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: powered land, then entitled shell, then developing and operating the data centre, then behind-the-meter or co-located generation and transmission. A very large company is possible if the smallest rung can be won.
scored.fatal_flaw: State trust boards lease commercial land by competitive RFP or auction at fair market value for the proposed use, and must approve and can reprice any assignment. The publicly noticed RFP also reveals the site. The step-up therefore goes to the trust, not to the applicant who read the substation data. A second problem: utilities will not issue a firm will-serve to a speculator with no named load.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer and the ladder are strong, and the relaxed C3 helps with an expensive proving step. But trust land is not sold at a fixed grazing-grade price: Montana and Wyoming require competitive RFPs at fair market value, and Arizona auctions at data-centre-appraised minimums. That destroys the cheap-unproven-right leg.

scored.name: Closed-loop pumped storage sites via FERC preliminary permits (federal, state trust and optioned private land)
scored.one_line: Use ML over decades of surrendered FERC preliminary permits (whose scanned filings say why earlier permittees gave up: geology, water, money), old USBR/USACE reconnaissance scans, LiDAR head and state geology/borehole files to rank off-river reservoir pairs with large head near HV substations. File FERC preliminary permits (first-to-file, essentially free, 4-year exclusive priority, transferable with FERC approval), plus BLM/USFS ROW or state trust land use at schedule rent, or land options on private parcels. Pay for geotech borings (dam and tunnel foundations, not mineral exploration), water-supply, interconnection screening and an NOI/PAD, then sell the de-risked project to a storage developer, utility or infrastructure fund that pays the step-up because a feasible, permitted site saves it years. Must sell at the permit-plus-geotech rung, since the build is enormous.
scored.unproven_right: FERC preliminary permit (4-yr exclusive priority to study and apply for a licence, granted by filing order, not sold at market value) plus a BLM/USFS ROW or state trust land use application at schedule rent; on private land, an option at farmland prices before head, geology and interconnection are validated
scored.proving_step: About $0.5-5M over 1-3 years: geotech borings and rock-mass testing at upper reservoir, dam, tunnel and powerhouse; head and volume survey; makeup-water study; interconnection pre-study or queue entry; environmental fatal-flaw screen; NOI and Pre-Application Document. Roughly 30-60% of ML-screened sites reach a licensable configuration; ML that drops dead sites before filing plausibly lifts cost per proven site 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Pumped storage and long-duration storage developers, western and eastern utilities with IRP storage needs (PacifiCorp, NV Energy, APS), and infrastructure funds (Rye Development-type developers, Brookfield, CIP, NextEra)
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary (thousands of issued and surrendered preliminary permits with scanned feasibility reports and surrender letters), USBR and USACE 1970s-80s pumped storage reconnaissance scans, USGS 3DEP DEMs/LiDAR, scanned USGS/Reclamation geologic reports, state dam-safety files and borehole logs, NREL and ORNL closed-loop PSH site atlases (legible screening only), BLM MLRS/LR2000 and ePlanning NEPA PDFs, EIA-860, FERC Form 715 and ISO/WECC transmission data
scored.rough_step_up: About $0-300k for the permit and land position becomes $3-50M for a de-risked 1-2 GW site (about $5-20k/MW): roughly 30-1000x on the right and about 5-15x on all-in proving spend. Weakness on private land: the land is priced. NREL's public screening reduces the ML edge. Ladder: licensing, EPC, ownership of the storage plant.
scored.frame: The rung is a closed-loop PSH site held by preliminary permit, with geotech, an interconnection screen and an NOI/PAD done. Inside that rung, discovery (picking the reservoir pair, head, geology and grid access) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is regulatory and interconnection process: NOI/PAD consultation, environmental screening, the queue, makeup-water rights. Geotech borings are real field campaigns, not a trivial physical step. Buyers do exist (TransAlta, AGL, Rye/CIP-type developers). But they pay mostly in staged milestone payments tied to licence and offtake, not cash on the proving result. So the rung can be sold, but discovery is not 80%+ of it.
scored.step_up: Comparable early-stage sales were all brownfield mine-pit sites. TransAlta paid C$8M upfront plus up to C$17M on milestones for 50% of the 320 MW Tent Mountain project in 2023. That implies about C$50k/MW upfront and up to about C$150k/MW with milestones. Hillgrove sold the 250 MW Kanmantoo rights to AGL for A$31M (about A$124k/MW), paid in stages over 18-36 months on milestones. Against $1-5M of proving spend on a 1 GW site, that is about 10-30x, and much of it only arrives at licence or offtake. On the permit itself (filing cost only) the multiple is huge, but that is an artifact of the permit being free. On real capital it falls in the 10-100x band, and it is not paid immediately.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $0.5-5M per site over 1-3 years, and a full licence costs another $10-30M over 5+ years. That clears the >=$50k bar. Base rate: most FERC PSH preliminary permits are surrendered or lapse without a licence application. Maysville (1,000 MW) was denied a successive permit for not filing an NOI/PAD, and Banks Lake needed a rehearing to keep its permit. Of ML-screened closed-loop sites, maybe 30-60% reach a licensable configuration. Mining surrender letters and old USBR/USACE reconnaissance for the reasons projects died (geology, water, interconnection, money) could plausibly drop dead sites before boring and give 1.5-2x on cost per proven site. NREL/ORNL closed-loop atlases already do the legible head and volume screening, so the remaining edge is in geology and failure reasons. Under the relaxed C3 that earns a 4, held below 5 because NREL already covers the geometric screen.
scored.data: The data really is illegible: FERC eLibrary scanned feasibility reports and surrender letters, 1970s-80s USBR/USACE reconnaissance, state borehole logs. On top of that, LiDAR and 3DEP are huge but legible. The outcome is not already written into a status field: permit status says surrendered or expired, but not why. On the other hand, NREL's public closed-loop atlas already gives everyone head, volume and distance to transmission, which narrows the edge to geology and failure modes.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought, so the information asymmetry has no seller to exploit. A FERC preliminary permit is issued by filing order, essentially free and first-to-file, and competitors can file competing applications. By statute it is non-transferable: 16 U.S.C. 798(d) says permits 'shall not be transferable'. In practice it can only move by selling the SPV that holds it, or by the buyer taking the licence application. The permit gives no land access. BLM/USFS ROW is charged at schedule rent with NEPA review, so there is no hope-value clawback, but also nothing to buy cheaply. State trust land can be auctioned or negotiated at appraised value once a competing interest appears. Private land is the only place an owner who 'cannot read the data' sells cheaply via an option. Even there, a 1-2 GW reservoir pair needs hundreds to thousands of hectares from several owners, and visible permit filings tip them off. Sites already on NREL's map are effectively public knowledge.
scored.buyer: The buyer pool is thin but capitalised: TransAlta, AGL, Rye Development (CIP-backed), Brookfield, NextEra, and utilities with IRP storage needs (PacifiCorp, NV Energy, APS). They pay largely through milestone-contingent deals tied to licence, offtake or FID, and US transactions are rare and opaque.
scored.ladder: The rungs run from site and permit, to FERC licence (5-7 yrs, $10-30M), to offtake/IRP contract, to EPC and construction ($2-5B per GW-scale plant), to owning and operating a long-duration storage fleet, then to a multi-site storage developer and IPP. The ladder is very large, but each rung needs heavy capital and long timelines, and it is dominated by regulatory process rather than discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right cannot be bought from an owner who cannot read the data. It is a free, first-to-file FERC preliminary permit that is statutorily non-transferable (16 U.S.C. 798(d)) and open to competing filers, and NREL's public atlas already maps the legible candidate sites. And most of the value step-up is paid only through milestone-contingent deals at licence or offtake, years and tens of millions of dollars after the permit-plus-geotech rung, not immediately on the proving result.
scored.one_line_reason: Under the relaxed C3, proving is expensive and ML on surrender letters could lift cost per proven site about 1.5-2x. But the free, non-transferable, first-to-file permit gives no cheap purchase to exploit. Early-stage sales (Tent Mountain, Kanmantoo) show only about 10-30x on proving spend, mostly paid on later milestones. And discovery is well under 80% of a rung dominated by regulation and interconnection.

scored.name: Crown land wind investigative licences with met-mast proof (BC, Ontario, Newfoundland)
scored.one_line: File fixed-fee Crown land wind investigative licences (BC Land Act about $675/yr plus schedule application fee; Ontario Crown site release; Newfoundland Crown wind reservations) on ML-selected ridges, pay for 12-24 months of met-mast/LiDAR measurement plus bird, bat and interconnection screens and early Indigenous engagement, then sell the licence plus bankable wind data to IPPs bidding into BC Hydro calls for power or the Newfoundland hydrogen-wind build-out. Ministry consent is needed to assign. Caveat: wind atlases (ERA5, Global Wind Atlas) are legible, so the ML edge comes mainly from illegible siting constraints (icing, caribou habitat, consultation areas, lapsed-licence histories).
scored.unproven_right: BC Land Act Investigative Licence (wind), Ontario Crown land site release, or Newfoundland Crown land wind reservation over Crown land, at fixed per-hectare or flat administrative rent, first-come (NL ran a nomination process), assignable with consent
scored.proving_step: 12-24 month met mast + LiDAR campaign, energy yield assessment (bankable P50), bird/bat screens, transmission/interconnection desktop study, early First Nations engagement; ~$150-800k per site; ~40-70% reach bankable-yield status
scored.proven_buyer: IPPs and utility-scale developers and infrastructure funds (Capital Power, Innergex, Pattern, EverWind, First Nations-led JVs) bidding BC Hydro calls or NL projects
scored.public_data: FrontCounter BC / BC Data Catalogue tenure layers incl. expired/abandoned wind investigative licences and scanned management plans and old met-tower records; archived 2000s-2010s BC Hydro EPA call submissions; Environment Canada station archives; BC Hydro transmission capacity maps; icing/turbulence reports; provincial LiDAR; caribou/ungulate habitat and First Nations consultation area shapefiles; ERA5 and Global Wind Atlas as baseline
scored.rough_step_up: Licence ~$1-20k; a proven early-stage 200 MW site trades ~$5-20k/MW = $1-4M (~10^2-10^3x on the right, ~3-10x on total spend)
scored.frame: The rung is a licence plus 12-24 months of bankable met-mast/LiDAR data, sold to an IPP. Discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work in that rung, well short of 80%. The wind resource can already be read from ERA5 and Global Wind Atlas, and the mast campaign is contracted out, so it is cheap and abstracted. What a buyer actually pays for at that stage is First Nations partnership, an interconnection position and a permitting path. In BC, Hydro's 2024 call required at least 25% First Nations equity, and 8 of 9 winning wind projects came in at 51%. A licence plus data with no Nation partner is not what IPPs buy.
scored.step_up: The right costs about $1-20k (BC investigative licence rent of about $675/yr plus application fee). Early-stage pipeline deals trade at roughly $5k/MW: Western Wind paid $20M for a 4,000 MW pipeline. Later-stage sites trade higher: Pattern paid $26.5M for King Pine's 600 MW, about $44k/MW, but only conditional on winning an offtake contract. Meanwhile, $1.9M/MW was offered for Windstar, which was near-built and had royalties attached. A 200 MW proven early site is therefore about $1-4M. That is roughly 10^2-10^3x on the licence, but only 3-10x on the total $150-800k spent proving it. The value also depends on winning a utility call, not just on the hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These figures are the candidate's estimates and industry norms, not verified by search. Proving costs about $150-800k and takes 12-24 months per site, so it clears the 'expensive' bar. About 40-70% of sites reach a bankable P50. Because the resource itself is legible, ML only adds value on screening out constraints (icing, caribou habitat, consultation conflicts, lapsed-licence history). That gives a plausible 1.2-1.5x improvement in cost per proven site, not 2-3x.
scored.data: This data is mostly legible. Tenure layers, habitat and consultation shapefiles, transmission capacity maps and wind atlases are all structured GIS that every IPP siting team already overlays. Only a thin layer is illegible: scanned management plans, old met-tower records and archived EPA call submissions. Abandoned or expired licences show up as status fields, which repeats the failure seen in earlier hunts where the regulator writes the outcome into a field.
scored.right_bought: The rights are not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. In BC the investigative licence is first-come at a fixed fee, but the Crown is a competent seller, sophisticated IPPs are filing too, and assignment needs ministry consent. Newfoundland ran a competitive Crown Land Call for Bids (Dec 2022 to Mar 2023). Bidders were screened on experience and financing and scored on grid, benefits, Indigenous engagement and financing. The winners got only an exclusive recommendation letter, with an EA required before the land award, which effectively auctions the hope value. Ontario Crown site release for wind is restricted and runs through IESO procurement. On top of that, First Nations effectively capture half the uplift through required equity.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: Capstone, Innergex, Capital Power, Pattern, EverWind and infrastructure funds. But they buy mainly sites that already have a First Nations partnership, and in BC they need to win a BC Hydro call, which pays 30-year EPAs.
scored.ladder: The ladder is solid: site, then develop and permit, then build, then own and operate as an IPP with 30-year EPAs, then aggregate a portfolio, possibly feeding hydrogen in Newfoundland. The ceiling is capped by the First Nations equity requirement and by provincial utility procurement volumes.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck in this rung. Wind resource is already legible from public atlases. The real value-making steps are a First Nations equity partnership (25% minimum, 51% typical in BC's 2024 call), interconnection, and winning a utility procurement. Newfoundland auctions the hope value through a scored call for bids. So the ML edge is thin and the cheap right doesn't capture the uplift.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little, since proving is expensive and the base hit rate is around 50%. But wind resource is legible, NL auctions sites through a scored call for bids, and BC buyers need a 51% First Nations partner rather than a licence plus mast data, so discovery is nowhere near 80% of the rung.

scored.name: Old-dam-site pumped hydro on Crown land (NSW/Qld)
scored.one_line: ML over scanned 1950s-1990s state water authority dam and storage investigations, with their geotech logs and hydrology, finds sites the state already partly proved but never built. The company takes a fixed-fee Crown Lands investigation licence over the site, pays for targeted geotechnical confirmation and a connection/hydrology feasibility study, then sells the feasibility-grade pumped hydro project to a capitalised genco. Caveat: the ANU pumped hydro atlas is legible and widely used, so the edge rests on the geotech in the old files.
scored.unproven_right: NSW Crown Land Management Act licence / Qld Land Act investigation permit over Crown land at a pumped-hydro site, at fixed administrative fees
scored.proving_step: Geotechnical confirmation (engineering boreholes, not mineral exploration), water-availability and connection studies, pre-feasibility design; ~$1-4M over 1-2 years; ~40-60% pass to feasibility when prior state investigations exist
scored.proven_buyer: Gencos and capitalised storage developers (EnergyAustralia, AGL, ACEN, Snowy Hydro, CleanCo, Quinbrook) and LTESA/CIS tender bidders
scored.public_data: Scanned WaterNSW / former Water Resources Commission and Qld Water Resources Commission dam investigation reports and borehole logs (state archives); AEMO ISP REZ and connection capacity data; ANU RE100 pumped hydro atlas as a baseline layer; Crown land cadastre
scored.rough_step_up: Licence <$10k; a feasibility-grade 500 MW / 8 h PHES site trades ~$10-50M (~10^3x on the right, ~5-15x on total spend)
scored.frame: The rung is a feasibility-grade pumped hydro project with a site right. Finding the site (good head, good geology, a past state investigation) is maybe 25-40% of the work. The rest is not discovery and not trivial: water entitlement, grid connection and transmission, environmental and planning approval, native title on Crown land, community licence and cost estimation. Snowy 2.0 and Borumba show that cost and buildability, not site identification, decide whether these projects live. Buyers with capital exist (AGL, ACEN, EnergyAustralia, CIS/LTESA bidders), so the frame is real but discovery is well under 80%.
scored.step_up: Comparable deal: Hillgrove sold AGL the right to develop the 250 MW / 8 h Kanmantoo PHES for A$31M (2019), about A$124k/MW. Only A$1M was paid on signing; the rest came over 18-36 months in stages tied to milestones, including confirming ground stability by drilling. Against a licence under $10k the step-up looks like 10^3, but against the A$1-4M proving spend it is about 5-15x, and much of it is deferred and conditional. Realised step-up on capital at risk is about 10x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about A$1-4M over 1-2 years (the candidate's own estimate, consistent with how the Kanmantoo milestones were set up), so the expensive leg passes. The candidate's base pass rate of 40-60% is unsourced. ML over old geotech could plausibly lift geotech pass rates, but most attrition comes from non-geotech factors (connection, water, approvals, economics), so the lift in cost per proven project is more like 1.2-1.5x than at least 1.5x.
scored.data: The illegibility leg is real: scanned 1950s-1990s state water authority investigation reports and borehole logs, with the ANU atlas as the legible baseline. But the owner of the data is the same state agency that owns the land, and it does read it. Queensland's state-owned Queensland Hydro ran its own Hydro Study, which identified 16 potential sites in 2017. WaterNSW is running its own pre-feasibility studies to pick which of its 41 dams are best suited for private developers. The outcome is not written in a legible field, but the incumbent holder of the files is actively doing this work itself.
scored.right_bought: Fails. The sites are not available at a fixed fee regardless of hope value. Old dam investigation sites mostly sit on WaterNSW or water-authority land, and WaterNSW allocated pumped hydro access by competitive tender (ACEN Phoenix at Burrendong, Upper Hunter Hydro at Glenbawn/Glennies Creek, ZEN at Burragorang), giving each winner a Development Agreement. NSW Crown Lands has allocated renewable energy land by state-run EOI followed by RFP (Balranald, 2023), and the state reportedly lined up the land itself rather than waiting for developers to bring sites. My searches did not confirm the licence, transfer or rent terms. From general knowledge, not checked here: Crown licences are generally personal, revocable and not freely transferable, and commercial uses are charged market rent. In Queensland the state builds through its own company, and the government cancelled Pioneer-Burdekin and said it will pursue smaller projects. The public body auctions or reserves the hope value rather than selling it cheaply.
scored.buyer: Gencos and storage developers with capital: AGL (paid A$31M for the Kanmantoo PHES rights), ACEN, EnergyAustralia, Snowy Hydro, CleanCo, Quinbrook, plus CIS/LTESA tender bidders.
scored.ladder: Strong in principle. The path runs from site rights and feasibility, to development approval and connection, to EPC and owning the storage asset, to a merchant and contracted storage portfolio, to a genco or retailer. The rungs above are multi-billion-dollar and capital-intensive (A$1-2M/MW or more to build).
scored.fatal_flaw: The state that holds the old dam investigation files also owns the land and reads those files itself. WaterNSW is running pre-feasibility on 41 dams and allocates access by competitive tender; NSW Crown Lands allocates renewable energy land by EOI/RFP; Queensland develops through its own Queensland Hydro. So the unproven right cannot be bought cheaply at a fixed fee, and the hope value is captured by the public owner.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive and the buyers have capital, but the state owner tenders these sites and reads its own files, discovery is a minority of PHES development work, and the realised step-up on capital at risk is only about 10x.
sources: https://hillgroveresources.com.au/uploads/downloads/224/190416 Hillgrove Sells Rights to Pumped Hydro Project.pdf

scored.name: BLM solar ROW applications outside designated leasing areas, cleared of NEPA fatal flaws
scored.one_line: Use ML over illegible BLM NEPA EAs/EISs, Class III cultural and protocol biological survey PDFs and the narrative records of withdrawn and rejected applications (why a ROW died is written in documents, not a status code) to find variance and non-exclusion parcels with low tortoise, cultural and visual risk near grid capacity. File ROW applications at schedule cost-recovery and the reduced per-acre rent and MW capacity fee (2024 Solar and Wind rule, cut ~80%). Pay for protocol biological and cultural surveys and an accepted plan of development, then sell the survey-complete, NEPA-ready ROW position to a utility-scale solar developer at $/MW.
scored.unproven_right: Pending BLM solar ROW application priority and resulting FLPMA grant, priced by fixed acreage rent and capacity-fee schedule rather than auction outside designated leasing areas. Assignable with BLM consent.
scored.proving_step: About $0.3-3M and 1-3 years: desert tortoise and plant protocol surveys, Class III cultural inventory, hydrology, glint and visual study, accepted POD and preliminary NEPA, optionally an interconnection feasibility or cluster study deposit. About 30-60% clear without a fatal flaw; ML over fatal-flaw records plausibly lifts that 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale solar and storage developers and IPPs (NextEra, Intersect, AES, Arevon, Primergy, Invenergy) and their infrastructure-fund and hyperscaler-backed procurement vehicles, buying NEPA-ready MW
scored.public_data: BLM ePlanning EA/EIS PDFs and appendices, MLRS/LR2000 case files incl. withdrawn and rejected solar applications, SHPO survey indices where accessible, USFWS ECOS tortoise habitat models and critical habitat, Western Solar Plan GIS exclusions and EIS appendices, NREL NSRDB, scanned BLM master title plats, EIA-860 substation data, FERC Form 715 and ISO queue study PDFs
scored.rough_step_up: About $10-100k for application rights becomes $20-150k/MW for 200-500 MW, i.e. $6-50M, roughly 10-1000x on the right. Risks: competing applications can trigger a competitive process; interconnection value is a separate track (killed earlier as a lookup-table problem); incumbent developers read this data well. ML edge sits in the fatal-flaw screen, worth about 1.5x.
scored.frame: Rung: a NEPA-ready BLM solar right-of-way (ROW) position outside the designated leasing areas, sold to a developer. Discovery (screening for fatal flaws and picking the site) is maybe 40-50% of the work in this rung. The rest is physical: contracted protocol tortoise and plant surveys, Class III cultural fieldwork, hydrology, glint and plan-of-development work with BLM. Those are routine but not trivial or abstracted. Worse, the step that actually makes the asset bankable is interconnection, which is a separate track (killed earlier as a lookup-table problem) that this rung does not own. A NEPA-ready site with no queue position sells at a steep discount. The capitalised buyer (IPPs, infrastructure funds) exists in principle. Since August 2025, though, Interior's capacity-density order and secretary-level review have put about 35 pending BLM solar projects in doubt. Demand for federal-land solar sites is therefore politically impaired, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's (OBBBA) wind down of solar tax credits shrinks it further.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $15/acre filing fee plus cost-recovery, about $10-100k per application. Proven: early-stage, pre-notice-to-proceed (pre-NTP) utility solar sites trade at roughly $20-80k/MW AC (weak source: ibinterviewquestions energy-IB guide; no hard transaction data found). For 200-500 MW that is about $4-40M. Measured against the fee alone that is 100-1000x. Measured against the $0.3-3M of survey and NEPA spend needed to reach 'proven', it is about 5-15x. The value is also not realised immediately on a hit: buyers price in interconnection and federal approval risk, so a clean survey does not deliver a jump like a drill hit does.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is about $0.3-3M and 1-3 years per site (candidate's estimate; it matches typical tortoise and Class III survey budgets). That clears the 'expensive' bar. The base rate of clearing without a resource fatal flaw is about 30-60% (candidate's estimate; no independent source found). ML over EA, EIS and withdrawn-case narratives could plausibly lift the resource-clearance rate 1.3-1.5x. But since 2025 the dominant failure modes are interconnection and political review (the capacity-density order, secretary-level sign-off), and document-trained ML cannot predict either. So the effective lift on cost per sold asset is about 1.2-1.4x, which scores 3 under the relaxed C3.
scored.data: Partly illegible: BLM ePlanning EA and EIS PDFs, survey appendices and case-file narratives are scattered and unstructured. But Western Solar Plan exclusion layers, USFWS tortoise habitat models and critical habitat are already legible GIS layers. MLRS/LR2000 case disposition (withdrawn or rejected) is a status field, and the reason often shows up in summarised BLM decision records. Cultural SHPO site data is restricted rather than public. Experienced desert-solar developers and consultants (the people who wrote these EAs) already read this material well, so the incumbent extraction gap is small.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a first-come application to the federal government, the most informed party, at fixed fees: a $15/acre filing fee, schedule rent, and the MW capacity fee (cut in 2024). On its face the fixed price ignores hope value, which is favourable. But under the 2016 rule (43 CFR 2804.30-31) BLM may run a competitive process on its own initiative, on public nomination, or whenever two or more competing applications are filed. That auctions away the hope value exactly when a good site attracts attention. The grant is assignable only with BLM consent, and the post-2025 Interior review adds discretionary denial risk. So the hope value is exposed both to competitive clawback and to discretionary denial.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale solar and storage developers and IPPs (NextEra, Intersect, AES, Arevon, Primergy, Invenergy) and the infrastructure funds behind them. They are capitalised, but their appetite for BLM land collapsed after the August 2025 capacity-density order, the July 2025 senior-level review requirement and the OBBBA tax-credit sunset. They now favour private land with a queue position.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: site origination, then NEPA-ready ROW, then an interconnection position, then a construction-ready project, then build-own-operate as an IPP, then storage and hyperscaler PPAs. It is a large but well-trodden path dominated by deep incumbents, and federal-land solar is currently politically disfavoured, which weakens the ladder from this particular entry point.
scored.fatal_flaw: Federal-land solar is effectively frozen by policy. Interior's August 2025 capacity-density order and secretary-level review of all solar and wind decisions, plus the OBBBA credit sunset, mean a NEPA-ready BLM ROW has no reliable path to grant and no eager buyer. Even in a friendlier regime, the value gate is interconnection rather than NEPA screening, and competing applications let BLM auction away the hope value.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving spend is real, but the step-up is about 10x against that spend and not immediate. ML lifts only the resource-clearance slice of the risk. The right is a fixed-fee federal application exposed to competitive clawback, not something bought from owners who cannot read the data. And Interior's 2025 orders have politically frozen demand for BLM solar ROWs.

scored.name: Philippine DOE wind and solar pre-development service contracts
scored.one_line: Apply for Renewable Energy Service Contracts (RESCs) on the DOE's fixed-fee schedule over sites an ML model ranks from scanned DOE/NREL wind atlases, PAGASA records and abandoned contractor filings. Run a 12-18 month LiDAR or met-mast campaign plus a grid study, then assign the bankable contract to an IPP (ACEN, Aboitiz, foreign entrants) under GEA auction pressure.
scored.unproven_right: A pre-development-stage RESC for an onshore wind or solar block. You get it from the DOE on application for fixed administrative and processing fees, with work-program commitments and no bidding on value. Assignment needs DOE approval.
scored.proving_step: A bankable resource assessment: 12+ months of met-mast or LiDAR data, energy yield at P50/P90, a grid connection study and an initial ECC screen. Roughly $150-400k and 1.5 years per site. Perhaps 40-60% of ML-picked sites reach a bankable capacity factor, versus about 20-30% for land-grab sites.
scored.proven_buyer: Capitalised Philippine and foreign IPPs bidding into DOE Green Energy Auctions, which need shovel-ready contracted capacity.
scored.public_data: DOE awarded and terminated RESC lists and work-program reports (scanned PDFs). NREL/DOE Philippine wind atlas. PAGASA station records. NGCP Transmission Development Plan. ECC filings on the DENR-EMB portal. Satellite reanalysis (ERA5).
scored.rough_step_up: Contract and application costs total about $10-30k. A proven 50-100 MW wind contract trades at roughly $30-80k/MW, about $2-6M. That is about 100-300x on the right, or ~10x on all-in cost. The ladder runs on to permitting, then financial close, then owner-operator IPP.
scored.frame: The rung is pre-development wind or solar, ending in a bankable RESC: a P50/P90 yield, a grid study and an ECC screen. Finding the wind resource is maybe 30-40% of the work at most. The rest is physical and permitting work that is neither trivial nor abstracted: siting and running a met mast or LiDAR for 12+ months, landowner consents, NCIP FPIC (Indigenous consent) in many upland sites, LGU endorsements, and NGCP grid capacity, which is often the binding constraint. Capitalised buyers do exist (ACEN, Aboitiz, foreign IPPs bidding into the GEA). But inside this rung the work is mostly permitting, land and grid, not discovery.
scored.step_up: The claim is a right costing $10-30k going to about $2-6M for a proven 50-100 MW contract (assumed $30-80k/MW). That would be about 100-300x on the right but only about 10x on all-in cost ($150-400k proving). I found no disclosed per-MW price for any Philippine development-stage wind deal. The one data point I found cuts the other way: ACEN bought out the remaining 60% of the 500 MW Unicorn wind project in July 2024 at a price below 10% of the company's book value. That suggests early-stage Philippine wind rights trade cheaply, closer to $5-20k/MW. A realistic step-up is about 10-100x on the right and 3-10x on all-in cost, so score 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $150-400k and 1.5 years per site (met mast or LiDAR, yield study, grid study), so it passes the cost test. The base hit rate of 20-30% for land-grab sites and 40-60% for ML-picked sites is the candidate's own estimate, not sourced. The resource itself is already mapped well by mesoscale models and reanalysis (Global Wind Atlas, ERA5, the NREL Philippine atlas), so ML adds little on wind speed. Most failures come from grid capacity, land or FPIC, and community opposition, which ML on scanned atlases barely predicts. Mining terminated-contract filings and NGCP TDP congestion data might give about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven asset, so score 3. DOE has terminated 163 RE contracts (17.9 GW) in 2024-25 for non-performance, which shows failure is mostly about execution, not resource.
scored.data: This is mostly legible. Wind and solar resource is published as clean global rasters (Global Wind Atlas, ERA5, NREL atlas) that every IPP already uses. Some signal does sit in illegible form: scanned DOE work-program reports, terminated-contract filings with partial met data, and ECC filings. But DOE publishes awarded, terminated and certificate-of-commerciality status lists, which put much of the outcome into legible status fields. Incumbents (ACEN, Mainstream and others) run their own GIS screening, so the edge from extraction is small.
scored.right_bought: This fails the rubric. The right is not bought from an owner who cannot read the data. It is a state grant under DC2024-06-0018: the OCSP (competitive selection) for DOE pre-determined areas, or direct application, effectively first-come, at fixed administrative fees with no price on hope value. The DOE then claws back idle value: it terminates non-performing contracts (84 in 2025, 5.3 GW) and rebids them through the OCSP, and it can forfeit performance bonds and blacklist developers. Transfer or assignment needs DOE approval. Secretary Garin has said publicly that DOE does not want applicants who hold service contracts only to flip them at a premium. So the right is cheap, but transferring it is politically contested, it carries use-it-or-lose-it work commitments, and the actual landowners still have to be bought out separately.
scored.buyer: Capitalised Philippine and foreign IPPs that need shovel-ready capacity for GEA rounds: ACEN, Aboitiz, Mainstream, Citicore, and others such as CIP or Copenhagen Energy for larger assets. These buyers are real and liquid, but many prefer to self-develop and buy distressed rights cheaply (for example ACEN on Unicorn).
scored.ladder: The ladder is clear: pre-development RESC, then development and permits, then financial close and EPC (construction), then owner-operator IPP, then a portfolio or utility-scale renewable platform. Offshore wind (57 contracts, about 42 GW) is a bigger rung above that. Score 4.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value-creating step is not discovery. The wind and solar resource is already legibly mapped by public global atlases. What decides success is grid, land and FPIC execution. And the right is a first-come state grant whose regulator explicitly opposes flipping, requires approval for assignment, and terminates and rebids idle contracts, so the uplift cannot be cleanly captured by a lean prover.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little (proving costs $150-400k), but the resource signal is already legible and failures are mostly about execution. The right comes from a regulator that is cracking down on flipping, and the realistic step-up is about 10-100x, not 10^3-10^4.

scored.name: Chilean maritime concessions with approved RCA for desalination and seawater intakes
scored.one_line: Apply to the Subsecretaría para las Fuerzas Armadas for maritime concessions at fixed per-m2 fees on coastal strips that an ML model ranks for bathymetry, outfall dispersion, grid and pipeline access to Atacama mining demand. Win environmental approval (an RCA), then sell the permitted intake/outfall site to miners or desalination developers.
scored.unproven_right: A Chilean concesión marítima (beach, seabed and water column) for an intake/outfall. It is granted on application at a regulated annual fee based on the fiscal valuation, and is transferable with authorisation.
scored.proving_step: Oceanographic and marine-biology baselines, outfall plume modelling, and an EIA/DIA through the SEA ending in a favourable RCA. Roughly $0.5-2M and 2-3 years. Perhaps 40-60% approval for well-chosen sites. Many sites fail on benthic or indigenous (ECMPO) conflicts, which ML can screen for.
scored.proven_buyer: Copper and lithium-hydroxide producers (Codelco, BHP, Antofagasta, AMSA), water utilities and desalination developers (Acciona, IDE). Permitting is their binding constraint for mandatory seawater use.
scored.public_data: SEA e-SEIA archive: thousands of scanned EIA/DIA files and adenda with baselines and rejection reasons. SHOA bathymetry charts. ECMPO indigenous-claim maps. DIRECTEMAR concession registry. Mining water-demand filings in Cochilco reports.
scored.rough_step_up: The concession plus application costs about $20-100k. An RCA-approved intake/outfall site for a 1 m3/s plant is plausibly worth $10-40M to a miner facing a 5+ year permitting delay. That is ~100-1000x on the right and ~10x on all-in. The ladder runs on to building, owning and operating the desal plant and the water-sale pipeline.
scored.frame: The rung is "a desal intake/outfall site that holds both a maritime concession and an RCA". It is sellable in principle: developer-stage desal projects do change hands, e.g. Patria sold Aguas Pacífico in Feb 2025 at an undisclosed price. But discovery (choosing the site) is maybe 15-25% of the work. Most of it is the bureaucratic and social path: a maritime concession that averages 52 months (CNEP 2023-24), indigenous Lafkenche/ECMPO claims that can be filed at any time before grant, marine baselines, the EIA, and court challenges after approval. Collahuasi C20+ lost its RCA in court even with the plant nearly built. The proving step is permitting, not a cheap drill, so the frame is not one where discovery is 80%+.
scored.step_up: Unproven: concession fees plus application costs of about $20-100k. Proven: a claimed $10-40M to a miner, but I found no disclosed sale price for any RCA-approved Chilean desal site (the Aguas Pacífico price is confidential). Against the $0.5-2M all-in cost that is ~10-30x, and the value depends on one nearby buyer and a pipeline route. Score 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: $0.5-2M and 2-3 years for the EIA, on top of ~4.3 years for the concession (CNEP average 52 months). The candidate's own estimate puts the base approval rate at 40-60%. ML screening of benthic and ECMPO conflicts, and of plume dispersion, could plausibly lift approval about 1.2-1.5x. Much of the failure risk is political or judicial, though: Lafkenche claims, a Committee of Ministers appeal, Environmental Tribunal annulments. ML cannot model that well. Score 3 under the relaxed C3.
scored.data: Public: the SEA e-SEIA archive (large, partly scanned EIA/DIA files and adenda), SHOA charts, ECMPO maps, the DIRECTEMAR registry. It is only partly illegible. Rejection reasons and conditions sit in RCA resolutions and ICSARA reports. ECMPO claims and existing concessions are mapped. The miners and desal developers who would buy the site (BHP, Codelco, Antofagasta, Acciona, IDE) file these very documents and have specialist consultancies reading them. Nobody is blind to the signal.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a discretionary state grant by supreme decree (Ministry of Defence). Under the new Law 21.813 (published 12 May 2026, in force 13 Nov 2027), a dedicated 'concesión de desalinización' needs a favourable prior report from the DGA. It runs at most 30 years. It lapses if works do not start within 2 years of handover (suspendable to a maximum of 4 while permits are processed). That is an explicit anti-speculation clawback. The law also sets priority for human consumption and sanitation. The fee is fixed and regulated, not auctioned, but the hope value is policed through discretion, a project-specific application, and use-it-or-lose-it caducity. Transfer requires authorisation, and I could not confirm the new law's transfer rule. Score 1.
scored.buyer: Real and capitalised. Copper and lithium producers need seawater (Codelco, BHP, Antofagasta Minerals/AMSA, Collahuasi), and desal developers and infrastructure funds (Acciona, IDE, Patria, Lumina) buy developer-stage projects. But the big miners usually permit their own intakes, as BHP did at Escondida and Codelco did with its own desal approval.
scored.ladder: Strong: permitted site, then build/own/operate the desal plant, then the water pipeline to altitude, then a regional water utility selling to several mines under take-or-pay. ENAPAC was an approved ~$500M independent water project, and Aguas Marítimas a ~$5B one. Each rung up is heavily capital- and construction-intensive, but it is a real path to a large infrastructure company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'cheap unproven right' does not exist in an exploitable form. The maritime concession is a discretionary, project-specific state grant that takes ~4+ years. Under Law 21.813 it now carries a requirement to start works within 2-4 years or lose the concession, so it cannot be cheaply banked for its hope value. The proving step is multi-year permitting and social-licence work, not discovery. Discovery is a minor share of the rung, and the well-funded buyers read the same e-SEIA data and permit for themselves.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer and the ladder are real, but the rung is dominated by permitting rather than discovery. The right is a discretionary grant with anti-speculation caducity, not something bought cheaply from owners blind to its value. The step-up on all-in cost is ~10-30x and has no disclosed comps.

scored.name: Build-ready cell tower entitlements (zoning permit at fixed fee on optioned land)
scored.one_line: Use ML to find coverage-gap parcels where towns approve towers and landowners will sign cheap ground-lease options. Buy the option, then win the conditional-use or zoning permit (a public body charges a fixed application fee) plus FAA and NEPA clearances, and sell the shovel-ready site to a tower REIT or carrier at a large markup. Honest view: C1 4, C2 4, C3 5, C4 4, C5 3. This industry already exists as build-to-suit developers; the ML edge is picking which towns will approve.
scored.unproven_right: A ground-lease option on a private parcel (typically $1-3k), plus a municipal or county zoning application at a fixed fee schedule
scored.proving_step: Zoning or conditional-use approval (hearings, balloon test, RF justification), FAA Determination of No Hazard, NEPA/SHPO/Tribal review and FCC ASR. Cost is about $50-150k and 9-24 months, with approval odds of roughly 40-60%. ML over hearing minutes can plausibly lift approval odds 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Tower REITs (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge) and carriers (Verizon, T-Mobile, AT&T, DISH/EchoStar)
scored.public_data: Municipal planning and zoning meeting minutes and denial records (scattered PDFs and video across about 19,000 jurisdictions), FAA OE/AAA filings, FCC ASR and ULS, TCNS/E-106 Section 106 notices, carrier coverage maps and the FCC Broadband Data Collection, and county parcel records
scored.rough_step_up: A ~$2k option plus about $100k of entitlement work becomes a site worth $300k-1M+ to a REIT: ~150-500x on the option, ~3-10x on total capital
scored.frame: The rung is an entitled tower site: an optioned ground lease plus zoning, FAA, NEPA/Section 106 and ASR clearances, sold to a tower REIT or carrier. Discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work inside this rung. Most of the effort is procedural and legal: RF justification, hearings, balloon tests, SHPO and tribal consultation, and litigation under the Telecom Act. The deciding input is also not discoverable from public data. A carrier issues a search ring based on its own RF and traffic data, and the developer competes to fill it. If the site has no carrier demand, nobody buys it. The physical tower (about $150-300k) is cheap compared with the leases on it, but it still has to be built, usually by the buyer.
scored.step_up: An unproven option costs about $1-3k. A tower's resale value of about $300-500k per site is real: SBA paid TeleCorp $327,500 per tower, SBA's average purchase price was about $309k per tower, and SBA's Mobilitie deal implied about $500k. That value comes from the carrier leases on a built tower, though, not from the permit. An entitled but unbuilt site in a carrier search ring typically sells to a build-to-suit buyer for a development fee of tens of thousands of dollars (my industry estimate; I found no published figure). Outside a ring it sells for close to nothing. Against the total capital of $50-150k, the realistic step-up is about 1-3x, or about 3-10x if a tenant is already lined up. The 150-500x figure on the option alone is misleading, because the option is not the gating cost.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $50-150k and takes 9-24 months (the candidate's figures, consistent with what the industry reports). I found no published national denial rate for tower zoning. Denials are common enough to produce steady Telecom Act litigation, such as Verizon v. Clifton Park and T-Mobile v. Roswell. Inside a carrier search ring, approval odds are probably already 60-80%, because experienced site acquisition firms pick their jurisdictions with care. ML over hearing minutes might plausibly improve cost per approved site by 1.2-1.5x, but the bigger uncertainty is carrier demand, which ML over public data cannot see. Under the relaxed C3 that gives a 3, not a 5.
scored.data: Planning and zoning minutes, video and denial records across about 19,000 jurisdictions really are illegible and scattered, and nobody extracts them systematically, so the ML read on approvability is real. FAA OE/AAA, FCC ASR/ULS and TCNS records are legible and already used by incumbents. FCC Broadband Data Collection coverage maps are legible and are carrier-reported. The demand signal that matters, carrier search rings and capacity plans, is private, so the outcome is held by the buyer rather than hidden in public data.
scored.right_bought: A ground-lease option on private land is bought, transferable and cheap, so it is not free first-come. The zoning application is a fixed fee with no auction and no clawback, and the conditional-use permit usually runs with the land. Landowners are not naive, though. Tower lease rates are widely known, lease-buyout firms (Landmark, Unison, TowerPoint) work the market, and the price gets negotiated once a carrier shows interest. The cheap option is real but not deeply discounted.
scored.buyer: Tower REITs (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge) and carriers are well capitalised. They buy entitled sites only where a carrier has committed as anchor tenant. New macro tower builds in the US are a few thousand per year, and carrier capex has been falling.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: build the tower and hold the leases (the developer becomes a TowerCo), then aggregate a portfolio and sell it to a REIT at 20-30x tower cash flow. Further rungs are small cells, fiber and edge sites. This path is proven: SBA, Vertical Bridge and TowerCo all started as build-to-suit developers. The end state is a mature oligopoly worth about $100B+, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value of a tower site comes from the carrier's anchor lease, not from the permit. The carrier decides where demand is, using private RF and traffic data, and buyers pay a modest development fee for entitled sites inside a search ring and almost nothing outside one. ML over public zoning minutes lowers entitlement risk, which is not the main risk, and the step-up on total capital is about 1-3x instead of 10^3-10^4x.
scored.one_line_reason: The tower-site build-to-suit business already exists. Value comes from carrier demand the developer cannot see, and the 1-3x step-up on capital comes from leases, not entitlement. Approval prediction lifts results only about 1.2-1.5x on a risk that is not the binding one.

scored.name: Chesapeake/Gulf oyster-ground leases picked by ML and proven by grow-out trials (VA VMRC, MD DNR, LA LDWF)
scored.one_line: Lease public oyster bottom at the fixed statutory rent (VA VMRC about $1.50/acre/yr, MD about $3.50/acre/yr, LA a few $/acre/yr), or buy idle leases from heirs, using ML over scanned Baylor/Yates surveys, sanitary surveys, closure histories and water-quality data to pick productive, open-to-harvest ground. Prove it with 1-2 seasons of cage and spat-on-shell grow-out plus sanitary sampling, then assign the proven lease (transferable with state approval) to a capitalised grower or seafood company. The company keeps the full sale price. The catch is that productive ground already trades, so the step-up is real but the buyer pool is small and only modestly capitalised.
scored.unproven_right: New, lapsed or idle state oyster-ground lease at a fixed administrative per-acre rent plus survey and application fees of a few thousand dollars, set by statute rather than auction, with a 10-year renewable term and assignability. Over 100k acres in Virginia are leased but idle, many held by watermen or estates that cannot assess productivity.
scored.proving_step: 1-2 seasons of triploid cage and bottom-culture trials, water-quality logging, MSX/Dermo disease monitoring, a bottom-hardness/substrate survey and a sanitary-classification check. Costs about $50-150k per lease block. Base success roughly 30-60%; ML plausibly gives about 2x on cost per proven acre by screening out siltation, low-salinity, closure and predation zones.
scored.proven_buyer: Established Chesapeake and Gulf growers and seafood processors expanding acreage, PE-backed aquaculture roll-ups, and restoration and nutrient-credit programs. Assignment needs state transfer approval (VMRC fee $300-1,000).
scored.public_data: VMRC scanned historical lease plats and Baylor public-ground charts (1892-94); Maryland Yates Survey (1906-12); LDWF lease GIS and historic oyster-ground maps; VIMS annual spatfall, disease and oyster stock assessment PDFs; Chesapeake Bay Program monitoring; NOAA/CBIBS and USGS salinity and DO series; VDH/LDH shellfish sanitary survey reports and condemnation shapefiles (legible, so a weak spot); NOAA bathymetry and sidescan.
scored.rough_step_up: Right cost of about $3-5k (fees plus rent), or $50-300/acre bought from heirs, becomes proven productive ground at about $2-10k/acre: 10^2-10^3x on the right, but only about 2-4x all-in including trials. Small TAM. Ladder: hatchery, farming, processing and branded distribution, possibly coast-wide via other fixed-fee shellfish lease states (WA, ME, NC, LA).
scored.frame: The rung is a proven, sanitarily open, productive oyster lease. Discovery (choosing ground) is maybe 40-50% of the work inside that rung. The proving step is 1-2 seasons of cage and bottom grow-out, which is really just farming. It is labour- and season-heavy, so it is neither trivial nor abstracted. Buyers are small growers and processors. Maryland's whole aquaculture dockside value was about $5.9M in 2024, so the buyer pool is thin and only modestly capitalised.
scored.step_up: Unproven: Virginia rent is $1.50/acre/yr (2025 VMRC application), riparian leases are free, and Maryland is about $3.50/acre/yr for bottom (2012 fiscal note), plus application and survey fees. Proven: no public sale-price data exists. VMRC posts a leases-for-sale list but stays out of pricing. The candidate's own estimate of $2-10k/acre is unverified and probably high. On the bare right that is roughly 10^2-10^3x, but new ground costs anyone almost nothing, so arbitrage caps the premium. All-in after the $50-150k trials it is about 2-4x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $50-150k per lease block and takes 1-2 seasons (candidate estimate; plausible given gear, seed and labour). That clears the relaxed bar of at least $50k or years per attempt. Base success is roughly 30-60%. ML could plausibly give about 1.5-2x by screening out low-salinity, siltation and predation ground. But much of the signal is already legible: VDH/LDH condemnation shapefiles, the VIMS spatfall and disease series, and CBP salinity data. Local watermen also hold the tacit knowledge. Realistic lift is about 1.3-1.6x, so the score is 3.
scored.data: Partly illegible: scanned Baylor (1892-94) and Yates (1906-12) surveys, old lease plats, and VIMS assessment PDFs. Much is legible: shellfish closure and condemnation shapefiles, LDWF lease GIS, and CBP and NOAA salinity and DO series. The outcome (open versus condemned) sits in a legible status field, which weakens the edge. Productivity is also driven heavily by the grower's own husbandry, not only by the ground.
scored.right_bought: Virginia sets the rent by statute at $1.50/acre/yr. It is not an auction and there is no clawback of the uplift. Leasing is first-come by application, limited to Virginia residents or companies that are 60% Virginia-owned, with a 250-acre cap per application. About 30% of over 400 new applications faced protests, often from riparian owners. Leases are transferable, but only with VMRC approval and a Commissioner's public-interest determination. The transfer fee is $300, $500 or $1,000 depending on acreage, and current rent must be paid. 2021 renewal guidelines push use-it-or-lose-it on idle ground. Fixed price and transferability are good. The weak point is that unproven ground is so cheap that anyone can lease next door, so the market pays little premium for 'proven' status.
scored.buyer: Established Chesapeake and Gulf oyster growers, a few seafood processors, and occasional PE-backed aquaculture roll-ups. These are small, thinly capitalised operators. Restoration and nutrient-credit programs mostly use public ground or pay for services, not lease purchases.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs hatchery and seed, then grow-out, processing, and branded distribution. It could extend to other shellfish-lease states (WA, ME, NC, LA). It is real but small: Virginia plus Maryland farmed oysters are tens of millions of dollars of dockside value a year. There is no trillion-dollar path, and seafood consumption caps the ceiling.
scored.fatal_flaw: Ground is not the scarce input here. New leases cost $1.50/acre/yr to anyone who applies, and an oyster lease's value is mostly the farming business run on it. A 'proven' lease therefore commands only a small premium (about 2-4x all-in after the trials), and the buyers who would pay it are small and lightly capitalised.
scored.one_line_reason: The right is cheap, fixed-price and transferable, and grow-out proving does clear the relaxed C3 cost bar. But the proving step is just farming, much of the signal is already in legible closure and salinity layers, and nearby ground is nearly free. That leaves only a 2-4x all-in step-up into a small, thinly capitalised market.

scored.name: State DOT outdoor-advertising permit to permitted billboard location
scored.one_line: Use ML over zoning code text, DOT spacing rules and scanned permit inventories to find the rare highway frontage that is legally conforming for a new or digital sign. Option the ground cheaply, win the state permit (fixed fee) and the local sign permit, then sell the permitted location to Lamar or Outfront. The right is administrative, but the land option comes from a private owner. That leg partly breaks the fixed-price thesis, and it sits outside the trust-land lens.
scored.unproven_right: An option on a ground lease for a frontage strip from a landowner who does not know it is permit-eligible (a few thousand dollars), plus a state DOT outdoor-advertising permit issued at a fixed schedule fee to whoever qualifies first.
scored.proving_step: Spacing and zoning legal analysis, survey, state permit and local sign or variance hearings. Costs about $20-60k and takes 6-18 months. Success is about 30-60%, and ML lifts conforming-site precision more than 1.5x.
scored.proven_buyer: Lamar, Outfront and Clear Channel Outdoor, plus regional operators. They buy permitted sites and structures at multiples of expected rent, often $200k-$1M+ where digital is allowed.
scored.public_data: State DOT outdoor-advertising permit inventories (many scanned). Federal Highway Beautification Act spacing tables per state. Municode zoning text. Local sign-variance minutes. State AADT traffic counts. Nonconforming-sign removal records.
scored.rough_step_up: A $5-10k option plus $30-60k of proving becomes a permitted site worth $200k-$1M. That is about 5-20x all-in and about 50x on the right. C2 is about 3, C1 about 3. Sign companies already canvass landowners, which caps the cheap option.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted, unbuilt billboard location: a land option plus state and local permits, sold to a sign operator. Finding legally conforming frontage is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is entitlement: local sign permits, variances and council or planning hearings that are political and contested, plus survey and legal work. The physical step (the structure) is left to the buyer, which is good. But the proving step is mostly a lawyering and lobbying fight, not reading data, so discovery is well under 80% of the work.
scored.step_up: The candidate's own figures: a $5-10k option plus $20-60k of proving becomes a permitted site worth $200k-$1M. That is about 20-100x on the right and about 5-20x all-in. One market reference: Lamar offered $75k/yr for 20 years for two digital faces in Lombard, IL, which supports $0.5-1M+ value for a digital site. I found no public prices for selling a bare permitted site. Static sites are worth far less, maybe $50-200k. So this is mid-range, about 10-100x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are the candidate's own figures; I found no external hit-rate data. Proving costs about $20-60k and 6-18 months per attempt, which only just meets the roughly $50k bar. The base hit rate is 30-60%. ML can screen out spacing and zoning non-conformers before options are signed (perhaps 1.5x precision). But the binding uncertainty is local discretion: variances, council politics and cap-and-replace credit availability. Data does not predict that well, so the realistic cost per proven site improves about 1.2-1.5x.
scored.data: Data is partly illegible. Some state DOT permit inventories are scanned, but many are already GIS or online registries. Municode zoning text and FHWA/state spacing rules (e.g. 500 ft in MA; 1,400 ft on MO primaries since 2001) are legible text the sign companies' own real-estate staff already parse. AADT counts are clean public data. No status field writes the answer, which is a plus, but the screen is a fairly simple rules engine (spacing buffers, zoning lookup), so ML has a thin edge over a GIS analyst.
scored.right_bought: The right is mixed and mostly fails the thesis. The land option is privately negotiated, and sign companies routinely canvass highway landowners, so landowners near viable sites know the hope value. Asking prices rise and option exclusivity is weak. The state DOT permit has a fixed schedule fee, goes first-come to whoever qualifies and generally transfers with the sign or site. But the local layer is the binding constraint. Over 3,000 US jurisdictions ban new billboards (2008 Georgia Planning newsletter), and 'most cities' use cap-and-replace (a Fort Smith official's claim, not a survey), where a new sign needs a removal credit banked by an incumbent operator. In effect the local body reserves the uplift for incumbents rather than selling at a fixed price.
scored.buyer: Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel Outdoor, Link and regional operators are capitalised buyers. Lamar guided $200-300M of acquisitions for 2026 and owns only about 11.2k of about 82.7k sites outright, so it does buy easements and sites. But these buyers are also the main competitors for the same sites, and in cap-and-replace markets they hold the credits a newcomer needs.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: build and own structures, operate an ad sales network, and roll up regional operators. That path ends at an outdoor-advertising company: Lamar is worth roughly $12-13B and US out-of-home is roughly a $9B market. That is a large company but nothing like a trillion-dollar chain, and the market is regulatorily capped, with no further rungs above operating signs.
scored.fatal_flaw: Scarcity here comes from regulation, not from hidden information. Most local codes ban new billboards or require cap-and-replace removal credits banked by incumbent operators. So the few conforming sites are decided by local discretion and incumbent-held credits, not by discovering what illegible data says. And sign companies already canvass the landowners, so the cheap option on mispriced land mostly does not exist.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but small arbitrage: about 10-100x on the right, $20-60k to prove each site, and outcomes set by local politics and incumbents' banked removal credits rather than by data. The relaxed C3 lifts it only to about 3, and C1/C4 stay weak.

scored.name: BC run-of-river power water licence + gauged hydrology
scored.one_line: File BC Water Sustainability Act power-purpose water licence applications (fixed schedule fee: $1/kW for the first MW plus $250 per additional MW) and Land Act investigative tenure on creeks that ML ranks highly, trained on scanned historic water-licence files, abandoned 2000s Clean Power Call applications and regionalised WSC gauge records. Pay for 1-2+ years of stream gauging, fish/environmental baseline and a feasibility study, then sell the priority-dated licence application plus hydrology to IPPs bidding BC Hydro's 2024-26 Calls for Power. The water priority date is the scarce part, and the company keeps the uplift. Surface water only, not groundwater.
scored.unproven_right: Water Sustainability Act power-purpose water licence application (priority date) plus Land Act investigative licence for the intake, penstock and powerhouse footprint; fixed administrative application and rental fees (low thousands of dollars), not auctioned, transferable with the site
scored.proving_step: 12-24+ months of continuous hydrometric gauging, fish/environmental baseline, head and energy feasibility, interconnection screen; ~$100-700k and 1-3 years; ~30-60% reach a financeable feasibility showing bankable firm energy with workable head, intake and road
scored.proven_buyer: Run-of-river IPPs and infrastructure funds (Innergex, Kruger, Sigma, Capital Power, First Nations-owned developers) bidding BC Hydro Electricity Purchase Agreements, who pay to skip 2+ years of their own measurement
scored.public_data: BC Water Licence and Point of Diversion records and scanned historic licence files incl. cancelled 2000s IPP applications and their engineering reports; Water Survey of Canada HYDAT plus discontinued gauges (sparse, so ML regionalises flow to ungauged basins); BC Hydro 2002-2010 call bid documentation; TRIM/LiDAR DEMs; fish habitat/barrier inventories; BC Hydro transmission maps; old FrontCounter BC tenure files
scored.rough_step_up: Fees ~$5-20k; a gauged, licensed 10-25 MW site sells ~$100-300k/MW = $1-7M (~10^2-10^3x on the right, ~3-10x on total spend). ML can lift the gauging hit rate 1.5-2x. Caveats: First Nations consultation is a real gate and BC Hydro call timing sets demand.
scored.frame: The rung is a gauged, licensed, early-stage run-of-river site. Inside it, hydrology and site selection are maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is First Nations consultation and equity negotiation, environmental flow and fish permitting under mandatory Water Sustainability Act factors, Land Act tenure, and interconnection screening. None of that is trivial or abstracted. The physical step (gauging) is cheap, but proving also takes permitting and partnership work that ML cannot shorten. A capitalised buyer exists in principle (Innergex and similar), but BC Hydro is effectively the only offtaker and it gates that buyer's demand.
scored.step_up: Application fees run about $5-20k. The candidate assumes a licensed, gauged 10-25 MW site sells for $100-300k/MW, or $1-7M. That is ~10^2-10^3x on the fees but only ~3-10x on total spend once $100-700k of gauging and feasibility is counted. The only real comp found is Innergex in 2008: C$8M for two-thirds of a joint venture holding 18 licensed BC run-of-river projects totalling more than 200 MW. My own arithmetic puts that at roughly C$60k/MW, below the candidate's assumption (the deal also included warrants). That gives about 30-100x on the right and about 2-5x on total spend.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $100-700k and takes 1-3 years per site (candidate estimate). That is expensive, so it passes the C3 cost bar. The base hit rate to a financeable feasibility is about 30-60%. ML regionalisation of WSC/HYDAT flows to ungauged basins is already standard practice (BC regional hydrology tools, consultants). Most of the extra lift would come from reading cancelled 2000s IPP engineering reports, so ~1.2-1.5x on cost per proven site is plausible and >=1.5x is not well supported. The bigger failure modes are non-hydrologic: First Nations consent, fish flows, road access and interconnection.
scored.data: Mixed. Water Licence and Point of Diversion records are a legible, mapped database, so incumbents already see which creeks are licensed, pending or cancelled. The scanned historic licence files and old Clean Power Call engineering reports are illegible and an under-used signal. The outcome (was the site viable?) is partly legible already, because cancelled or abandoned applications and awarded EPAs are public. HYDAT is clean data. Hydrology on the best Lower Mainland and coastal creeks was heavily mined during the 2000s IPP boom, so much of the edge has already been picked over.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a first-in-time application to the Crown with fixed administrative fees: not auctioned, no hope-value pricing, and no direct clawback found. That is cheap and fixed-price, which is good. But it is the 'free first-come' type the rubric discounts. The licence is appurtenant to the land/works and can be transferred with the project; developer portfolio sales such as Plutonic to AltaGas included water-use applications. Constraints: the decision maker must weigh environmental flow needs, and objections can kill a licence. A ministry official said there is normally no deadline to complete a project unless someone else applies, so dormant old applications can block creeks. Post-2010 investigative-licence rules add requirements. UBCM has passed resolutions calling for moratoria on run-of-river licences.
scored.buyer: Run-of-river IPPs and funds (Innergex, Kruger, Capital Power, First Nations-owned developers). Their demand comes almost entirely from BC Hydro Calls for Power. The 2025 Call set a 40 MW minimum capacity and a 25% minimum First Nations equity requirement, scored up to 51% (all four first-round awardees had 51%). Proposals ran 63-496 MW and were overwhelmingly wind. No Standing Offer replacement exists for smaller projects; Clean Energy BC is asking for one. So the candidate's 10-25 MW sites have no current offtake route and no capitalised buyer today.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are permit, then build (owning a $3-6M/MW construction business), then own and operate as an IPP. Real, but capped: BC Hydro is the single monopsony buyer, total run-of-river demand is a few TWh per call, and wind is outcompeting it. The 25-51% First Nations equity requirement caps the ownership share on every rung. This is a mid-size IPP path, not a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: No buyer for the rung. BC Hydro's 2025 Call for Power requires at least 40 MW and 25% minimum First Nations equity, and small hydro has no standing offer, so a gauged 10-25 MW creek licence has no capitalised buyer. Even when it does, only about half the proving work is hydrologic discovery: First Nations consent and fish-flow permitting are the real gate, and ML does not help there.
scored.one_line_reason: The right is cheap, fixed-fee and transferable, and proving is expensive, so the relaxed C3 helps somewhat. But the target 10-25 MW sites are ineligible for BC Hydro's only offtake (40 MW minimum, First Nations equity required), the step-up on total spend is only about 2-10x, and consultation and permitting rather than discovery dominate the rung.

scored.name: Federal mountaintop communications-site leases (USFS/BLM fixed population-strata rent) sold as tower assets
scored.one_line: Use ML over FCC ULS/ASR, terrain viewsheds and coverage-gap data to find Forest Service and BLM ridgetops where a new site would anchor several carrier, FirstNet and BEAD tenants. Obtain a communications-use lease or new site designation, where rent comes from a CPI-indexed schedule set by use type and population served rather than site value. Prove the site with RF propagation against carrier coverage holes, NEPA/SHPO and FAA clearance plus anchor-tenant LOIs, then assign the entitled site to a tower REIT. Build (~$300k) can be left to the buyer. Main risks are agency discretion and NEPA timelines.
scored.unproven_right: USFS special-use or BLM ROW communications-use lease or authorization at a designated or newly proposed site, at the published population-tiered rent schedule (typically a few thousand dollars a year). Assignable with agency consent.
scored.proving_step: About $75-250k and 1-3 years: RF propagation study, NEPA categorical exclusion or EA with SHPO review, FAA no-hazard determination, FCC clearance and an anchor-tenant LOI. Perhaps 40-60% reach an authorized, buildable site with a tenant.
scored.proven_buyer: Tower REITs and private tower funds (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge), carriers, FirstNet/AT&T, utilities and broadcasters who need high sites
scored.public_data: USFS and BLM communications site management plans (scanned PDFs, one per forest), BLM MLRS/LR2000 ROW case files, the BLM/USFS rental fee schedule and population strata lists, FCC ULS and ASR, the FCC National Broadband Map (BEAD coverage gaps) and carrier coverage maps, USGS 3DEP terrain, NEPA decision memos on Forest Service SOPA lists
scored.rough_step_up: About $2-10k a year in schedule rent becomes $0.5-3M for an entitled, anchored site, roughly 100-1000x on the annual right cost. Physical build and tenant sales are not trivial, so C1 is roughly 3-4. Ladder: own towers, then a regional tower platform.
scored.frame: The rung would be selling an entitled but unbuilt federal ridgetop communications site to a tower company. Discovery (picking the ridge and modelling RF) is about 30-40% of the work. The rest is not trivial: NEPA designation, which on undesignated land often needs a forest-plan amendment or an EA; SHPO, FAA and FCC clearance; and winning an anchor carrier. Carriers set demand through their own "search rings", so which ridge to pick is often decided by the buyer, not found by the seller. Tower buyers pay mainly for built towers with leases in place. An unbuilt entitlement is worth far less, and the $300k build plus tenant leasing is where most of the value is created. A capitalised buyer exists (AMT, CCI, SBA, Vertical Bridge, carriers), but under build-to-suit contracts the tower company or carrier usually controls site acquisition.
scored.step_up: The "100-1000x" figure is the right's annual schedule rent ($2-10k/yr) compared with a built, anchored tower ($0.5-3M). That is the wrong comparison. The cash actually spent to prove a site is $75-250k, and an entitled unbuilt site with an LOI plausibly sells for low hundreds of thousands. That is roughly 1-3x on cash in, perhaps 3-10x on a portfolio basis. Reaching $0.5-3M requires the $300k build and signed leases. I found no published price for entitled unbuilt sites (search came up empty), so these figures are my estimate.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs $75-250k and takes 1-3 years (candidate's estimate). It is longer when the forest plan must be amended to designate a new site, as in the Toiyabe/Humboldt-Toiyabe and Triangle Mountain EA examples. Simple co-located or designated sites clear in months via categorical exclusion (Mines Peak: scoping Aug 2020, decision Sept 2020). The base rate of 40-60% reaching an authorized, tenanted site is a guess. Under the relaxed C3 an expensive proving step qualifies. However, demand is set by carriers' known coverage holes and the FCC broadband map, so ML ranking of ridges plausibly gives about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven site, not more.
scored.data: The signal is mostly legible. FCC ULS/ASR is structured, the National Broadband Map is public and machine-readable, USGS 3DEP is clean, and carriers already know their own coverage gaps. Only the per-forest communications site plans and the SOPA/decision memos are scanned or scattered. No regulator status field gives the outcome directly, but the main input (carrier demand) is held privately by the buyer, not hidden in public files.
scored.right_bought: This is not a cheap purchase from owners who cannot read the data. The authorization is issued by the agency on application after initial and second-level screening, at its discretion. Rent does come from a fixed schedule by use type and population strata (BLM IM-2025-013; FS rent depends on type of use and largest community served), not from site value. There is no auction, but competitors can also apply and the agency favours co-location. It is not a property right and is assignable only with agency consent. Clawback risk: the Forest Service has solicited a Communications Uses Market Rent Study so that rental fees "reflect market economics", which threatens the fixed-price edge. A speculative holder with no intent to build may fail screening for financial and technical capability.
