scored.buyer: Tower REITs and private tower funds (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge), and carriers including FirstNet/AT&T. They buy built, leased towers at high cash-flow multiples. For unbuilt sites they mostly prefer their own build-to-suit pipelines driven by carrier search rings, so the market for entitled-only sites is thin.
scored.ladder: Entitled site, then built tower, then multi-tenant leasing, then a regional rural/federal-land tower platform. A full-chain tower company is large (AMT is about $90B+). The market is mature and crowded, and this ladder ends at tower ownership rather than a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not where the value is. Carriers decide which ridges they need from their own known coverage holes, so there is no hidden asset for ML to find. The value jump comes from the $300k build and signed tenant leases, not from proving the site. The agency issues the right at its discretion and is studying a move toward market rent, so it is not a cheaply bought, mispriced asset.
scored.one_line_reason: Fixed schedule rent and assignability help, but the proving step is entitlement paperwork whose value depends on the build and the tenants. Demand data is legible to the buyers themselves, and the step-up on cash actually spent is only about 1-10x.

scored.name: Wind and solar site control on fixed-rate state trust land leases, proven with measured bankable data
scored.one_line: Lease state school-trust land (WY, MT, NM, SD) at the statutory per-acre or per-AUM schedule rate, or take wind/renewable option leases at fixed per-acre rents, in places where public wind and solar models are known to be biased. Use ML over archived met-tower records, model residuals, transmission maps and scanned land-office records to pick sites, run a 12-month LiDAR/met or solar resource campaign with an independent energy assessment plus a transmission and environmental fatal-flaw desktop, then assign the lease or option with the bankable data package to a utility-scale developer.
scored.unproven_right: An assignable state trust land agricultural lease, wind option or renewable planning lease at a fixed schedule rent (a few $/acre per year). Verify per state: some trusts require a separate competitive renewable lease.
scored.proving_step: A 12-month met tower or LiDAR wind campaign (or solar resource study) with an independent bankable P50, plus a desktop transmission and environmental fatal-flaw analysis. Cost is about $100-400k, over 12-18 months. About 40-60% of sites prove bankable or beat the public model enough to be developable.
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale wind and solar developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, Pattern) who pay for site control backed by bankable data.
scored.public_data: NREL WIND Toolkit and NSRDB, residuals of WIND Toolkit and ERA5 against old tall-tower data, archived met-tower records in scanned state energy office and NREL reports, HIFLD transmission lines and substations, scanned state land office lease files and plats, FAA obstruction filings, USFWS species range maps.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-100x on the lease's value (a $2-20/acre/yr lease becomes a renewable option or development position worth roughly $50-2,000/acre). Risks: the trust may require a competitive renewable lease; developers price site control quickly; wind data is fairly legible and incumbents model it well.
scored.frame: The rung is greenfield site origination: securing wind or solar site control plus a bankable resource assessment, then selling it to a developer. Inside that rung, finding the resource is maybe 30-50% of the work. The rest is what decides whether a site is worth anything: transmission and interconnection headroom, permitting and wildlife, offtake, and assembling contiguous land. The physical step (a met tower or LiDAR, about 12 months) is cheap and routine. The buyers are developers and IPPs, and they are well capitalised. But they value interconnection position and permits far more than a resource campaign, so the frame is not one where discovery is 80% or more.
scored.step_up: The step-up is modest. The candidate quotes $2-20/acre/yr growing to $50-2,000/acre, but the real entry price is not schedule rent. New Mexico auctions wind leases: Pattern bid $9.295M for 147,684 acres, about $63/acre in bonus (my arithmetic). Cedarvale paid a $340k bonus on 10,160 acres (about $33/acre) plus $2/acre/yr rent. Early-stage wind site control with met data typically trades at a few thousand $/MW to about $10-30k/MW before interconnection. At roughly 50-80 acres per MW that is about $100-500/acre, so a hit is worth roughly 3-15x over the auction price, not 10^3. The large value jumps come from an interconnection agreement and permits, not from resource data.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $100-400k plus 12-18 months for a met tower or LiDAR campaign and an independent energy assessment, so it meets the relaxed expense test. The base hit rate is roughly 40-60% (the candidate's estimate; plausible). ML lift is likely only about 1.1-1.3x. NREL WIND Toolkit, ERA5 and NSRDB are already well calibrated and developers run mesoscale and residual modelling in-house, especially for solar, where public irradiance data is close to bankable. Most sites fail on transmission, permitting or wildlife, which a map overlay already screens. Score 3 at best.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. The WIND Toolkit, NSRDB, ERA5, HIFLD transmission, FAA obstruction filings and USFWS ranges are all structured and widely used by incumbents. Only the archived met-tower reports and scanned land-office plats are illegible, and they add little. The outcome is effectively already summarised in public layers: NREL wind-speed rasters plus HIFLD substations give developers the answer.
scored.right_bought: The right cannot be bought cheaply at a fixed rate. Wind and solar rights on state trust land are not part of the grazing or agricultural schedule lease; they are a separate lease. New Mexico competitively auctions renewable leases to the highest bidder (the Pattern deal above, plus bonus payments such as Cedarvale's $340k). In Wyoming, Chapter 6 wind leases must be at fair market value. In 2009 the board rejected an application 29% below nearby leases, and it caps bids at 120% of fair market value, so prices are pegged to comparables. A court vacated the Pronghorn H2 wind lease in Dec 2025 for violating board rules, and rulemaking reopened in Jan 2026. Montana issues these leases by competitive bid or RFP. Assignments need board or director approval, and boards may refuse transfers that diminish the beneficiaries' interest. The trusts have a fiduciary duty to capture hope value, and the sellers can read the same NREL maps.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale wind and solar developers and IPPs such as NextEra, Invenergy and Pattern. They have plenty of capital, but they originate their own sites, bid directly in state auctions, and pay up mainly for interconnection-advanced projects rather than resource-proven greenfield leases.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong. It runs from site origination to development (permits, interconnection, PPA), then to construction and ownership as an IPP, and finally to a transmission-integrated renewable utility. That path does lead to a very large company (NextEra-scale).
scored.fatal_flaw: The state trusts do not sell renewable rights at a fixed schedule price. Wind and solar rights are a separate lease, auctioned or bid at fair market value (New Mexico auctions, with Pattern at about $63/acre in bonus; Wyoming pegs to fair market value against comparables with a 120% cap; Montana uses competitive bid or RFP), and assignments need board approval. So the trust captures the hope value, and the signal sits in legible NREL and HIFLD data that every bidder already uses.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails mainly on C4: renewable rights on trust land are auctioned or priced at fair market value rather than at schedule rent, wind and solar resource data is legible and well modelled by incumbents, the realistic step-up is about 3-15x rather than 10^3, and site value depends mostly on interconnection, not on discovering the resource.

scored.name: Large-load utility service capacity on optioned farmland (data-center power proof)
scored.one_line: Company options rural land near substations with spare capacity identified by ML. It pays the utility's tariff large-load study deposit to get a confirmed MW service commitment, then assigns land plus capacity commitment to hyperscalers and data-center developers at powered-land prices.
scored.unproven_right: Utility tariff large-load or transmission-service study request, at a fixed deposit and study fee set in the tariff, not auctioned. Bundled with an option on farmland at agricultural price. Assignable with the land and customer of record.
scored.proving_step: Utility system-impact and facilities study confirming X MW by a date. Costs about $100k-1M in deposits and studies over 6-18 months, with a roughly 30-60% chance of a usable MW and date. ML over substation loading and planned upgrades plausibly lifts that about 2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers and data-center developers (QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, Stack, CyrusOne) who pay about $0.5-3M/MW-equivalent for powered land.
scored.public_data: FERC Form 715 and 1 filings, utility IRP appendices, scanned state PUC dockets on load forecasts and substation upgrades, ISO transmission-planning study PDFs, and EIA-860/861.
scored.rough_step_up: Land at $5-15k/acre goes to about $300k-1M/acre powered, a 30-100x step-up. Weakness: closely mirrors the killed powered-brownfields idea, landowners increasingly price hope, and utilities are adding commitment-fee tariffs that limit assignment. Ladder: powered shell, data center owner-operator, on-site generation.
scored.frame: The rung is to option farmland, run the utility large-load study, and assign land plus a MW commitment as powered land. Finding the site and capacity is only about 40-50% of the work in that rung. The rest is collateral, a creditworthy customer of record, entitlement and zoning, and dealing with the utility. None of it is trivial or abstracted the way a drill hole is. Data-center developers do buy the output (QTS, Vantage, Stack). But the rung is already crowded with powered-land developers (Tract and others) and the hyperscalers' own site-selection teams.
scored.step_up: The 30-100x claim is overstated. Texas rural land averaged about $5,214/acre in 2025 (Land Report). Reported offers from data-center buyers for farmland run about $12k-35k/acre, roughly 3-10x (Bullvine, Texas A&M). Powered entitled land in Northern Virginia is about $6M/acre versus $4M unpowered, so power alone adds about 1.5x there (Avison Young via Data Center Knowledge). An unverified estimate puts the premium for confirmed capacity at about $150-400k/MW (Acres). For about 100 MW on 100 acres, that is roughly $15-40M of uplift on about $1M of land, so 10-40x at best and only if the commitment is firm and assignable. Realistically the step-up is 10-30x, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive and getting more so. Texas SB6 draft rules set study fees of $100k (75-250 MW) or $300k (over 250 MW), plus a $50k/MW non-refundable interconnection fee and $50k/MW in security before the study starts. That is about $5M non-refundable plus $5M security for 100 MW. Dominion GS-5 requires $1.5M/MW collateral and a 14-year minimum contract. The 30-60% base hit rate is plausible. ML over substation loading could lift it about 1.3-1.6x. But utility hosting-capacity maps and newly required published large-load queues (PA model tariff, April 2026) already narrow the search, so ML is close to a lookup table here, the same failure as the interconnection-queue candidate. I scored C3 at 3, not 5.
scored.data: FERC 715/Form 1, IRP appendices, PUC dockets and ISO planning PDFs are public and partly illegible. But the outcome is increasingly summarised in legible form. Utilities publish hosting-capacity maps, PA now requires each utility to publish its large-load queue, and ISO planning reports list substation upgrades with their dates. The large hyperscalers and brokers already mine these sources, so there is little extraction edge left.
scored.right_bought: The utility does not sell this right at a fixed price regardless of hope value. Tariff reforms are designed to tax speculation and capture the uplift: $50k/MW non-refundable fees, collateral of $50k/MW up to $1.5M/MW, 12-14 year minimum take-or-pay contracts with 60-85% minimum bills, exit fees, and site control lasting 5+ years past the peak-demand date. All of these load the cost onto whoever holds the commitment and push out flippers. I found no tariff that explicitly bans assignment. But the commitment is tied to a creditworthy customer of record, so a land-banker with no balance sheet cannot hold it cheaply and pass it on. Farmland near substations is also no longer cheap to option, because landowners are already pricing hope (offers of $12-35k/acre). Both halves of the bundle fail the buy-cheap test.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers and data-center developers (QTS/Blackstone, Vantage, Stack, CyrusOne) are well capitalised and do pay powered-land premiums. Committed utility load is the strongest predictor of land price (Altus Group, 80 deals).
scored.ladder: There are real rungs above this one: powered shell, data-center developer and owner-operator, and on-site generation. Incumbents occupy each rung and capital is the binding constraint, so winning the land rung gives only a modest edge for climbing.
scored.fatal_flaw: Utilities and regulators now capture or tax the hope value directly. The cost of proving rises with the megawatts requested (SB6 $50k/MW non-refundable plus security, Dominion $1.5M/MW collateral and 14-year take-or-pay), so the gap between unproven and proven value is shrinking. The commitment is tied to a creditworthy customer of record, and published queues and hosting maps make the outcome legible. That leaves no buy-cheap, prove-cheap arbitrage, and this is the same failure as powered brownfields and interconnection queue positions.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the killed powered-brownfields and queue-position idea again. Relaxing C3 helps a little, but tariffs that charge per MW and require collateral push most of the uplift to the utility or the creditworthy customer of record, and the real step-up is about 10-30x, not 10^3-10^4.

scored.name: Sovereign submerged-land marina leases with environmental permit proof (Florida)
scored.one_line: Company acquires or options under-used riparian parcels with existing state sovereign submerged-land leases (rent fixed by the state schedule). It pays for the ERP and USACE permit to expand slips, then sells the permitted marina expansion to a capitalised marina consolidator.
scored.unproven_right: Florida sovereign submerged lands lease, with rent set by an administrative formula (percentage of revenue or per sq ft) and not auctioned, transferable with the riparian upland. Many small holders cannot assess permit feasibility.
scored.proving_step: Environmental Resource Permit plus USACE Section 10/404 permit for slip expansion: seagrass and manatee surveys, hydrographic and flushing studies. Costs about $150-500k over 1-3 years, with roughly 30-50% success. ML over past permit decisions plausibly lifts that about 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Marina roll-ups and REITs (Safe Harbor/Sun Communities, Suntex, Morningstar) paying $50-150k per permitted wet slip.
scored.public_data: Scanned FDEP ERP permit files and denials, Florida DEP lease and BTIIF records, FWC seagrass and manatee data, USACE Jacksonville District public notices, and county property records.
scored.rough_step_up: Permitted slips are worth about $50-150k each versus near-zero unpermitted. On a 100-slip expansion that is about $5-15M against about $0.5M in permit cost plus the upland. The upland is private and partly priced, so the realistic step-up on the right is about 10-30x. Ladder: a marina operating platform and coastal waterfront real estate.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted marina expansion, meaning the riparian upland plus the sovereign lease plus the ERP/USACE approvals, sold to a consolidator. Permitting is real proving work. But most of the capital goes into buying or optioning private waterfront upland, which is the scarce asset, and the buyer still has to build the docks. Discovery and proving is perhaps 40-60% of the rung, not 80% or more. The physical step is abstracted only because it is handed to the buyer, and the land position itself is expensive.
scored.step_up: The headline claim is near-zero to $50-150k per permitted slip. The one comp found is Safe Harbor's $6.9M purchase of One Particular Harbour (55 wet and 128 dry slips), which is roughly $125k per wet slip but overstated because the price includes dry storage. Measured against the actual entry cost (waterfront upland already priced as waterfront, plus a $0.15-0.5M permit), the realistic uplift on the whole position is about 2-5x. On the permit spend alone it is about 10-30x. It is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate estimates the proving step at $150-500k and 1-3 years per attempt, with a base success rate of about 30-50%. That counts as expensive, so it qualifies under the relaxed C3. ML over FDEP/USACE decisions could lift the hit rate, but county Manatee Protection Plans (Lee, Naples, Miami-Dade, Charlotte) already publish boat-facility siting maps. These grade shorelines as preferred, moderate or protected and set slip-per-shoreline-foot density limits, and projects that match them get programmatic USFWS consultation. Much of the outcome is therefore already legible, and the plausible ML gain on cost per proven asset is about 1.2-1.5x, not 2x.
scored.data: Scanned ERP files and USACE Jacksonville public notices are genuinely messy. However, the decisive siting variables (seagrass, manatee risk, water depth, slip density caps) are already mapped in county MPPs and FWC layers, so the regulator has largely written the answer into legible siting categories. That undercuts the illegible-data edge.
scored.right_bought: The sovereign submerged-land lease is not auctioned. Rent is set administratively under Fla. Admin. Code 18-21.011 as the greater of 6% of gross wet-slip income, a base fee or a minimum fee, with an extended-term multiplier, and the lease transfers with the riparian upland. That part fits the rubric. But the state takes an ongoing 6% revenue share, which is a partial clawback, and an expansion needs lease modification and Board of Trustees review. The thing actually being bought is private waterfront upland, which Florida marina brokers and consolidators already price for expansion potential. The cheap-and-illegible-to-owner premise is weak.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist and are active, including Safe Harbor (owned by Sun Communities until its 2025 sale), Suntex (Conch Harbor in Key West in 2025, Two Georges in Shalimar with 134 wet slips) and Morningstar. They do pay per-slip prices for operating and permitted marinas.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs from permitted expansion to marina operator to a coastal waterfront real-estate and hospitality platform. That is a real path to a multi-billion-dollar roll-up, as Safe Harbor shows, but it is a capped and crowded market rather than a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset that is actually scarce and expensive is private waterfront upland, which is already priced competitively for its expansion potential. Meanwhile county Manatee Protection Plan siting maps legibly encode which shorelines can be permitted and at what slip density. There is no 10^3 step-up on a cheaply bought right and little hidden signal for ML to extract.
scored.one_line_reason: Permitting is expensive and buyers are real, but the right that matters (private upland) is market-priced, county manatee siting maps already publish the outcome, and the realistic step-up is 2-5x on the position (10-30x on the permit spend).

scored.name: Peruvian SERFOR conservation and ecotourism concessions proven into REDD+ or ARR carbon projects
scored.one_line: Take SERFOR conservation or ecotourism forest concessions, which carry low fixed per-hectare fees and are granted on application with a management plan. ML picks concessions with high deforestation-threat baselines and clean tenure from scanned SERFOR/OSINFOR files and Landsat history. Pay for Verra/ART validation, then sell the validated project or its forward credits to carbon buyers.
scored.unproven_right: A SERFOR conservation or ecotourism concession: a 40-year renewable forest use right at a fixed administrative fee. It is transferable or cedable with SERFOR approval, and carbon rights are attributable to the holder under Peruvian rules.
scored.proving_step: Carbon baseline and inventory plots, a PDD, and validation by a VVB under VM0048/ART-TREES-compatible methods. Roughly $200-600k and 1.5-3 years. Perhaps 40-60% reach validation; failures come from tenure overlaps and leakage. ML screens overlap and threat to lift the hit rate about 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Carbon project developers and offtakers (South Pole, Mercuria, airlines under CORSIA, corporate buyers) that prepay or buy validated projects.
scored.public_data: SERFOR/GERFOR concession files and management plans (scanned). OSINFOR inspection reports. Global Forest Watch and Hansen loss data. MINAM Geobosques. Indigenous territory overlap maps (SICNA).
scored.rough_step_up: A concession is near-zero, about $10-30k. A validated 50-100k ha REDD+/ARR project with 1-3M issuable credits trades for roughly $3-15M. That is ~100-500x on the right and ~10x on all-in. The ladder runs on to integrity-rated issuance, then forest management, then a regional carbon/timber platform. Carbon-market integrity risk is high.
scored.frame: The rung is a validated REDD+/ARR project on a SERFOR concession. Screening the site is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is not trivial: carbon inventory plots, the PDD, FPIC and community consultation, and 40 years of forest protection (patrols, leakage control, permanence buffer). For ARR it also includes planting. The holder must actually deliver avoided deforestation, so the physical and social step is ongoing and bespoke. That is closer to the geothermal counter-example than to drilling.
scored.step_up: Unproven: concession costs roughly $10-30k, mostly management-plan preparation and admin fees (candidate's estimate; I found no fee schedule). Proven: a validated 50-100k ha REDD+ project with 1-3M issuable credits might trade for $3-15M. That is ~100-500x on the right but only ~10x on all-in cost of $0.3-1M+. Credit prices are currently ~$3-10/t for REDD. A developer claims ~$50/t is possible under Article 6 (Carbon Pulse, June 2025), but that is speculative. These are candidate estimates, not verified transactions.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs ~$200-600k and 1.5-3 years per project (candidate estimate, consistent with industry norms). The candidate assumes ~40-60% reach validation. Under VM0048 the baseline is not chosen by the developer: Verra allocates activity data from jurisdictional deforestation risk maps. Peru's final maps were released 24 Nov 2025, with open-access 100m versions published for due diligence. So the threat-picking part of the ML lever is mostly already done by Verra for free. What is left is screening tenure and indigenous-territory overlaps, which plausibly gives ~1.2-1.5x.
scored.data: Partly illegible: scanned SERFOR/GERFOR files and OSINFOR inspection reports. But the main value driver, deforestation threat, is now a legible public product (Verra's VMD0055 risk maps for Peru, open-access for due diligence), along with Hansen/GFW and MINAM Geobosques. Indigenous overlap maps (SICNA, BDPI) are public GIS layers. Any carbon developer can screen these, so the edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Not bought from uninformed owners. Concessions come from the state (SERFOR or regional forestry authorities) on application with a management plan and public notice. That makes them first-come or contested, not a discounted purchase. Transfer or cession needs SERFOR approval. Conservation concessions are historically meant for non-profit holders. Carbon credits must also be registered in RENAMI, and Peru's Article 6 and corresponding-adjustment framework gives the state room to take or condition part of the uplift (MINAM rules for protected areas, Dec 2025). The fee is fixed and does not price in hope value, but the state can reserve land or reject the application, and indigenous claims compete.
scored.buyer: Carbon developers and offtakers (South Pole, Mercuria, CORSIA airlines, corporates) are capitalised, but demand for REDD is impaired by integrity scandals, and buyers prefer pre-issuance offtakes at a discount over paying 100x for a validated project.
scored.ladder: Ladder: issuance and integrity rating, then forest management or sustainable timber, then a regional carbon and land platform, then Article 6 sovereign deals. It exists but is capped by the size of the carbon market and by policy risk. A trillion-dollar path is not plausible.
scored.fatal_flaw: The ML edge has been taken over by the methodology. Under VM0048 the threat baseline comes from Verra's published jurisdictional risk maps (Peru's are final and open-access), so picking high-threat land is a legible public lookup. Proving also requires decades of real forest protection, not one cheap physical step. The rights are granted by the state on application, not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up on the right is real, but the ML lever is weak: Verra's public risk maps already set the baseline. Tenure is state-granted and contested, not bought from uninformed owners. Carbon delivery is a 40-year operational obligation, so discovery is not 80% of the work.

scored.name: LEO/MEO gateway earth station sites (FCC Part 25 licence at fixed filing fee)
scored.one_line: Option cheap rural land near fiber that ML ranks as RF-quiet and coordinatable. File and win a Part 25 Ka/V/E-band gateway earth station licence (fixed FCC fee) with completed frequency coordination, then sell the licensed, coordinated site to a constellation operator racing to deploy hundreds of gateways. Honest view: C1 4, C2 3, C3 4, C4 3, C5 4.
scored.unproven_right: A land option (~$5-20k) plus an FCC Part 25 earth station application (fixed schedule fee, a few thousand dollars), assignable with FCC consent
scored.proving_step: An RF interference measurement campaign, a frequency coordination report with terrestrial Part 101/UMFUS and federal NTIA users, zoning and FAA review, and FCC grant. Cost is about $75-200k and 6-18 months. Success odds are perhaps 50-70%, and ML can raise them by avoiding coordination conflicts and quiet zones.
scored.proven_buyer: Amazon Kuiper, SpaceX Starlink, Telesat Lightspeed, SES O3b mPOWER, AST SpaceMobile, and ground-station-as-a-service operators (AWS Ground Station, KSAT, Viasat RTE)
scored.public_data: FCC ICFS/IBFS earth station filings and coordination exhibits (unstructured PDFs), ULS Part 101 and UMFUS licences, NTIA federal protection zones, NRAO and radio-quiet zone boundaries, fiber route maps, the USGS 3DEP DEM, and county parcel and zoning records
scored.rough_step_up: A ~$10k option becomes a coordinated, licensed gateway site worth perhaps $0.5-3M: ~50-300x on the option, ~5-15x on total capital
scored.frame: The rung is a licensed, coordinated gateway site: a small leased parcel (about 500 m2 for an Amazon site in New Zealand; an 88x153 ft gravel pad for a Starlink site in Port Matilda, PA) holding a Part 25 grant. Inside that rung, siting, coordination and permits are perhaps 60-75% of the work. Pouring a pad and running fiber are minor. But the licence names specific space stations as its points of communication, so the site has to be filed together with, or for, a particular operator. That breaks the "prove it first, sell it later" pattern. Buyers are well capitalised (SpaceX, Amazon Leo, Telesat, SES). Third-party hosts already serve them: Northwood, PSSI, and United Teleports (which operates an Amazon Leo gateway teleport in Florida). These hosts mostly build to order on a lease; they do not prove sites on speculation and then sell them. So the frame exists, but discovery is not 80%+ of it, and most of what is sold is a service or lease.
scored.step_up: I found no published price for a licensed gateway site. Starlink and Amazon Leo lease small rural pads from landowners like Countryside Estate Properties LLC, and those parcels are worth a few thousand to tens of thousands of dollars. A coordinated, granted site might plausibly be worth $0.2-1M to an operator in a hurry, for the time it saves. That is about 20-100x on a $10k option, but only about 2-5x on the $100-250k of total capital once proving costs are included. The parcel itself gains little, because rural land near fiber is plentiful and interchangeable.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $75-200k and takes 6-18 months, which clears the expense bar. The base success rate is already high. FCC grants for NGSO gateways are routine: SpaceX filed for about 99 US gateway sites by 2022 and Amazon Leo keeps filing 6-antenna sites. Failures come from local zoning opposition (Ketchikan, AK; Selle Valley, ID) more than from RF problems. The interference and coordination analysis is already done deterministically by coordination firms working from structured ULS/UMFUS data and the 47 CFR 25.136 county and population counts. Like the interconnection-queue candidate, a lookup table matches ML here. ML might help predict local opposition. Plausible gain is about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven site.
scored.data: The interference signal is mostly in legible, structured data: ULS Part 101 and UMFUS licence records, IBFS/ICFS earth station records with coordinates, and NTIA and quiet-zone boundaries, which are published maps. Coordination exhibits are PDFs, but the key facts (site, band, how many stations per county) appear as fields or follow from simple counts under 25.136. Incumbents and coordination firms already extract this.
scored.right_bought: The land option is bought cheaply, but landowners sell no hidden hope value: the parcel is interchangeable and its value is just rural rent. The licence is a fixed FCC filing fee, granted largely in filing order. It is not auctioned and the uplift is not clawed back. The one scarce piece is 25.136's cap of three protected earth stations per county in 27.5-28.35 GHz, but that slot comes from the FCC, not from an owner who cannot read the data. The FCC can also deny filings that look speculative or lack a real point of communication. Assignment needs prior FCC consent under 25.119, which is routine; an example is a PSSI-to-Lowery assignment involving a Kuiper site in Voca, TX.
scored.buyer: Starlink, Amazon Leo (Kuiper), Telesat Lightspeed and SES are all capitalised, but they site and file gateways in-house at low marginal cost. Ground-station-as-a-service hosts (Northwood, PSSI, United Teleports, AWS Ground Station, KSAT) are the other route to market, and they mostly lease rather than buy proven sites at a premium.
scored.ladder: Coordinated site, then owned teleport with antennas, then multi-operator ground-station-as-a-service, then a network of fiber-connected points of presence and possibly edge data centres at the gateways. That is a real but crowded ladder (Northwood, KSAT, AWS, Viasat). It leads to a large infrastructure business, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no hope-value asymmetry to capture. The site is interchangeable rural land, the licence costs a fixed fee, is tied to a named operator and is easy for that operator to get directly, and coordination feasibility is already computed deterministically from structured FCC data. So a proven site is worth only a few times what it cost to prove, and buyers can repeat the process themselves.
scored.one_line_reason: Not excluded, but weak (12/25). Proving does cost $75-200k. However, the base success rate is already high, coordination is a lookup over legible ULS data, land is interchangeable, and operators file their own gateways cheaply. The likely result is a 2-5x return on capital, not 10^3x.

scored.name: DOE national-lab patent options at $1k, proven by prototype validation
scored.one_line: Use DOE's fixed-price option programs (e.g. the 'Next Top Energy Innovator' style $1,000 option on up to 3 lab patents) and standard lab option terms. ML over OSTI technical reports, lab notebooks-derived publications and patent claims finds orphaned inventions whose buried performance data suggest commercial viability. Fund an independent prototype/validation test, then exercise and assign or sublicense the proven exclusive license to a strategic, keeping equity and cash.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive option on federally owned lab patents at a fixed nominal fee set by program schedule, not by invention value
scored.proving_step: Bench-to-pilot validation at a third-party lab or user facility, plus a techno-economic analysis (about $100-500k, 6-18 months); perhaps 30-40% hit commercial thresholds
scored.proven_buyer: Strategic corporates in energy, materials and industrial sectors, plus growth-stage VCs funding a NewCo around the license
scored.public_data: OSTI.gov full-text technical reports (huge and unstructured), DOE Lab Partnering Service patent listings, USPTO full text, ARPA-E/EERE project final reports
scored.rough_step_up: $1k option goes to a $1-10M license or assignment value on a validated hit, roughly 10^3x on the right (about 10x on total capital incl. proving)
scored.frame: The rung is: hold an option on a lab patent, validate the invention, then sell or sublicense the exclusive license. Discovery (reading OSTI and patent text to find orphaned inventions that work) is perhaps 40-50% of the work inside this rung, not 80%+. The proving step is real engineering: building a bench or pilot prototype, scaling it up and writing a techno-economic analysis, all different for every technology. It is neither trivial nor abstracted, unlike a standardised exploratory drill hole. There is a buyer (strategic corporates and VCs), but strategics usually want to license directly from the lab, or buy a team and company, not a bare sublicense.
scored.step_up: Nominally the step-up looks like $1k to $1-10M, but that is wrong in two ways. First, the $1,000 fee is only for a 6-month option, extendable once by 6 months (the Brookhaven and 2011 'America's Next Top Energy Innovator' terms). The program ran only from May to 15 December 2011. Second, the commercial license is negotiated after the option, with royalties and equity set case by case under 35 USC 209 / 37 CFR 404. The real unproven right therefore costs close to nothing but also captures little. Typical university and federal license deals are worth well under $1M up front, so a validated lab license selling for $1-10M is optimistic. Realistic gain on all capital including proving: about 3-10x on hits.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $100-500k and takes 6-18 months, so it clears the 'expensive' bar. The candidate puts the base hit rate at 30-40% (an estimate, not sourced). ML over OSTI reports and claims could plausibly lift the share of picks that pass validation 1.5x or more, by screening out inventions whose buried data show poor performance. Under the relaxed C3 this counts as a strong lever. It is scored 4 rather than 5 because 'commercial threshold' is a soft, subjective outcome and has no labels to train on.
scored.data: The data really is public and illegible: OSTI full-text technical reports, ARPA-E and EERE final reports, and USPTO full text. Lab technology transfer offices do not systematically mine performance data from them, and no legible field summarises 'commercially viable'. That part works.
scored.right_bought: This part is weak. The fixed-price $1k option was a time-limited 2011 program. Standard lab options now cost a negotiated fee. More importantly, the hope value is clawed back at exercise. The exclusive license is negotiated later (royalties, equity, diligence milestones, a share of sublicense income), and the lab sees the same validation results. Grants require 15-day public notice in the Federal Register with an objection period. Small businesses with a 'practical application' plan get first preference, which favours an operating company over an IP flipper. Assignment and sublicensing need lab consent. Most DOE lab patents are owned by the contractors that run the labs (e.g. Battelle, UT-Battelle), not the government, and those contractors license on their own negotiated terms. So the right is not bought at a fixed price regardless of hope value, and it is not freely transferable.
scored.buyer: Strategic corporates in energy, materials and industry, and VCs forming NewCos. Both are capitalised, but they are not a dependable bid for a bare sublicense. They can go directly to the lab, and they usually pay for a team and a de-risked company rather than for an option holder's validation report.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Each invention is a different technology and market, so winning one rung does not set up a repeatable chain like explore, develop, mine, refine. The upward path is to become a venture studio or an operating company in each vertical. That is a portfolio, not vertical integration toward one trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The cheap right is an option, not the license. The licensor negotiates the exclusive license terms (royalties, equity, a share of sublicense income, consent to assignment) after validation, with full sight of the results, and public notice is required. So the lab captures the step-up the company paid to create, and no fixed-price, transferable right exists to hold and flip.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is illegible and ML could raise validation hit rates, but the $1k option was a 2011 one-off. The real license is renegotiated after proving, which claws back the uplift. Proving is bespoke engineering, and there is no coherent ladder.

scored.name: USDA GRIN germplasm accession to proprietary trait line
scored.one_line: Order accessions from the USDA National Plant Germplasm System, which ships at a fixed nominal cost of zero under standard terms. ML over decades of scattered evaluation notes, field-day observations, herbarium/passport data and climate-of-origin pick accessions likely to carry heat, drought or disease tolerance. Fund multi-site field trials and marker work, introgress the trait into elite lines under PVP or a utility patent, and sell or license the proven trait line to a major seed company.
scored.unproven_right: Germplasm accession plus the right to develop and protect derived lines, acquired at fixed nominal cost regardless of latent trait value
scored.proving_step: 2-3 seasons of multi-location phenotyping, marker mapping and introgression (about $200k-1M per trait program); 30-50% of ML-prioritised accessions confirm the trait
scored.proven_buyer: Seed majors and regional breeders (Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, KWS, Limagrain)
scored.public_data: GRIN-Global evaluation and observation records (inconsistent, partly digitised), legacy USDA plant introduction inventories (scanned), herbarium specimens, WorldClim/soil data for collection sites, published screening trial PDFs
scored.rough_step_up: Near-$0 accession goes to a $2-20M trait license or line sale on a hit, at least 10^3x on the right (about 10x on proving capital)
scored.frame: The rung would be "exotic accession to a validated trait line licensed to a seed major". It fails the 80%-discovery test. Picking the accession is maybe 10-20% of the work. Most of it is physical and slow: multi-location phenotyping, mapping, backcrossing into elite backgrounds, and breaking linkage drag (wild segments that carry bad genes along with the useful one). Breeders resist exotic germplasm for exactly this reason (Frontiers/Hohenheim pre-breeding reviews). Realistic timelines are 5-10+ years, not 2-3 seasons. This looks like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: making the product is harder than finding the input.
scored.step_up: On the right itself the step-up is effectively infinite, because the accession costs $0. But that is meaningless when the right is non-exclusive. On proving capital it is about $0.2-1M in versus a hoped-for $2-20M license, so 3-20x. I found no published license fees for traits sourced from wild or exotic germplasm, so the $2-20M figure is unverified and probably optimistic for a single native-trait introgression. Seed majors pay big money for transgenic or event-level traits, not for raw introgressions. Score 3, on proving capital rather than on the right.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt is expensive ($200k-1M and several years per trait program), so the relaxed C3 expense bar is met. The candidate's own 30-50% confirmation rate fits the relaxed window. A 1.5x ML lift is plausible but not unique. The Focused Identification of Germplasm Strategy (FIGS), which picks accessions by climate of origin, is already public and used by ICARDA, CGIAR and others. Seed majors also run their own genomic prediction over genebank collections. So the marginal ML edge over existing methods is about 1.2-1.5x. No source gave a hit-rate figure; this is an estimate.
scored.data: GRIN-Global evaluation and observation data is partly structured and searchable. Legacy plant introduction (PI) inventories and screening PDFs are illegible, which is a real but modest edge. Climate-of-origin and passport data are already exploited by FIGS. Trait outcomes are often written into GRIN descriptor fields (e.g., disease ratings), so part of the answer is already in legible fields.
scored.right_bought: No exclusive right is acquired. NPGS ships accessions free to any bona fide research or commercial entity. A 2025 briefing from the Swiss NGO ProSpecieRara says 20% to over 50% of distributions in crops like sorghum and soybean already go to commercial firms; this is advocacy material, not USDA data. Bayer, Corteva and every competitor can order the same accession the day they see your interest or your trial results. The fixed zero price is not a hope-value discount you can capture, because the asset is never locked up. For accessions covered by the standard material transfer agreement (SMTA) of the international seed treaty (ITPGRFA), you cannot claim IP over the material in the form received. Derived lines must pass SMTA terms on, and restricting access triggers benefit-sharing payments. The right is not transferable as an asset. The only things you can own are the derived line (through a PVP certificate or utility patent) and the know-how.
scored.buyer: The buyers are real and well capitalised: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, KWS, Limagrain and regional breeders. But they buy traits already in elite, adapted backgrounds with demonstrated yield neutrality. They largely run this kind of pre-breeding in-house or source it from public programmes at low cost.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: trait lines lead to an own-germplasm seed company, then a branded seed and trait platform. The seed market is about $50-60B. But it is highly consolidated, climbing is slow (decades of breeding pipeline), and distribution moats favour incumbents. The path is plausible but not trillion-dollar.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right is non-exclusive and free to everyone, including the buyers. Nothing is locked up at a hope-value discount, so any discovery signal can be copied instantly by ordering the same accession. Meanwhile the dominant work (multi-year introgression and breaking linkage drag) is physical breeding, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap input but no exclusivity, and breeding, not discovery, dominates the rung. The relaxed C3 helps only modestly because FIGS and in-house genomic selection already cover the ML lever.

scored.name: Wind site-testing ROWs on BLM land with ML-picked met campaigns
scored.one_line: Use ML over scattered old met-tower records, BLM case files and reanalysis data to find BLM parcels where the wind resource is underestimated and conflicts are absent. Take short-term site-testing ROWs at schedule rent (non-competitive outside designated leasing areas). Run a 1-2 year LiDAR/met campaign plus avian and cultural baselines. Sell the bankable-resource site, with its ROW application priority, to a utility-scale wind developer.
scored.unproven_right: BLM wind energy site-testing and monitoring ROW (3-yr term, schedule rent of a few thousand dollars a year), which gives priority for the development ROW application. Assignable with BLM approval.
scored.proving_step: About $150-400k and 12-24 months: met mast or LiDAR campaign for a bankable P50/P90, eagle and avian use surveys, preliminary cultural survey. About 40-60% of ML-picked sites hit a bankable resource with no fatal flaw.
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, Pattern, AES) that buy development-stage projects per MW
scored.public_data: BLM MLRS serial register and case abstracts (including lapsed met ROWs), BLM ePlanning environmental assessments, legacy DOE/NREL and university met-tower archives, NREL WIND Toolkit, USFWS eagle nest and critical habitat layers, FAA obstruction filings, FERC/EIA interconnection data
scored.rough_step_up: About $10k of rent and filing becomes $20-50k/MW for a 200-400 MW proven site, i.e. $4-20M, roughly 100-1000x on the right. ML that avoids eagle or cultural fatal flaws and finds underrated resource gives about 1.5-2x cost per proven site. Ladder: development ROW, then build, then own and operate.
scored.frame: The rung is a site-testing ROW with a bankable resource and no fatal flaw, sold to a developer. Inside that rung, discovery (picking the site and screening for fatal flaws) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is a real physical and regulatory campaign: a met mast or LiDAR, 1-2 years of eagle and avian use surveys, and a cultural survey. More important, what a wind site is worth is set by interconnection position, offtake, NEPA and the development ROW, not by wind discovery. So no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of what creates value. There is a capitalised buyer class, but its appetite for new early-stage federal wind is collapsing (see fatal flaw).
scored.step_up: Unproven: a few thousand dollars a year in schedule rent plus filing, about $10k all-in. Proven, meaning resource data plus baselines but no interconnection, no development ROW and no NEPA: early-stage wind sites typically trade at low single-digit $k/MW (my estimate; I found no public transaction comps). The candidate's $20-50k/MW is a late-stage, interconnection-secured price. For 200-400 MW at $1-5k/MW that is about $0.2-2M. That is 20-200x on the rent, but only about 1-5x on total capital once the $150-400k proving spend is counted. Score 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $150-400k and 12-24 months per site (candidate's estimate; consistent with LiDAR plus eagle-survey norms), so the expensive leg of the relaxed C3 is met. The base hit rate is claimed at 40-60%. ML lift is likely modest, about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven site. The wind resource is already well modelled (NREL WIND Toolkit, commercial wind maps), and eagle nest and critical habitat layers are already legible GIS that every developer screens against. The edge left is mostly in scanned BLM case files and lapsed met-ROW data. Score 3.
scored.data: Weak. The main signals (wind resource, eagle nests, critical habitat, FAA obstructions, interconnection queues) are public and largely legible, and incumbent developers and consultants already use them. Only the legacy met-tower archives and BLM case abstracts are illegible, and they add little beyond the reanalysis models. The outcome is partly summarised already: designated leasing areas and land-use-plan exclusion and avoidance zones encode BLM's own judgment.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a government ROW filed first-come at schedule rent, which is the free first-come pattern the rubric disfavours. Under 43 CFR 2804.30 and IM 2021-026, BLM may offer land outside designated leasing areas competitively whenever it sees competitive interest, so a valuable site can be pulled into a bid. The 2024 Renewable Energy Rule cut rents and fees but did not remove this discretion. The grant is assignable only with BLM approval. Since the July 2025 Interior memo, every wind ROW decision needs sign-off from the Secretary's office, so assignment and conversion to a development ROW face political review. The rent is fixed, but the uplift is not safe from competition or from denial.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale wind developers and IPPs (NextEra, Invenergy, Pattern, AES). They have capital, but post-OBBBA projects that missed the July 4, 2026 construction-start deadline must be in service by end-2027 to keep tax credits. Wood Mackenzie describes the early-stage pipeline as weakening, and Interior is hostile to federal-land wind. Demand for brand-new, early-stage BLM wind sites is close to the weakest it has been.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: development ROW and interconnection, then construction, then own and operate as an IPP. In principle that is a large company path. It is capped by the current federal policy hostility toward wind and by intense competition among IPPs. Score 3.
scored.fatal_flaw: The wind resource is not the scarce, illegible thing; interconnection, permitting and offtake are. On top of that, federal-land wind is now gated by the Interior Secretary's office and loses tax credits after 2027 if construction did not start by July 4, 2026. So a proven-resource BLM site carries no 10^3-10^4 step-up, and its buyers are pulling back.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the rubric on several counts: discovery is a minor share of what makes a wind site valuable, the resource data is already legible (NREL WIND Toolkit), the ROW is first-come and BLM can put it to competitive bid, and the proven value is about 1-5x on capital rather than 10^4. Federal wind is also politically frozen and losing its tax credits.

scored.name: Atlantic salmon marine site origination (Maine and Atlantic Canada leases)
scored.one_line: Use ML over oceanographic and old lease records to find unleased bays that can carry finfish, apply for a provincial or state aquaculture lease at fixed fees, fund the baseline environmental survey and hydrographic modelling, and sell the approved site to Cooke or Mowi, who pay heavily for scarce new licensed biomass. Honest rough score: C1 3, C2 4, C3 4, C4 3, C5 4.
scored.unproven_right: Nova Scotia, Newfoundland or Maine DMR marine aquaculture lease and licence. These are granted at fixed application and rental fees per hectare (not auctioned), and are transferable with regulator approval.
scored.proving_step: Environmental baseline survey, current and dispersion modelling, benthic sampling and the full application and hearing (e.g. NS ARB): $300k-1.5M over 2-3 years. A hit is an approved lease. Approval odds are roughly 40-60%, depending on social licence.
scored.proven_buyer: Cooke Aquaculture, Mowi Canada East and Grieg NL. Licensed marine capacity is the binding constraint on their growth, and Norwegian licence equivalents trade at about NOK 150-250M per 780t MTB.
scored.public_data: NS Aquaculture Review Board decisions and transcripts, and DFO site-application archives (long PDFs). Maine DMR lease decision documents. DFO and CIOOS oceanographic buoy and temperature data. Historical sea-lice and disease reports. CHS bathymetry.
scored.rough_step_up: About $10-50k in fees becomes a licensed finfish site worth $5-20M+ to a major, roughly 100-1000x on the right and about 10x on all-in proving cost. ML lifts approval odds by avoiding sites likely to fail on temperature, current or social opposition. Caveat: Canadian politics around new open-net sites is hostile.
scored.frame: Rung: originate an approved marine finfish lease and sell it. Inside that rung, site discovery (temperature, current, bathymetry, avoiding sites likely to fail) is perhaps 20-30% of the work. Most of it is permitting, social licence and hearing work, and that is politics more than discovery. The rung is also hard to sell. Nova Scotia will not normally approve a lease assignment until the site has been in production for at least a year. Maine bars transfers made for speculative purposes, and an applicant there must show a source of fish (DMR ended American Aquafarms' applications over this). To realise the step-up you would in practice have to stock and farm the site yourself, and that physical step costs tens of millions of dollars (smolts, pens, boats). It is not trivial.
scored.step_up: Unproven: fixed application and rental fees, about $10-50k. Proven: Cooke is buying Mowi Canada East for C$225M on about 9,000 t/yr of production, roughly C$25k per annual tonne (my own arithmetic, which includes hatcheries and processing plants). A licensed site of 1,000-2,000 t is maybe C$5-20M within a whole business, but I found no evidence of standalone trades of unstocked approved sites in Atlantic Canada. Against fees that is about 10^3. Against all-in proving cost ($0.3-1.5M) it is about 10x. Norwegian licence prices do not carry over, because Canadian sites are not a separately traded capacity market.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs $300k-1.5M and takes 2-3+ years, which clears the expensive threshold. Base approval odds of maybe 40-60% fall within the relaxed band. But the main failure mode is social opposition and policy (the Nova Scotia pause, Maine's Frenchman Bay fight), not physical suitability. ML over oceanography might give about 1.2-1.5x on cost per approved site, not clearly 1.5x or more. Sources: CBC and SeafoodSource reporting on the Nova Scotia pause, plus NS ARB decisions.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: ARB transcripts, DFO application archives and Maine DMR decision PDFs. The oceanographic data (CIOOS, CHS bathymetry) is already legible and is used by the incumbents' own siting teams. Outcomes are written into legible decisions. Nova Scotia has paused new marine finfish applications since 2023 until it builds its own coastal classification system, which maps and rates the coast for suitable locations. That means the regulator itself is producing the suitability map, which kills the information edge. The 2025 NS lease regulation also allows calls for proposals that set how many options will be issued, so the best areas can be allocated by competitive call rather than first-come at a fixed fee.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a lease from the Crown or the state at fixed fees, but it comes with strong anti-flip rules. In Nova Scotia an assignment needs the Minister's consent, a change of corporate control counts as an assignment, and the Minister normally refuses until the site has a year of production. Maine's transfer statute requires that the transfer is not for speculative purposes, and an applicant must show a fish source. The regulators therefore block a non-operator from taking the hope-value uplift. New open-net sites in Nova Scotia are also paused.
scored.buyer: There are capitalised buyers: Cooke (which now also owns Mowi Canada East, agreed C$225M in June 2026) and Grieg NL. Cooke's purchase of Mowi Canada East consolidates the region down to essentially one or two buyers, which gives them monopsony pricing power over any originated site.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: farming, then hatchery, then processing, then brand. That is a real vertical chain, but the market is mature, very capital-heavy and politically shrinking (BC is phasing out open-net pens, and Nova Scotia has paused new sites). This is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The approved lease cannot be flipped. Nova Scotia normally refuses an assignment until the site has a year of production, and Maine bars speculative transfers and requires a fish source. On top of that, Nova Scotia has paused new marine finfish applications while it builds its own coastal suitability map. So a non-operator cannot realise the step-up, and the regulator is producing the discovery output itself.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up on fees is real, but anti-speculation transfer rules, the Nova Scotia pause and a state-built suitability map turn this into a capital-heavy salmon farming business decided by social licence, not a discovery rung.

scored.name: Landlocked tax-forfeit parcels plus a court-won easement by necessity
scored.one_line: Buy landlocked tax-defaulted parcels at the statutory minimum bid (back taxes, often $100-$2,000). Use ML over scanned deed chains to find the parcels that were once under common title with a neighbouring parcel that touches a road, since that history is what lets a court grant an easement by necessity. Win the access easement in court, then sell the now-buildable parcel to an adjacent developer or a homebuilder.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to a landlocked tax-forfeited parcel, sold by the county at a formula minimum (taxes plus costs) in states like MI, MN, AR (COSL negotiated sales) and PA repository sales. Hope value is not priced because the county sells by fixed schedule and bidders cannot see an access path.
scored.proving_step: Quiet title plus a declaratory action for an easement by necessity or implication, backed by a title abstract and a survey. Cost is about $40-80k with surveying and appeals risk, over 12-24 months. Success is roughly 40-70% where unity of title and strict necessity are documented.
scored.proven_buyer: Adjacent landowners and developers assembling sites, regional homebuilders, and solar or wind developers needing contiguous site control.
scored.public_data: County register-of-deeds scanned instruments and grantor-grantee indexes (many pre-1950 handwritten), historic plat books, county GIS parcel fabric (to flag parcels with zero road frontage), state tax-forfeiture lists, and USGS historical topo maps for old roads.
scored.rough_step_up: About 20-100x on the parcel (for example a $1-3k landlocked parcel becomes a $40-150k buildable one). Most of the uplift is kept because the company owns the fee title.
scored.frame: The rung is buying one landlocked parcel, winning a court-declared access easement and reselling the parcel as buildable. Discovery means reading the deed chain to find unity of title, and it is maybe 30-50% of the work. The proving step is contested litigation against a hostile neighbour plus a survey, title abstract and appeals risk, at $40-80k over 12-24 months. That step is neither trivial nor abstracted, so this fails the 80%+ discovery test the same way the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example does. Capitalised buyers (homebuilders, solar developers) exist, but they buy assembled sites, not single remnant lots. The most natural buyer is often the servient neighbour, the same party being sued.
scored.step_up: Appraisal evidence puts the landlocked discount at 46-90% against comparable road-access land. That is about 2-10x, not the claimed 20-100x. Paired sales of Montana trust land averaged a 46% discount. A 2020 upstate NY appraisal paper used discounts of up to 90%, and up to 75% for land with a right-of-way or restricted access. One NC county applied 70-90%. Parcels that sell for $1-3k at tax sale are cheap mainly because they are tiny, nonconforming or remnant strips, not only because they lack access. Adding an easement does not make an undersized lot meet zoning, and Orono, MN notes that such parcels stay subject to minimum lot area and width rules. A realistic step-up is 2-10x on a parcel worth a few thousand dollars.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive enough to qualify: about $40-80k in quiet title, declaratory action and survey per attempt (the candidate's own estimate), over 12-24 months. The base win rate of 40-70% is now acceptable under the relaxed C3. ML that screens deed chains for unity of title before purchase could plausibly lift wins per attempt 1.3-1.6x, since many claims fail on unity. In Creagan v Stein (NY App Div 2021), a tax-sale purchaser lost for failing to prove unity by clear and convincing evidence. The lever is real but modest, because a paid title abstract is required for the lawsuit anyway. It also does not fix the economics: $40-80k spent to add perhaps $5-50k of value on most such parcels.
scored.data: The deed data really is illegible: handwritten pre-1950 grantor-grantee indexes and plat books that nobody structures. The outcome itself is not written into any status field. But the trigger is legible: county GIS already shows zero road frontage, and Michigan DNR auction notices say outright that a parcel has no legal access. Pricing is less fixed than claimed. Michigan sells at competitive auction above the minimum bid, so hope value is bid up. In Minnesota, tax-forfeited land sells at no less than appraised value, and nonconforming parcels can go to adjoining owners only by sealed bid (282.01 subd. 7a) and must be combined with their land, so an outsider often cannot buy them at all. Minnesota's cartway statute (164.08) also lets any landlocked owner of 5+ acres force a town to establish access for damages, with no unity of title needed. That makes the ML edge moot in the main 'fixed price' state and also offers the neighbour a statutory route. Arkansas COSL negotiated sales and PA repository sales come closer to a fixed price, but they need county or taxing-body approval. Fee title is transferable, and nothing claws back the uplift.
scored.right_bought: Fee title to a tax-forfeited landlocked parcel. It is transferable, but the sale mechanism varies by state. Michigan: open auction above the minimum bid. Minnesota: appraised-value floor, with nonconforming parcels limited to adjoining owners and required to be combined. Arkansas: COSL negotiated sale. Pennsylvania: repository bid subject to taxing-body approval. Hope value is partly priced through competitive bidding, and adjoining owners, who know the history, are the usual bidders.
scored.buyer: In theory, adjacent landowners, site assemblers, regional homebuilders and solar developers. In practice the adjacent owner is both the most likely buyer and the defendant in the easement suit. Homebuilders buy parcels in the $40-150k range only as part of larger assemblies, not one at a time.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs: parcel access arbitrage, then land assembly, then entitlement, then homebuilding or development. These are real but fragmented local businesses with thin edges. Scale is limited by state-by-state property law and the cost of litigating each parcel. There is no credible path to a very large company from this rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a $40-80k adversarial lawsuit, while the value it unlocks is only the landlocked discount of 2-10x (46-90%) on parcels worth low thousands of dollars. On most parcels, legal cost per win exceeds the uplift. The physical step dominates, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The deed data is illegible, but proving means litigating (expensive and dominant), the real step-up is 2-10x rather than 20-100x, and Michigan and Minnesota auction, appraise or restrict these parcels to adjoining owners rather than selling them at a fixed minimum.

scored.name: Entitled subdivisions from tax-forfeited acreage
scored.one_line: Buy tax-forfeited raw acreage at the formula minimum price (MN, WI and MI county tax-forfeit sales use appraised or statutory minimums and over-the-counter sales after the auction). Use ML over scanned zoning board minutes, past plat approvals and soil and wetland data to predict which parcels will win preliminary plat or rezoning approval. Obtain the entitlements, then sell the entitled lots or tract to a production homebuilder.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to tax-forfeited acreage sold over the counter at a fixed post-auction price. Unsold forfeit land is often listed at the minimum indefinitely, with no premium for entitlement probability.
scored.proving_step: A preliminary plat or rezoning application with traffic study, wetland delineation, perc and septic or utility capacity letters, and an engineering layout. Cost is about $75-250k, over 12-30 months. Approval runs about 35-65%, and ML-screened parcels should do better.
scored.proven_buyer: Production homebuilders (DR Horton, Lennar and regional builders) and land bankers who pay a premium for entitled lots.
scored.public_data: Scanned planning commission and zoning board minutes and staff reports (PDF agendas), recorded plats, comprehensive plan future land-use maps, NRCS SSURGO soils, the National Wetlands Inventory, sewer service-area maps, and county tax-forfeit lists.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-40x per acre (forfeit rural or edge acreage at $500-3k/acre becomes entitled land at $20-80k/acre in exurban growth corridors).
scored.frame: The rung is "entitle a raw tract and sell it to a builder". It is real and sellable. But picking the parcel is maybe 20-30% of the work. The other 70-80% is the proving step itself: engineering layout, traffic and wetland studies, utility capacity negotiation, neighbour opposition, conditions of approval and public hearings. That work is political and procedural, not a cheap physical act like a drill hole. The rung is not discovery-dominated the way Terranox's is.
scored.step_up: The claimed 10-40x mixes two different land pools. Forfeit land at $500-3k/acre is mostly northern forest, swamp, landlocked or remnant parcels (Aitkin, Lake and St. Louis county lists) with no development demand. Edge acreage in real growth corridors trades at ag/transition value of roughly $10-25k/acre. Entitled but unimproved tracts sell at roughly 2-4x raw, because builders pay the big premium for finished lots after horizontal development. Option structures value finished lots at 20-40% of home price (Builder Online). So the realistic immediate step-up on a hit is about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $75-250k and 12-30 months per application (the candidate's own figures; consistent with trade sources citing 2-3 years for entitlements). The candidate gives a base approval rate of 35-65%. Under relaxed C3 that rate is fine. The doubt is the ML lift. Approval is largely predicted by legible inputs: the comprehensive-plan future land-use designation, whether the parcel is inside the sewer service area (MUSA in the Twin Cities), and NWI wetlands. A lookup on those fields probably captures most of the signal, as with interconnection queues. Mining the minutes for neighbour opposition and council temperament plausibly adds ~1.2-1.4x on cost per approved tract, not >=1.5x.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scanned planning commission minutes and staff reports are scattered PDFs. But the outcome is largely already summarised in legible public layers: future land-use maps, MUSA/sewer boundaries, zoning GIS, SSURGO soils and NWI wetlands. Homebuilder land teams and brokers read all of these routinely, so the illegible part adds only marginal signal.
scored.right_bought: Bought, transferable fee title, but not cheap relative to hope value. After Tyler v. Hennepin (2023), Minnesota changed its process for land forfeited after 12/31/2023 (Minn. Stat. 282.005). There is first an estimated-market-value (EMV) auction within six months of forfeiture. Unsold parcels go over the counter at EMV until a minimum-bid auction, and surplus goes back to the former owner. Dakota County (a metro growth county) sells over the counter at the estimated market value shown on the list, plus a 3% state surcharge. So the price is set by an assessor's market value and tested by a public auction where builders and land speculators can bid. Hope value is not fully priced, but there is no deep discount. Local governments can also request conveyance for public use before sale. Wisconsin and Michigan run auctions too. Growth-corridor forfeits are rare and small, because owners near development pressure sell or refinance during the multi-year redemption period. The sellers are counties pricing at market, not owners who cannot read the data.
scored.buyer: Production homebuilders (DR Horton, Lennar, Pulte and regional builders) and land bankers (Varde, Millrose and similar) are well capitalised and buy entitled land or finished lots, typically through options with roughly 15% deposits. They are real, deep buyers, but they pay mostly for finished lots rather than paper entitlements.
scored.ladder: Entitlement leads to horizontal development (finished lots), then vertical homebuilding, then possibly a build-to-rent portfolio. Climbing gives a large homebuilder or land developer (DR Horton has a market cap of about $50B), but each rung is a capital-heavy commodity business with no compounding discovery edge. That is a large but not trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The cheap land and the land worth entitling are different pools. Forfeit land priced at $500-3k/acre is undevelopable rural or remnant land. The rare forfeit parcels in growth corridors are sold at assessor market value through a public auction first (Minnesota's post-Tyler 282.005 process), so there is no discounted hope-value purchase. The entitled step-up is also only ~2-5x and is driven by process rather than discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little, since entitlement is expensive and slow. But the real step-up is only ~2-5x, approval is mostly predicted by legible comprehensive-plan and sewer maps, and growth-corridor forfeit land is rare and sold at assessed market value by auction. That leaves no cheap unproven right.
sources: https://www.aitkincountymn.gov/board/2024/09-24-2024/pdf/5B- Adopt Resolution - Set Date Time and Pricing of Tax Forfeited Land Sale.pdf

scored.name: FERC permits on non-powered federal dams (hydro retrofit)
scored.one_line: File FERC preliminary permits or conduit exemptions (free or nominal-fee, first-to-file, transferable) at USACE and Reclamation non-powered dams ranked by ML from scanned water-control manuals, daily release logs, dam safety reports and surrendered-permit histories at the same dams, since release patterns that set real generation are buried in PDFs. Fund flow-duration, structural/outlet-works and dissolved-oxygen screens plus USACE Section 408 pre-consultation and an interconnection screen, then sell the licensable project to a small-hydro IPP, fund or utility. The dam is public, so no private landowner prices hope.
scored.unproven_right: FERC preliminary permit or conduit exemption at a federal non-powered dam: a nominal-fee, first-to-file exclusive study priority that FERC can approve for transfer
scored.proving_step: Flow-duration and head analysis on historical releases, structural and outlet-works assessment, DO screen, USACE Section 408 pre-application and interconnection screen. About $150-500k over 1-2 years; roughly 30-60% feasible, and ML plausibly lifts that ~2x by avoiding dams whose release regimes kill capacity factor.
scored.proven_buyer: Small-hydro IPPs and funds (Rye Development and backers, Enel Green Power NA, Eagle Creek, Brookfield Renewable), municipal utilities wanting firm low-carbon capacity, utilities seeking firm clean MWh for data-centre PPAs, and ITC-driven tax-equity buyers
scored.public_data: USACE National Inventory of Dams, scanned USACE water-control and operating manuals, daily release logs and periodic inspection reports, BoR records, USGS NWIS flow records, the ORNL non-powered dam assessment, and FERC eLibrary histories of lapsed and surrendered permits on the same dams
scored.rough_step_up: Permit about $0-50k. A feasibility-proven 5-40 MW pre-licence project sells for about $0.5-10M (about $50-150k/MW), roughly 10-100x on proving spend. Weakness: the ORNL inventory already summarises much of the potential (legible-outcome risk). Ladder: licence, construction, owned small-hydro fleet, pumped-storage add-ons.
scored.frame: The rung is a feasibility-screened, permit-held, pre-licence project at a federal non-powered dam. Inside that rung, discovery and screening is perhaps 50-60% of the work, not 80% or more. Even before the licence, a lot of the cost is regulatory and consultation work that has nothing to do with discovery: FERC ILP/TLP pre-filing, USACE Section 408, state 401 water quality, ESA and fish passage, and interconnection. The value-defining step is building bespoke civil works at someone else's dam, which costs roughly $4-8k/kW. That makes this the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure pattern: building is much harder than finding. Buyers for pre-licence NPD projects are thin. Rye/FFP has sat on its portfolio for more than 10 years, and it took CAI and Crestline funding to move the projects forward, not an outright purchase.
scored.step_up: The right itself costs about $0, since preliminary permits carry no fee, so the meaningful comparison is proving spend against project value. About $150-500k of screening produces a pre-licence project worth perhaps $0.5-3M for typical 5-20 MW NPD sites at roughly $50-150k/MW. That is about 3-10x, and the candidate's own 10-100x estimate is optimistic. I found no disclosed sale prices for development-stage NPD portfolios: the CAI deal with Rye for 22 projects (about 250 MW) and the Crestline loan to FFP New Hydro had undisclosed terms. Most of the value step comes at licence plus PPA plus financing, years later and after much larger spend. It is not an immediate jump on a hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $150-500k over 1-2 years, which passes the relaxed expense test. The base feasible rate is perhaps 30-60% (the candidate's estimate; I found no sourced figure). ML lift is limited because the key inputs are already legible: USGS NWIS gauge flows below dams, NID head and height, and the ORNL 2012 NPD assessment of about 54,000 dams with per-site MW estimates. Release-regime nuance from scanned water-control manuals could plausibly give about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven project, not a clear 2x.
scored.data: This is the legible-outcome trap. ORNL's NPD resource assessment already publishes per-dam potential capacity and energy. USGS daily flow records and NID head data are structured and machine-readable. USACE has also published its own hydropower-potential studies of its dams. Scanned water-control manuals add marginal detail on minimum flows, drawdown rules and DO, but they do not hold a hidden answer that incumbents miss. Sophisticated filers such as Rye/FFP, Lock+ Hydro and municipal utilities have already permit-banked the top-ranked USACE sites, many of them repeatedly.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from an owner who cannot read the data. It is a free, first-to-file FERC preliminary permit, which is exactly the free first-come right C4 penalises. The FPA statute (16 USC 798(d)) makes preliminary permits explicitly non-transferable and cancellable for good cause. The only route to selling one is selling the permittee SPV, and FERC can still cancel the permit or award priority elsewhere. Municipal and state preference under FPA Section 7(a) lets public utilities beat private filers on competing applications. Reclamation dams mostly go through Lease of Power Privilege instead. That is a competitive solicitation with scoring, a preference-entity right to match within 90 days, a first right to the power for WAPA, a lease term capped at 40 years, and an ongoing per-kWh lease charge. The public body therefore effectively auctions, reserves, or claws back the uplift. Permit terms of up to 4 years plus one extension also limit how long priority can be held.
scored.buyer: Small-hydro IPPs and infrastructure funds: Rye/FFP New Hydro with CAI and Crestline, Brookfield, Enel Green Power NA, and Eagle Creek/Ontario Teachers'. Also municipal utilities and data-centre offtakers, such as Iron Mountain's 150 MW PPA with Rye. These buyers are capitalised but mostly buy operating or licensed assets with PPAs. Appetite for pre-licence permit-stage projects is low, and they are valued near cost.
scored.ladder: Preliminary permit, then licence or LOPP, then PPA and financing, then construction, then an owned small-hydro fleet, then pumped-storage add-ons and firm clean capacity sales. The ladder is real but bounded. Total US NPD potential is about 12 GW, concentrated in fewer than 100 large sites that are mostly already claimed. This is a good mid-size IPP outcome, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck and its outcome is already legible. ORNL's NPD assessment, USGS gauge flows and NID head data already rank the dams, so the top sites are permit-banked by Rye/FFP and municipal utilities. Value comes from the hard physical and regulatory build at a federal dam, not from finding the dam. On top of that, the permit is a free first-to-file right that the statute makes non-transferable, subject to municipal preference, and at Reclamation sites competitively solicited with a lease charge. No cheap right is being bought from someone who cannot read the data.
scored.one_line_reason: Like the geothermal-in-coal-mines case, building beats finding: the dam-ranking outcome is already published by ORNL/USGS/NID, and the free FERC permit is statutorily non-transferable and preference-contested, so the step-up from proving spend is only about 3-10x.

scored.name: Nepal hydropower survey licences to generation-licence-ready projects
scored.one_line: Acquire DoED survey licences, which carry fixed per-MW fees, for run-of-river sites an ML model picks from digitised DHM hydrology, scanned old feasibility studies and DEM/landslide data. Fund the hydrology, geotechnical work and detailed project report, then sell the licence with a PPA-ready DPR to capitalised IPPs and Indian or Chinese developers.
scored.unproven_right: A Department of Electricity Development survey licence for a hydropower site. It is issued on application at a schedule fee per MW, not auctioned. Licences change hands through company share transfers, which happens actively in Nepal.
scored.proving_step: A feasibility study and detailed project report: discharge measurement, geotech drilling at headworks and powerhouse (ordinary civil drilling, not exploration), and an IEE/EIA. Roughly $200k-1M and 2-3 years. Perhaps 40-60% of ML-picked sites prove economic, versus a large fraction of speculative licences that lapse.
scored.proven_buyer: Listed Nepali IPPs, NEA subsidiaries, and Indian developers (SJVN, GMR) under the India-Nepal power export agreements. They pay premiums for DPR-complete licences with connection agreements.
scored.public_data: DoED licence registers and lapsed-licence lists. DHM gauge records, partly scanned. JICA and NEA master-plan studies (scanned PDFs). ICIMOD glacier/landslide inventories. SRTM/ALOS DEMs.
scored.rough_step_up: A licence costs about $5-20k. A DPR-complete, PPA-ready licence sells for roughly $50-150k/MW, so a 20-50 MW site is worth $1-7M. That is ~100x on the right and ~5-10x on all-in. The ladder runs on to construction, then IPP ownership, then cross-border export.
scored.frame: The rung is a survey licence carried through to a DPR-complete, generation-licence-ready project. Discovery is maybe 15-25% of the work inside it.
