Nepal's good run-of-river sites are already mapped in the JICA/NEA master plans and DoED registers. Most of the work is engineering and permitting: a year or more of discharge measurement, geotech drilling, IEE/EIA, the grid connection agreement and chasing a PPA. That physical and bureaucratic work is not trivial. A capitalised buyer exists in principle (listed IPPs, SJVN, GMR). In practice the step that creates value is the NEA PPA, which neither the developer nor ML controls.
scored.step_up: The claimed step-up is ~100x on the licence fee and 5-10x all-in. Real figures are worse. Developers report spending Rs5-6M/MW (~$37-45k/MW) on survey licences, feasibility studies, EIAs and other preparatory work (Kathmandu Post, Jul 2026). For a 30 MW site that is about $1.1-1.4M in. A sale at the claimed $50-150k/MW would be roughly 1.2-3x all-in. That price is also unverified: searches found no per-MW secondary-market price for licences. With ~16.4 GW (281 projects) of licensed projects waiting for PPAs, a DPR-complete project without a PPA is not scarce, so the premium is likely thin. The one hard price point found is a DoED auction of six already-studied licences: 142 MW for Rs937M, about Rs6.5M/MW for Lower Solu. That suggests the state captures the hope value on studied sites itself. Realistically about 1.5-3x all-in, well short of 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving cost is expensive enough: about $40k/MW, so roughly $0.8-2M and 2-3 years per 20-50 MW site (Kathmandu Post, Jul 2026). The relaxed C3 admits a 40-60% base hit rate. But most failures come from outside the site. Sites do not mainly fail on hydrology or geotech. They fail on NEA's PPA freeze since 2022, grid absorption limits, transmission readiness and take-or-pay exposure. ML on hydrology, DEM and landslide data might lift technical-economic quality about 1.2x. It cannot lift the PPA hit rate, so the gain in cost per proven, sellable asset is likely under 1.3x.
scored.data: Some data is illegible: partly scanned DHM gauge records and scanned JICA/NEA master plans. But the outcome is largely already written down in legible form. The master plans rank sites. DoED registers list every licence, its MW, its holder and its status. NEA publishes PPA and connection-agreement status by project, and the ministry is now required to publish milestone and progress lists. Nepali developers and NEA know the river sites well, so incumbents are not blind to the signal.
scored.right_bought: The rights are not cheaply buyable and are not reliably fixed-price. (1) DoED switched to tiered fees in 2012 (Rs1M for 1-5 MW up to Rs6M for >500 MW) specifically to stop people taking licences in order to resell them. Bilateral MOUs like Arun-3 charge Rs100k/MW. (2) Studied projects are auctioned: six licences totalling 142 MW went for Rs937M, so hope value is clawed back on the best-known sites. (3) Since April 2026 (3 Baisakh 2083) the Energy Minister has frozen new survey permits pending a review, with cure notices and cancellations for licensees who miss milestones. (4) Licences are first-come applications, not purchases from owners who cannot read the data. Taking over existing licences means a share transfer of the holding company subject to DoED/ministry oversight, and current holders know what they have. Transfer works only through the company wrapper, and the anti-flipping regulatory posture reduces it further.
scored.buyer: Listed Nepali IPPs, NEA subsidiaries and Indian PSUs/developers (SJVN, GMR, NHPC) under the India-Nepal export arrangements. They are capitalised, but they already sit on large licence portfolios themselves and face the same PPA bottleneck. No evidence was found that they pay $50-150k/MW for licences that are DPR-complete but have no PPA.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is strong: generation licence and PPA, financial close, construction, operating IPP (equity listed on NEPSE), then cross-border export to India and Bangladesh, which earned Rs29.3B in FY2025/26. The ceiling is regional-utility scale rather than trillion-dollar, and every rung above sits behind NEA/state gatekeeping.
scored.fatal_flaw: The bottleneck is the state's PPA and grid gate, not discovery. About 16.4 GW across 281 licensed projects already waits for NEA PPAs, with signings stalled since 2022. New survey permits have been frozen since April 2026. Proven-ish projects are therefore in glut, not scarce, so no 10^3 step-up exists for a better-picked DPR. ML cannot move the PPA hit rate, and DoED auctions or anti-speculation fees claw back hope value on well-known sites.
scored.one_line_reason: The best sites are already mapped and licensed. Proving costs ~$40k/MW for at most ~1.5-3x all-in. The value step comes from an NEA PPA that is frozen behind a 16 GW backlog. New licences are suspended and studied sites are auctioned. This fails as a Terranox analogue.

scored.name: Chilean fiscal-land wind and solar measurement authorisations (Bienes Nacionales)
scored.one_line: Take Ministry of National Assets study/measurement authorisations and onerous-use concession applications on state land at administrative rates. ML ranks parcels from scanned CNE/Explorador Eólico data, abandoned SEA projects and transmission plans. Run measurement and prepare the concession dossier, then sell the proven site rights to developers or the large PV/wind/storage players.
scored.unproven_right: A Bienes Nacionales authorisation to study renewables on fiscal land, with a preferential path to an onerous-use concession. Rent is set at a regulated percentage of fiscal valuation. Some areas go to tender, which needs filtering.
scored.proving_step: A 12-24 month wind measurement or solar/soiling campaign, a geotechnical and archaeology survey, and a grid connection solicitation to the Coordinador Eléctrico. Roughly $150-500k. Perhaps 40-60% of sites prove bankable, given heavy curtailment risk that ML can model from CEN data.
scored.proven_buyer: Enel Green Power, Colbún, AES Andes, Engie, and European and Asian funds building storage hybrids. They pay for permitted, grid-adjacent, measured sites.
scored.public_data: Explorador Eólico/Solar (Universidad de Chile), CEN curtailment and nodal price data, the SEA e-SEIA archive of scanned wind/solar EIAs and abandoned projects, the Bienes Nacionales catastro, and CNE transmission expansion plans.
scored.rough_step_up: A fiscal-land authorisation is near-zero, about $5-20k. A measured, grid-solicited site sells for roughly $20-60k/MW, so $2-10M for a 100-200 MW site. That is ~100-500x on the right and ~10x on all-in. The ladder runs on to RCA, then a PPA, then IPP ownership and storage.
scored.frame: The rung is an early-stage renewable site on fiscal land: a concession, measured resource and a grid request, sold to an IPP. Discovery is perhaps 20-30% of the work inside it. The solar resource is already mapped in the clean, public Explorador Solar/Eólico GIS. The real work is grid access and curtailment, archaeology and environment, and the RCA permitting path, all of which is process work rather than discovery. Wind measurement is a cheap mast or LiDAR, but it takes time. Capitalised buyers exist (Enel, Colbún, AES Andes, Engie, funds), but they bid on Bienes Nacionales tenders directly.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a concession on fiscal land is not near-zero. Recent Bienes Nacionales tenders set minimum annual rents of about 1,300-3,400 UF per lot (roughly US$50-130k/yr), bid up competitively, plus guarantees. Proven: early or mid-stage Chilean PV and wind sites change hands at roughly US$10-50k/MW. Northern solar prices are depressed by curtailment and zero or negative nodal prices; this is my estimate, not a sourced comp. A 100-200 MW site might fetch $1-6M against $0.3-1M all-in (rent, bid, measurement, studies, guarantee). That is about 3-10x, not 100-500x. The 100-500x in the pitch assumes a near-free right, which no longer exists.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $150-500k and takes 12-24 months per site, so it passes the relaxed 'expensive' bar. The base bankable rate of 40-60% is the candidate's assumption, unsourced. The ML lift is weak. Resource quality is already legible in public GIS, and curtailment and nodal prices are clean CEN datasets that every developer already models. Abandoned SEA projects do give some signal on kill reasons, but my estimate is at most about 1.2x on cost per proven site.
scored.data: The core signals are legible. Explorador Solar and Explorador Eólico are structured, public GIS tools. CEN curtailment and marginal-cost data are clean downloads. CNE expansion plans are published and widely read. Only the e-SEIA scanned EIAs and abandoned-project files are somewhat illegible, and incumbent developers already mine them. Worse, the land outcome is effectively decided in the open: Bienes Nacionales publishes which lots it tenders and to whom it awards them.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data. Bienes Nacionales moved from direct assignment to public tender as the default for ERNC land. Lots go to the highest rent and investment bids, with a minimum rent plus a variable rent in wind tenders, so the state auctions away the hope value. Concessions carry build deadlines of 24-48 months with guarantees and fines, explicitly to deter speculation. Under DL 1939, transfer or assignment of a CUO needs Ministry authorisation. A direct-application path survives only for storage near specified Norte Grande substations, and it has a hard execution deadline (June 2027). Measurement or study authorisations are not a clean, transferable, preferential right.
scored.buyer: Enel Green Power, Colbún, AES Andes, Engie, CVE, and Asian and European storage-hybrid funds. They are capitalised, but they are the same parties bidding in the Bienes Nacionales tenders, so they can buy the land straight from the state rather than from a flipper.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: site → RCA environmental approval → grid connection → PPA or tender → IPP ownership → storage hybrid → transmission. Climbing it means becoming a full IPP, which is crowded and capital-intensive in Chile, and the thin, competitive bottom rung makes it hard to fund the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: The state auctions the hope value. Bienes Nacionales now allocates renewable fiscal land by competitive public tender on rent and investment, with build deadlines, guarantees and transfers subject to Ministry approval. So there is no cheap, transferable unproven right to buy from an owner who cannot read the data, and the key resource and grid data is already legible to every bidder.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive enough for the relaxed C3, but ML gives little edge on public, legible resource and curtailment data. The state auctions the land competitively with anti-speculation build deadlines and approval-gated transfers, so the real step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3.

scored.name: Crown land communications-site tenure at schedule rent (Canada and Australia)
scored.one_line: Apply for communications-site tenure where a government sells it at a fixed administrative rent, as with Crown land in BC, Ontario and Australian states. Use ML to pick hilltops that fill coverage gaps for new rural 5G, LEO backhaul or rail and mining private LTE, prove the site, and sell the tenure to a tower company. Honest view: C1 4, C2 4, C3 4, C4 4, C5 3. It extends the US federal comm-site idea to jurisdictions with less tower REIT competition.
scored.unproven_right: Crown land communications-site tenure, for example a BC Crown Land Communication Site licence, Ontario MNR land use permits, or NSW/QLD state land licences. Each is priced from a published fixed fee schedule and is transferable with consent.
scored.proving_step: A coverage and propagation study, environmental and First Nations consultation, ISED/ACMA site approval and an anchor-tenant LOI. Cost is about $50-150k and 1-2 years, with roughly 40-60% success.
scored.proven_buyer: Tower companies (Rogers/Freedom tower JVs, TELUS Communications Inc. towers, Indara, Amplitel, Axicom), carriers and mining companies
scored.public_data: Provincial and state Crown land tenure registries (scanned files), the ISED Spectrum Management System and Site Data, the ACMA RRL register, government coverage gap maps (CRTC/ISED Universal Broadband Fund, the Australian Mobile Black Spot Program), and terrain DEMs
scored.rough_step_up: $1-5k a year in schedule rent becomes a $0.3-2M site value: ~100-1000x on the annual rent
scored.frame: The claimed rung is getting an unbuilt Crown comm-site tenure to the point of an anchor-tenant LOI. Inside that rung, choosing the hilltop is perhaps 30-40% of the work. Consultation (environmental and First Nations), ISED/ACMA approvals and winning the anchor tenant make up the rest. Value is only realised when a $250-500k tower is built and leased, which makes the physical step larger than the discovery, as in the geothermal counter-example. Towercos and carriers do their own site acquisition through contracted site-acquisition firms, which are paid fees and do not capture a step-up. So a separate sellable rung for unbuilt licences is thin.
scored.step_up: The 100-1000x figure in the pitch compares an annual rent to a capital value, so it is not a like-for-like step-up. Rents are also far higher than claimed. NSW's 2023-24 standard comm-site rent was $9,362 (Low density) to $42,132 (Sydney) a year, per the IPART issues paper, not $1-5k. BC charges rent for each communication user on a site, using a CPI-indexed formula. The fair comparison is acquisition cost against sale value. Acquisition is roughly the cost of the application plus proving ($50-150k). A permitted raw site with an LOI might sell to a towerco for about $50-300k, since ground leases trade at around 10-20x rent (my estimate). That is a 2-5x step-up on capital, not 10^3. The $0.3-2M value belongs to a built, tenanted tower.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims proving costs about $50-150k and 1-2 years, with a 40-60% success rate; this is an unsourced estimate. That cost clears the relaxed bar for an expensive proving step. The binding constraint is getting a carrier or mining anchor tenant, which depends on carrier capex plans and government subsidy rounds (UBF, Mobile Black Spot), not on terrain. Carriers already run propagation tools such as Atoll and Planet, and the subsidy programs publish their own gap maps. ML plausibly lifts cost per proven site by only about 1.2-1.5x, so C3 scores 3.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible already. ISED SMS/Site Data and the ACMA RRL are structured, queryable registers. The UBF and Black Spot gap maps are published, and DEMs are free. Only the provincial tenure files are partly scanned. The answer to where coverage is needed is already summarised in the government gap maps that carriers bid against. This is the same failure seen in earlier hunts, where the regulator has already written the outcome down.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. It is applied for from the Crown, first-come, which is the excluded free-first-come pattern. The fixed price does not hold either. NSW sets rents through IPART reviews explicitly aimed at market-based commercial returns. Telstra and TPG are contesting co-user fees in the current review. BC charges rent per communication user, prices Crown land sold for comm use at full market value, and holds reserved sites through government agencies. All of this claws back co-location uplift. Assignment needs Crown consent, and tenures generally require the site to be built and used, so holding a site speculatively is fragile.
scored.buyer: Towercos are capitalised and do buy sites: Indara, Amplitel and Axicom in Australia, and the Rogers/TELUS/Bell tower assets in Canada. Carriers and mining companies with private LTE also buy. But they mostly buy built, tenanted towers or commission build-to-suit work, not unbuilt Crown licences.
scored.ladder: The path runs from site tenure to build-to-suit towers to a towerco portfolio, and from there to fibre backhaul and neutral-host or private LTE operator. That is a real ladder up to a multi-billion towerco, but it is a crowded one with low margins, competing against infrastructure funds.
scored.fatal_flaw: The Crown does not sell blind to hope value. Comm-site rent is set at market through IPART's market-based reviews in NSW ($9-42k a year per site) and charged per communication user in BC, so the government captures the co-location uplift. The value is only realised by building a $250k+ tower, which is a bigger task than finding the hilltop.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the rubric: the rights come free first-come but carry market-indexed, per-user rent; the gap data is already legible; and the real step-up needs a tower build. The result is about a 2-5x uplift, not 10^3.

scored.name: Washington DNR aquatic-lands shellfish/geoduck lease to permitted farm
scored.one_line: Apply for a Washington DNR state-owned aquatic-lands aquaculture lease, where rent follows the statutory aquaculture schedule rather than auction. Prove the site with a seed trial and obtain the shoreline and Corps permits, then sell the permitted, seeded lease to a large Puget Sound grower. Permit risk is the thing ML predicts.
scored.unproven_right: DNR aquatic-lands aquaculture lease application on state tidelands and bedlands, priced at the DNR schedule rent for aquaculture use. Assignable with DNR consent.
scored.proving_step: Sediment and eelgrass survey, a seed growth trial, a county Shoreline Substantial Development permit and Army Corps NWP 48 or an individual permit. Costs about $100-300k and takes 2-4 years. Success is about 30-60%, mainly limited by permits.
scored.proven_buyer: Taylor Shellfish and other large Pacific Northwest growers, plus aquaculture investors. Permitted geoduck acreage is scarce and is worth $100k+/acre per harvest cycle.
scored.public_data: DNR aquatic lease records and scanned plats. County shoreline permit decisions and hearing-examiner PDFs. Corps public notices. WDOH shellfish growing-area classifications (legible). DNR eelgrass (SVMP) surveys. Tribal usual-and-accustomed fishing-area rulings.
scored.rough_step_up: Application, rent and survey of about $10-20k become a permitted, seeded lease worth about $0.3-2M. That is 30-100x the right's cost but only about 3-8x all-in. C2 is about 3, C3 is 5 because ML plausibly picks permit-winnable sites at more than 1.5x.
scored.frame: The rung is 'state tideland lease to permitted, seeded site'. Discovery, meaning site selection plus predicting whether the permit can be won, is maybe 50-60% of the work. The rest is physical and slow: eelgrass and sediment surveys, seeding, PVC tube installation, and a growth trial on a crop that takes 5-7 years for geoduck. It also runs through adversarial permit fights (SEPA EIS, hearing examiner, Ecology conditional-use approval, Shorelines Hearings Board). There is a buyer, Taylor Shellfish and a few other growers, but they are mid-sized family firms, not deep-capital buyers. Most Puget Sound geoduck farms also sit on private tidelands, so growers have alternatives to buying state leases.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the cost of applying for a lease plus surveys, about $10-20k. Proven: a permitted, seeded lease the candidate claims is worth $0.3-2M. I found no transaction comps for sales of permitted geoduck leases. Against the full proving cost of $100-300k plus 2-4 years, the step-up is about 3-8x, and DNR rent based on bids or negotiation takes part of it. The Taylor back-rent dispute ($481k back rent, $630k total) shows the state charges real rent on productive geoduck ground. So C2 = 2, not the 10^3-10^4 jump that Terranox gets.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs $100-300k and takes 2-4 years (candidate estimate, consistent with Pierce County records). Taylor's Burley Lagoon project went through an FEIS in 2023, an 8-day hearing, and a December 2024 examiner approval, and is still subject to Ecology and SHB review. The Henderson Bay permits were denied by the SHB in 2014 after a 6-day hearing. The base success rate is about 30-60%. Under relaxed C3 the step is expensive enough. But outcomes hinge on organised local opposition and how individual hearing boards decide, and that is only partly predictable from eelgrass maps, WDOH classifications and past examiner decisions. A 1.2-1.5x gain is plausible; >=1.5x is not established. Score 3.
scored.data: The data are hearing-examiner PDFs, Corps public notices, DNR plats and SVMP eelgrass surveys. They are somewhat illegible, but each permit decision is itself a public document stating the outcome. The incumbent growers (Taylor and others) are the people who file these permits and know the opposition landscape better than any model would, so there is no edge over buyers who cannot read the data. WDOH classifications are already legible fields.
scored.right_bought: This fails. The candidate's premise is that rent 'follows the statutory aquaculture schedule rather than auction', and RCW 79.135.100 says the opposite: rents and fees for aquaculture on state-owned aquatic lands 'shall be established through competitive bidding or negotiation'. DNR has offered geoduck aquaculture sites through scored Request-for-Offers or bid rounds (nine sites in one round), and the legislature capped the acreage (15-25 acres a year in the 2007-08 bills). DNR also sells wild geoduck harvest rights by competitive auction to get 'the highest price'. Commissioner Goldmark refused to sign a negotiated Taylor lease. So the state picks which sites are offered, prices in the hope value through bidding or negotiation, and can refuse or claw back the uplift. Assignment needs DNR consent. The 'owners who cannot read the data' are a state agency that runs the process and growers who generate the data.
scored.buyer: Taylor Shellfish and a small number of Puget Sound geoduck and oyster growers, plus some aquaculture investors. This is real but thin demand from mid-sized private firms. Washington farmed geoduck is roughly a $50-100M a year market, and it depends on export to China and Hong Kong, which tariffs and the PSP closures of 2018-2019 have disrupted.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are permitted sites, then growing, harvest, processing and export to Asian live-seafood markets. That is a real chain but small, a regional niche worth hundreds of millions of dollars, constrained by acreage caps, tribal treaty rights and local opposition. There is no plausible path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The cheap fixed-price right does not exist. RCW 79.135.100 makes DNR set aquaculture rents by competitive bidding or negotiation, and DNR chooses and caps the geoduck sites it offers. The state captures the hope value, and the incumbent growers, the natural buyers, already read the permit record better than any model.
scored.one_line_reason: The proving step is expensive and somewhat predictable, so relaxed C3 gets a 3. But rent is set by bid or negotiation, not a fixed schedule, the all-in step-up is only 3-8x, the buyers are the people who already hold the information edge, and the ladder tops out at a regional shellfish niche.

scored.name: Maine DMR limited-purpose to standard aquaculture lease flip
scored.one_line: Use Maine's fixed-fee experimental and limited-purpose aquaculture licences (about $50-100 per year) to prove growth and social licence, convert to a standard lease at schedule rent of about $100/acre/yr, and sell the transferable standard lease to a capitalised grower. ML predicts which sites survive the DMR hearing and grow well.
scored.unproven_right: DMR LPA or experimental lease at a fixed administrative fee, rather than bid. The standard lease that follows is at a fixed per-acre rent and is transferable with DMR approval.
scored.proving_step: 1-3 seasons of grow-out data, a site survey, scoping and public-hearing preparation, plus legal and biological reports for the DMR standard-lease decision. Costs about $50-200k and takes 2-3 years. Success is roughly 40-70%, and the hearing outcome is the main risk.
scored.proven_buyer: Larger Maine oyster farms and consolidators, and out-of-state seafood investors. Approved standard leases are scarce and change hands for six figures.
scored.public_data: DMR lease decision PDFs and hearing transcripts (objections, riparian and fishing-conflict findings). DMR water-classification maps (legible). NERACOOS buoy temperature and chlorophyll data. Maine Sea Grant grow-out reports. Lobster-landings proxies for conflict.
scored.rough_step_up: Fees of under $5k become an approved 10-50 acre standard lease worth about $100k-$1M. That is 30-200x the right's cost and about 2-5x all-in. C2 is about 3.
scored.frame: Rung: get an approved Maine DMR standard aquaculture lease, then transfer it to a grower. Picking the site is maybe 25-35% of the work inside this rung. The rest is physical and regulatory: actually growing oysters for 1-3 seasons, gear, the site survey, the scoping meeting, the public hearing and the legal/biological reports. The physical step is not trivial. Running a farm is the proof, and DMR's transfer test requires that real aquaculture took place on the site (Ch. 2.60(3)(C)). Capitalised buyers (bigger Maine farms and consolidators) do exist, but they are few and the market is small.
scored.step_up: State charges for the unproven right: LPA about $50-300/yr, a standard-lease application of roughly $1-2k, then rent of about $100/acre/yr (older Penobscot Bay leases were at $50/acre). A proven, farmed 5-10 acre lease, sold as part of a going farm, is plausibly worth $50k-$500k. That is about 30-200x the state fees but only about 2-5x the all-in proving cost of $50-200k. My searches found no recorded arm's-length sale prices for leases, so the six-figure value claimed for approved leases is unverified. Scored on the all-in multiple: C2 = 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt costs $50-200k and takes 2-3 years (candidate estimate, which fits the DMR process of survey, scoping, hearing and 20-year lease decision). Base success is roughly 40-70%. Most Maine standard-lease applications that reach decision are granted, and the main risk is hearing objections from lobstermen and riparian owners (e.g. the 2019 Mere Point litigation). ML over hearing transcripts and objections could plausibly lift approval by about 1.2-1.5x, mostly by avoiding conflict sites. The growth-prediction side is weaker, because legible buoy and water-classification data already does most of that job. Under the relaxed C3 this is about 3.
scored.data: Public data is split. Decision PDFs, site reports and hearing transcripts are semi-illegible and scattered. However, DMR publishes legible decision-history tables (granted/denied/withdrawn) and legible water-classification maps, so the outcome label is easy to get and the predictors (conflict density, depth, classification) are largely legible too. Experienced local growers and Maine Sea Grant already know which coves are contentious. The ML edge is modest.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is a public application at a fixed administrative fee, and the state does not price hope value, which is good. But it is not an auction, and DMR gives preference to competing applicants and to riparian/existing users. Transferability is real but conditioned. Under 12 MRSA 6072(12-A) the commissioner approves a transfer only if it is not for speculative purposes, judged by whether the lessee conducted 'substantially no research or aquaculture'. The transferee must also show financial and technical capacity, stay under the 1,000-acre cap, and the transfer must not circumvent the competing-application preferences. Examples: CASSI Maine Scallop to Wild Ocean (2022), PEN LD2 Weed to Long Cove. A pure flip is barred. You must actually farm first. LPAs and experimental leases are not transferable stepping stones in any meaningful sense, and a buyer could simply apply directly.
scored.buyer: Larger Maine oyster and mussel farms and consolidators (e.g. Mere Point, Pemaquid Mussel Farms, Long Cove), plus a few out-of-state seafood investors. The pool is thin. Maine farmed oyster landings are on the order of tens of millions of dollars a year, so buyer capital is small. These buyers can also apply for leases themselves at the same fixed fee.
scored.ladder: Lease, then grow-out farm, then hatchery/seed, then processing and wholesale/brand. Each rung is small, and the whole Maine aquaculture chain is maybe $100M or more. Expansion to other states would be possible, but their lease regimes differ. Not a path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step IS operating a real oyster farm. Maine's anti-speculation transfer rule (Ch. 2.60, which looks for 'substantially no aquaculture') blocks a discovery-only flip. And because any buyer can apply for the same lease at the same fixed fee, there is no 10^3x step-up asset: it is about 2-5x all-in, in a tiny market.
scored.one_line_reason: A fixed-fee public right with conditioned transferability, but the proving work is physical farming plus a hearing. The transfer rule bars speculative flips, buyers can apply directly, and the all-in step-up is only 2-5x, so the relaxed C3 does not rescue it.

scored.name: WA pastoral/UCL renewable investigation licence + wind campaign
scored.one_line: Company holds a WA Land Administration Act s91 licence to investigate wind/solar over unallocated Crown land or pastoral leases at a fixed administrative fee (diversification leases follow later). It pays for a 12-month LiDAR/mast campaign and a constraints study, then sells the investigated area to hydrogen or large renewables developers. Caveat: WA increasingly releases large areas through an EOI process, which erodes the fixed-price advantage.
scored.unproven_right: WA LAA s91 investigative licence over UCL or pastoral Crown land at a fixed fee, convertible to a diversification lease
scored.proving_step: 12-18 month wind measurement campaign, heritage and environmental constraints study, transmission/port access screen; ~$400k-$1M; ~50-70% yield bankable data
scored.proven_buyer: Green hydrogen and gigawatt-scale renewables developers (InterContinental Energy, BP/Australian Renewable Energy Hub, Fortescue, Province Resources partners) and Pilbara/Mid West offtakers
scored.public_data: DPLH pastoral lease and UCL tenure records with scanned historic lease files; Aboriginal Heritage Inquiry System; BoM station archives; Western Power and NWIS network data; scanned 2010s wind farm proposal EPA referrals
scored.rough_step_up: Licence ~$1-5k; investigated 1 GW-scale area can command ~$2-10M premium (~10^3x on the right, ~3-10x on total spend)
scored.frame: Rung: 'investigated, consented renewable site' sold to a GW-scale developer. Discovery (finding where the wind is good) is maybe 20-30% of the work inside this rung. Most of the work is negotiating with native title holders: DPLH requires consent from the Prescribed Body Corporate / Common Law Holders before it will even grant the s91 licence. The rest is ministerial discretion, plus transmission and port access, which are relationship and infrastructure problems rather than signal-extraction problems. The physical step (a mast or LiDAR) is cheap. Buyers exist but have shrunk: BP left AREH in July 2025, and the hydrogen offtake thesis has weakened.
scored.step_up: The headline step-up only holds on the fee. Licence fee about $1-5k vs a $2-10M premium for an investigated GW area is ~10^3x, but that fee is not the real cost of the right. Real cost = fee + PBC consent negotiation (often equity or benefit-sharing) + the $0.4-1M campaign, so the uplift on capital at risk is ~3-10x (the candidate's own estimate). The premium is also not immediate: it depends on a developer committing, with no grid or offtake in hand. I found no transaction comps that confirm the $2-10M figure.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs ~$400k-1M and takes 12-18 months (the candidate's estimate; consistent with the ACEN/Yindjibarndi 1,000 km2 s91 licence being used for wind/solar monitoring masts). Base yield is 50-70%. The relaxed C3 accepts expensive proving with a moderate hit rate, but ML adds little. Wind resource across the Pilbara/Mid West is already modelled well by mesoscale reanalysis (ERA5, Global Wind Atlas). Sites usually fail on heritage, native title or grid, not on the wind. Plausible ML gain is ~1.1-1.3x on cost per bankable site.
scored.data: Mostly legible. Wind data is public and gridded (BoM, ERA5, Global Wind Atlas). The Aboriginal Heritage Inquiry System is a structured database. NWIS and Western Power network data are published. Scanned pastoral lease files and old EPA referrals give some illegible signal, but it is marginal, and incumbent developers (ACEN, CWP, InterContinental) already do this desk screening in-house.
scored.right_bought: Weak. An s91 licence is granted at the Minister's discretion and creates no estate, interest or exclusive possession. It can be amended or terminated by the Minister, and granting it requires prior consent from the native title PBC. The Traditional Owners can read the hope value and capture it through equity or benefit-sharing terms, so the price is not fixed regardless of hope value. The State is also moving to EOI releases (and SA uses competitive release areas), which auctions away the uplift. Transferability is unconfirmed and likely needs ministerial consent. A 2021 Liberal opposition statement (partisan) said only four companies held more than 25,000 km2, with about 90 applications queued, which suggests strategic allocation rather than cheap first-come rights.
scored.buyer: GW-scale renewables and green hydrogen/ammonia/iron developers (AREH, now run by InterContinental after BP's 2025 exit; Western Green Energy Hub; ACEN; Fortescue) and Pilbara miners decarbonising operations. These buyers are capitalised but have retreated since 2024-25.
scored.ladder: A ladder exists: consented site, then diversification lease and development approval, then build, own and operate generation, then green iron/ammonia or Pilbara mining offtake and transmission. That is a large path, but every rung above is capital-heavy construction where discovery is negligible.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right is not a cheap, fixed-price, transferable asset. An s91 licence is discretionary, non-exclusive and creates no interest in land. It cannot be granted without the native title holders' consent, and they (and the State, through EOI releases) capture the hope value. Meanwhile the 'discovery' (where wind and solar are good) is already legible in public gridded resource datasets, so ML has nothing illegible to unlock.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is expensive and a ladder exists. But the right is a discretionary licence that needs native title consent and is increasingly released by EOI. The wind signal is already legible, and hydrogen buyers have retreated, so the step-up on capital at risk is only ~3-10x.

scored.name: Queensland land-based prawn/aquaculture site approval
scored.one_line: ML over scanned EIS documents, discharge-licence decisions and the GBR water-quality record finds state-land parcels likely to receive a nutrient-neutral discharge approval. The company takes a fixed-rent state land lease or investigation permit inside or near an Aquaculture Development Area, pays for the EPBC and environmental authority approvals, and sells the approved site to a capitalised aquaculture operator. Approved sites near the Reef are very scarce, so they are valuable. Caveat: approval outcomes are partly written into the public register.
scored.unproven_right: Qld Land Act state land term lease / investigation permit at a fixed administrative rent, plus a pending environmental authority (ERA 38) application
scored.proving_step: Environmental baseline, nutrient-offset design, EPBC referral and state environmental authority; ~$1-3M over 2-3 years; ~30-50% approved
scored.proven_buyer: Large aquaculture operators (Tassal/Cooke, Pacific Reef Fisheries, Australian Prawn Farms, Mainstream) and agri-infrastructure funds
scored.public_data: Scanned Qld DES environmental authority decisions and EIS documents; EPBC referral archive; Qld Aquaculture Development Area mapping; GBR Marine Monitoring Program water quality; state land tenure records
scored.rough_step_up: Lease/permit ~$5-20k/yr; approved 100+ ha prawn site ~$10-30M (~10^3x on the right, ~5-10x on total spend)
scored.frame: The rung is 'an approved land-based prawn site'. Discovery (picking the site) is perhaps 20-30% of the work at most. Most of the cost and risk sits in the proving step: environmental baselines, engineering a nutrient-offset or nil-net-discharge design, EPBC and ERA approvals, and negotiating politically with the Department, GBRMPA and NGOs. That step is neither trivial nor abstracted; it is bespoke engineering plus regulatory negotiation, close to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. The state has already done the coarse discovery by publishing 8 Aquaculture Development Areas pre-screened as suitable (Townsville, Whitsunday, Mackay, Rockhampton, Gladstone, Hinchinbrook). Capitalised buyers exist (Tassal/Cooke, Mainstream, ag funds), but they tend to buy land in ADAs and run approvals themselves; Tassal at Exmoor Station in the Mackay ADA did exactly that. A market for pre-approved greenfield sites as a standalone rung is thin.
scored.step_up: The right itself might show ~10^3x (a $5-20k/yr lease against a claimed $10-30M approved site), but this is misleading. The asset you sell is land plus approval, and you have to put in $1-3M of approval spend plus land or lease costs, so the step-up on capital is ~3-10x at best. The $10-30M exit value is unverified. Comparables are small: Pacific Reef's 1,221 ha operating business sold in 2021 at an undisclosed price, operating Qld prawn farms are listed from ~A$1M upward (realcommercial/bsale listings), and greenfield ADA land trades near rural value. No source shows approved-but-unbuilt sites selling at a 10^3x premium. Score 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is clearly expensive: ~$1-3M over 2-3+ years (candidate estimate, consistent with Guthalungra running 2001 to 2015 for its GBRMPA discharge permit). The candidate puts the base approval rate at ~30-50%. Under relaxed C3 that is acceptable, but the ML lift is weak. Approval depends mostly on the conditions imposed (Guthalungra got 'nil net discharge', which industry says pond farms cannot technically meet in the dry tropics) and on whether the proponent can buy nutrient offsets. That is engineering, politics and offset economics, not a hidden signal in the documents. ADAs already pre-screen sites, so ML might pick somewhat better parcels and offset partners, maybe ~1.2-1.5x on cost per approved site. Score 3.
scored.data: Legibility is mixed. The EIS documents and older EPBC referral PDFs are unstructured, but outcomes are legible. EPBC decisions and their conditions are published in the referral register, Qld environmental authorities and their conditions are in the DES public register, ADAs are mapped publicly, and MMP water-quality data is already structured. The candidate itself concedes approval outcomes are partly in the register. Little latent signal is left that incumbents (consultants, Tassal and the like) can't already read.
scored.right_bought: This is weak. Most ADA land is freehold (Exmoor was a private cattle station), so you buy it at market from rural owners, and the ADA designation already advertises its hope value. Unallocated Qld state land under the Land Act is usually offered by competitive tender or auction, or it needs a purpose and an 'appropriate use' assessment with rent set on valuation. It is not handed out first-come at a fixed admin rent. A resource allocation authority for tidal land confers no tenure and can't be used without a development approval. Transfer of state leases needs Ministerial consent. Nothing confirms a fixed-price right the state won't reprice.
scored.buyer: Tassal/Cooke, Mainstream Aquaculture, Australian Prawn Farms, Pacific Reef Fisheries and agri-infrastructure funds. They are capitalised, but they have usually acquired land and run approvals in-house rather than buying pre-approved greenfield sites at a premium.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are pond construction, hatchery and broodstock, grow-out, processing and branded export. The ladder exists, but every rung is capital-heavy, biologically risky and low-margin, and the Australian farmed prawn market is roughly A$100-200M a year in production value. That makes a large company possible, but not a trillion-dollar path. Score 2.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving here is a bespoke engineering and political job, not discovery: designing and negotiating a nutrient-neutral discharge solution. The state has already done the site discovery through its published Aquaculture Development Areas. So ML has no illegible signal to exploit, the land is bought at market prices that already reflect ADA hope value, and an approval returns only ~3-10x on the capital spent.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 only lifts the hit-rate lever to a moderate 3. Everything else fails the rubric: pre-mapped ADAs, approval outcomes in public registers, market-priced land and engineering-heavy proving give a ~5x return on capital, not 10^4.

scored.name: Unbuildable tax-forfeit lots proven buildable (septic, wetland and setback relief)
scored.one_line: Buy the many 'unbuildable' substandard lots that counties sell at fixed minimum or side-lot prices. Use ML to predict which ones actually pass a septic perc test, a wetland delineation (finding no jurisdictional wetland) and a setback variance, then prove buildability and sell permit-ready lots to builders.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to a substandard tax-forfeited lot sold at a statutory minimum (often $100-1,500), usually priced as if unbuildable.
scored.proving_step: A soil perc test and septic design approval, a professional wetland delineation with Army Corps or state jurisdictional determination, and a variance hearing, giving a building-permit-ready status. Per lot this is only about $10-25k but takes 6-18 months. Batching 5-10 lots per program reaches about $50k+, with a 40-60% hit rate per lot.
scored.proven_buyer: Spec homebuilders, manufactured-home dealers and lake-lot buyers. Capitalisation is moderate; these buyers are less strong than the others on this list.
scored.public_data: NRCS SSURGO soils, LiDAR elevation, the National Wetlands Inventory, scanned historic septic permits and perc logs at county health departments, variance decision minutes, and FEMA flood maps.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-30x (a $500-2k lot becomes a $20-60k permit-ready lot). C3 is marginal because the per-attempt cost is below $50k unless batched.
scored.frame: The rung is 'tax-forfeit lot proven permit-ready'. Prediction (soils, wetlands, setbacks) is maybe 50-60% of the work. The rest is not trivial or abstracted: perc and septic design, wetland delineation and jurisdictional determination, and above all a discretionary variance hearing that depends on neighbours and local politics. ML cannot predict that last step well. Buyers are spec builders and lake-lot buyers. They do buy permit-ready lots, but they are thinly capitalised and local. The frame exists but is weaker than the 80%+ discovery-share test.
scored.step_up: About 10-30x on paper ($500-2k to $20-60k per the candidate). Netting out the $10-25k proving cost and holding time leaves about 2-5x on capital deployed. This is far from 10^3-10^4. Proven lots are priced in local market comps, so the step-up is visible to everyone.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate the candidate gives is 40-60% per lot, and proving costs about $10-25k and takes 6-18 months per lot (candidate estimates; perc tests and delineations usually run $1-5k each, and the variance is the slow part). Each attempt is below the ~$50k bar. Batching 5-10 lots does not make one attempt expensive; it only adds up spending. ML could plausibly lift picks 1.5x on soils and wetlands, but cannot lift the variance outcome. The relaxed C3 removes the low-hit-rate penalty, but the expensive-proving leg is still not met, so the score is 2.
scored.data: Mixed. SSURGO soils, LiDAR, NWI and FEMA flood maps are legible, free and already used by every county planner and builder. Scanned septic permits, perc logs and variance minutes are the genuinely illegible edge. The outcome is partly written into legible fields: counties already label parcels 'unbuildable' or 'substandard' on sale lists, and zoning lot-area and width minimums are coded. Little hidden outcome remains to extract.
scored.right_bought: Weak. In Minnesota, counties route small 'unbuildable' parcels to adjoiner-only private sales (Renville County). Cities condition those releases on legally combining the parcel with the adjoining property (Orono resolution), so an outside buyer cannot get them, and once merged they cannot be resold as separate building lots. Parcels that do go to public sale are auctioned 'to the highest bidder' from a minimum bid. After Tyler v. Hennepin, states are moving to mandatory public auctions (MN HF 4822, Illinois HB 4537) and appraisal at fair market value (Oregon), so local builders and neighbours will bid up any lot with visible hope value. Fee title is transferable when bought at public auction, but the cheap fixed-price channel mostly is not open to outsiders. Merger doctrine and substandard-lot rules add more clawback risk.
scored.buyer: Spec homebuilders, manufactured-home dealers and lake-lot end users. They are fragmented, local, moderately to thinly capitalised and price-sensitive. No deep-pocketed buyer like a mine developer is in for $40k/ha.
scored.ladder: Lot to permit-ready lot, then to vertical construction, then to scattered-site build-to-rent or a homebuilder. These rungs exist, but they lead into commodity homebuilding where discovery is not the bottleneck. The market is large, but there is no compounding discovery moat, and scattered infill lots do not aggregate into a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The cheap right is not actually buyable by an outsider at a fixed price. Substandard 'unbuildable' tax-forfeit lots are routed to adjoiner-only sales with mandatory combination into the neighbour's parcel. Lots that look buildable go to competitive public auction, which post-Tyler reforms are strengthening. On top of that, the gating proving step, a discretionary variance, is political rather than predictable, and each attempt is cheap, under $50k.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up is modest (10-30x gross, about 2-5x net) and proving is cheap and discretionary. The 'unbuildable' lots are mostly sold only to adjoiners with forced merger, or auctioned to the highest bidder, so the cheap transferable right that the thesis needs mostly does not exist.

scored.name: New-corridor microwave latency networks (FCC Part 101 first-come, fixed-fee licences)
scored.one_line: Use ML over terrain, structures and existing licences to find the near-geodesic microwave path on a newly valuable trading corridor, for example NJ/Chicago to the Dallas Texas Stock Exchange. Lock it up with Part 101 prior coordination notices and fixed-fee licences plus tower lease options, prove end-to-end latency, and sell the path to an HFT firm. Honest view: C1 3, C2 4, C3 4, C4 2, C5 2. ULS is structured, so the edge sits in path optimisation more than in illegible data.
scored.unproven_right: FCC Part 101 point-to-point licences (first-come, coordinated, with filing fees of a few hundred dollars per link) plus tower space lease options, assignable
scored.proving_step: Path engineering and coordination, tower leases, a temporary link build and a measured latency and availability test. Cost is roughly $0.5-3M and 6-12 months. A shortest-path claim succeeds maybe 40-60% of the time against competing filers.
scored.proven_buyer: HFT and latency network firms (Jump, Citadel Securities, Virtu, McKay Brothers, Vigilant Global/Go West)
scored.public_data: FCC ULS Part 101 licence and PCN data (huge), FCC ASR, state DOT and utility tower records, the USGS 3DEP and LiDAR terrain, and FAA obstruction data
scored.rough_step_up: About $1M of licences, options and test spend becomes a $10-50M path value to an HFT buyer when it is the fastest route: ~10-50x
scored.frame: The rung is a licensed, tower-optioned and latency-proven microwave path, sold to an HFT firm. Discovery (path finding) is perhaps 20-30% of that work. The rest is physical and commercial: tower leases, radios, frequency coordination, a test build, and holding off competing filers. The physical step is the bulk of the work, not a trivial one, so this fails the 80% test. The buyer is real and well capitalised: HFT firms and latency-network operators.
scored.step_up: Using the candidate's own figures, about $1M of licences, options and test spend becomes a $10-50M path, roughly 10-50x. No disclosed sale prices could be found: TMX/StrikeNet, CFN and the McKay-Tower Capital stake all closed at undisclosed prices. The Chicago-NJ race cost more than $500M in total across 6-15 networks (arXiv 1302.5966). That suggests a winning path is worth tens of millions, which is the 10-100x band, not 10^3 or more. The value is also winner-take-all: second place is worth close to zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt is expensive, about $0.5-3M and 6-12 months, so the proving-cost leg passes. The stated base hit rate is 40-60% against competing filers. The ML lever is weak, though. Finding the near-geodesic path over towers, terrain and Fresnel clearance is a solved shortest-path problem that incumbent RF engineers (McKay, Jump, Vigilant) already run with standard tools. Win-or-lose depends on filing speed and tower access, not prediction. A plausible ML gain is about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven path.
scored.data: The data is legible. ULS Part 101 licence and prior coordination notice (PCN) records, FAA/ASR tower data and 3DEP terrain are all structured and machine-readable. Academics have already reconstructed every Chicago-NJ HFT network from ULS (Laughlin; the IMC 2020 paper). Incumbents extract this data intensively, and coordinates and frequencies are written in clear fields, so there is no illegibility edge.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought cheaply from naive owners. Part 101 licences are free, first-come and coordinated (a fixed filing fee of a few hundred dollars, no auction and no clawback). The fixed price ignores hope value, but the competing filers are the most sophisticated latency buyers in the world, who watch PCNs in real time. Licences can be assigned with FCC consent, so they are transferable. Tower space comes from American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA and others, who price it commercially and are not owners blind to its value. The candidate's own honest view also gives C4 a 2.
scored.buyer: HFT firms and latency-network operators: Jump, Citadel Securities, Virtu, McKay Brothers, Vigilant/Go West, plus exchange groups such as TMX, which bought StrikeNet. They are well capitalised, but they also build in-house, so they compete with the startup as well as buying from it.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are limited: operate the network, sell bandwidth (as McKay does), and add more corridors or transoceanic shortwave. Exchange corridors are few and largely saturated. Revenue is capped by HFT latency budgets (low billions industry-wide), not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The new-corridor premise is false, and there is no hidden edge. TXSE runs its primary matching engine at Equinix NY6 in Secaucus, NJ, and uses Dallas only for disaster recovery, so no NJ/Chicago-Dallas latency arbitrage exists. More generally, Part 101 rights are first-come and free, the data (ULS) is fully legible, and incumbent HFT engineers already solve the path problem. ML adds almost nothing over standard shortest-path tools in a race decided by filing speed and tower access.
scored.one_line_reason: Path finding is a solved, legible problem on structured ULS data, rights are first-come rather than bought from owners who cannot read the data, the build dominates the work, and the flagship Dallas corridor does not exist because TXSE's primary engine is in Secaucus.

scored.name: BC shellfish tenure + sanitary classification
scored.one_line: ML over scanned CSSP shoreline sanitary surveys, oceanographic data and old tenure files picks foreshore sites likely to pass harvest-area classification. The company files a fixed-rent Land Act aquaculture licence of occupation and the DFO licence, pays for the sanitary classification and growout trials, then sells the approved, producing tenure to established growers. Smaller step-up and smaller ladder.
scored.unproven_right: BC Land Act aquaculture licence of occupation (fixed schedule rent) plus a federal DFO shellfish aquaculture licence, transferable with approval
scored.proving_step: CSSP sanitary/water-quality classification sampling, 1-2 year growout trial, siting/navigation review; ~$100-300k and 2-3 years; ~40-60% pass
scored.proven_buyer: Established shellfish growers and integrated seafood firms (Taylor Shellfish BC, Mac's Oysters, Indigenous-owned aquaculture companies)
scored.public_data: CSSP sanitary survey reports (scanned PDFs); DFO aquaculture licence registry; BC tenure archive incl. abandoned shellfish tenures; DFO oceanographic and satellite SST/chlorophyll archives
scored.rough_step_up: Tenure ~$1-5k; proven, classified, producing tenure ~$100k-1M (~10^2x on the right, ~2-4x on total spend)
scored.frame: The rung is a classified tenure that is producing shellfish. Discovery (picking the site) is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of it is physical and procedural: 1-2 years of growout with gear and seed, the harmonized DFO/Transport Canada/BC application with navigation review, First Nations consultation, and local opposition (for example the Islands Trust commenting on licences). The physical step is not trivial or abstracted. The buyers are small family growers, plus a few larger players such as Taylor Shellfish and some Indigenous-owned companies. That is a thinly capitalised buyer pool, not mine-developer money.
scored.step_up: An unproven tenure costs about $1-5k in application fees and fixed rent. BCSGA classified listings ask much more for operating farms: Deep Bay 15.74 ha at $1.025M (about $65k/ha), Kilo Seafarm in Malaspina Inlet 4.85 ha at $680k (about $140k/ha), and two Sechelt tenures totalling about 7.3 ha at $180k (about $25k/ha). These are asking prices, not sales, and they include gear, stock, upland property and goodwill. Against the right alone the step-up is about 10^2x. Against the $100-300k actually spent proving it, it is only about 1-4x, and the value comes 2-3 years later, not immediately.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $100-300k and takes 2-3 years per site (candidate estimate; growout gear, seed, labour and the application process). That clears the "expensive" bar under the relaxed C3. The ML lever is weak, though. ECCC/DFO already publish the CSSP harvest-area classification (Approved / Conditionally Approved / Restricted / Prohibited) as open GIS polygons. A grower can screen sites against that map for free, so ML adds perhaps 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven site, mainly through growth and temperature/chlorophyll modelling. The 40-60% base pass rate is the candidate's estimate; I found no source for it.
scored.data: This fails the central C4 test. The outcome is already written into a legible public field: ECCC's Shellfish Water Classification Program polygons (open.canada.ca, ArcGIS REST, with daily closure updates through BCCDC). The sanitary surveys are run by ECCC on the government's side, and their result is exactly that classification layer, so the scanned survey PDFs add little beyond it. Oceanographic, SST and chlorophyll data are legible and widely used. There is some residual signal in the abandoned-tenure archives, but it is thin.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought from owners who cannot read the data. It is applied for from the Crown first-come, at fixed schedule rent with no auction. That means no hope-value discount is being captured from anyone; it is a cheap permit, which makes it easy to copy. Assignment needs approval from both BC (Land Act) and DFO, so transfer is possible but discretionary. Approval is also gated by First Nations consultation and local opposition, which ML cannot predict from the data. There is no clawback, but the regulators' discretion caps how fast the company can scale.
scored.buyer: Established BC shellfish growers. They are mostly small operators (BCSGA classifieds show retirement sales at $180k-1M), plus a few larger buyers such as Taylor Shellfish and Indigenous-owned aquaculture companies. The pool is small and capital-limited, and many buyers would sooner apply for their own tenure cheaply.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is short and small: hatchery and seed, processing and depuration, and distribution. BC farmed shellfish is a niche market of tens of millions of dollars a year at the farm gate, with about 486 licensed facilities in 2020. Even the whole chain is far from a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving outcome (sanitary harvest-area classification) is already published as an open, legible government GIS layer. The right itself is a cheap first-come Crown permit, not something bought below hope value. So ML has no information edge, and no step-up is captured from owners who cannot read the data.
scored.one_line_reason: Weak (8/25). The sanitary classification is already in public open-data polygons, proving is mostly physical growout and permitting, the step-up on actual spend is only 1-4x, and the buyers and the ladder are small.

scored.name: Reclamation Lease of Power Privilege conduit and canal hydro
scored.one_line: Use ML over scanned USBR canal, drop and dam operating records to find conduit drops with firm head and flow. Apply for USBR Lease of Power Privilege preliminary leases (an administrative process with fixed charges, not an auction) on BLM/USBR land. Pay for feasibility and an interconnection study. Sell the de-risked lease to a small-hydro IPP or the local irrigation district's power partner.
scored.unproven_right: USBR LOPP preliminary lease (exclusive study priority) plus associated BLM ROW at schedule rent
scored.proving_step: About $100-300k and 1-2 years: flow and head measurement, turbine design, interconnection study. About 50% are feasible.
scored.proven_buyer: Small hydro IPPs and infrastructure funds; utilities buying firm renewable capacity
scored.public_data: USBR HydroData and scanned project histories, USBR Hydropower Resource Assessment at existing reclamation facilities (2011/2012), USBR canal operating records, USGS NWIS gauges, FERC eLibrary conduit exemptions
scored.rough_step_up: About $50k becomes $1-5M, roughly 20-100x. The ML edge is moderate because USBR already published a site-level assessment, which partly legibilises the outcome. The ladder is short.
scored.frame: The rung is a development-ready LOPP conduit lease (preliminary lease plus feasibility and interconnection study), sold to a small-hydro IPP. Discovery is only about 30-50% of the work in this rung, because head and flow are mostly known from USBR gauges, the 2011/2012 Hydropower Resource Assessment and canal records. The rest is NEPA, interconnection, turbine design and contract negotiation, all done under a 15-month deadline to sign the LOPP. The build itself (powerhouse and turbine, roughly $3-6k/kW) is a large, bespoke physical step that the buyer has to take on. There are buyers, but they are small and few, and the projects are under 5 MW.
scored.step_up: I found no market comps. My estimate: the unproven right costs only application and study fees, but its value is held down by the irrigation district's first-refusal right. A proven, development-ready lease for a sub-5 MW conduit project probably sells for about $50-250k/MW, so a typical 0.5-2 MW site is worth $100k-$1M. Against $100-300k sunk in proving, that is about 3-10x on the capital spent. The candidate's 20-100x counts from fees alone. It also does not account for the fact that the buyer still has to build the plant to realise most of the value. The LOPP term is capped at 40 years, and Reclamation charges an annual fee of a few mills/kWh (FAC 04-08; older documents cite 2 mills/kWh).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $100-300k and 1-2 years per site (candidate estimate; consistent with the 15-month preliminary-lease window for conduits under FAC 04-08). The base feasibility rate is about 50%. Proving is expensive enough to pass the relaxed C3 cost test. But ML lift is weak: USBR has already screened sites and published estimated kW and energy in its 2011/2012 resource assessments, and NWIS and HydroData flows are digital. Realistically ML gives about 1.1-1.3x on cost per proven asset, mainly by reading scanned canal records to estimate seasonal flow firmness. The relaxed C3 removes the failure-rate penalty, but it cannot create a lift that the published assessment has already taken.
scored.data: The data is only partly illegible. Scanned project histories and canal operating records exist, but the outcome (candidate site, head, flow, estimated MW) is already written into legible public documents: USBR's site-level Hydropower Resource Assessment (2011) and its conduit assessment (2012), USGS NWIS gauges, and FERC conduit exemption filings. This is the pattern prior hunts flagged, where the regulator has already written down the answer.
scored.right_bought:
The right is not cheaply buyable by an outsider. The charges are fixed and administrative, but access is not open first-come.
(1) For conduits under P.L. 113-24, Reclamation must first offer the LOPP to the irrigation district or water users' association that operates the conduit or receives water from it. They have 60 days to accept and 150 days to submit a proposal, and Reclamation does not solicit anyone else in that time.
(2) Dams and reservoirs go through a competitive solicitation with scoring criteria.
(3) The 1939 Act gives public "preference entities" a chance to match a superior proposal from a non-preference entity.
(4) The district can also get a reduced charge (for example 2 mills/kWh on Central Utah transferred works), so the uplift tends to go to the district.
(5) A preliminary lease is a time-limited (15-month) exclusive study priority. I found no free-assignment provision, so transfer most likely needs Reclamation approval.
Net effect: the irrigation district that "cannot read the data" has a statutory first-refusal right rather than being a seller you can bargain with, and the government does not sell the hope value at a fixed price to all comers.
scored.buyer: Small-hydro IPPs (for example Rye Development and Natel-type developers), irrigation districts' power partners, and a few infrastructure funds. Utilities buy the PPA, not the lease. The pool is thin and the projects are small, under 5 MW.
scored.ladder: Short. The rungs are lease, then build and own small conduit hydro, then possibly a portfolio of sub-5 MW plants. The total addressable resource on Reclamation conduits is a few hundred MW nationally. That gives no path to a very large company, and climbing means taking on construction risk, which is the hard part.
scored.fatal_flaw: The rights cannot be bought cheaply on an information edge. Under P.L. 113-24, conduit leases go first to the irrigation district that operates or receives water from the conduit, with a 60-day accept and 150-day proposal window and no outside solicitation in that time. Dam sites are competitively solicited, and public preference entities can match a better proposal. On top of that, USBR's own site-level resource assessments already make the outcome legible, so ML adds little.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 does not save it. Proving is expensive, but ML lift is small because USBR already published site-level assessments. The irrigation district's first-refusal right and competitive solicitation block cheap acquisition of the right. The step-up is about 3-10x on proving capital, and the build is a heavy physical step, with a ladder capped at a few hundred MW.
sources: https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/web/20161226091602/https:/www.usbr.gov/power/LOPP/PL 113-24 Revision/Reserved Conduit - Request through Preliminary Lease.pdf

scored.name: Tax-foreclosed buildings proven eligible for historic tax credits
scored.one_line: Buy vacant tax-foreclosed or land-bank buildings at the fixed minimum bid or land-bank schedule price. Use ML over scanned historic surveys and Sanborn maps to pick the buildings likely to be eligible for the National Register. Get NPS Part 1 certification (and state listing), then sell the certified shell to a historic tax credit developer. Certification unlocks the 20% federal credit plus state credits (up to 25-45% combined in MO, OH, GA, MI and others).
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to a tax-defaulted or land-bank building sold at a statutory minimum or a fixed side-lot or structure price (Detroit, Cleveland/Cuyahoga, St. Louis LRA, Philadelphia land bank, Ohio county land banks). The price ignores eligibility for credit-bearing rehab.
scored.proving_step: An architectural historian's nomination or Part 1 (Evaluation of Significance) filing plus a SHPO determination. Cost is about $30-80k with condition and stabilisation docs, over 6-18 months. Approval runs about 40-70% for candidates screened inside or next to districts.
scored.proven_buyer: Historic tax credit syndicators and developers (bank-backed tax-equity investors such as US Bancorp CDC and regional developers), and opportunity zone funds.
scored.public_data: Scanned state historic resource survey forms, NRHP nomination PDFs and district boundaries, Sanborn fire insurance maps (Library of Congress), county assessor build-year records, land-bank inventories, and street-view imagery.
scored.rough_step_up: About 10-50x on the acquisition price (a $2-10k shell becomes a $100-300k credit-eligible project site). The step-up comes from the credit value the developer can monetise on a $2-10M rehab.
scored.frame: The pitched rung is buying a shell and getting it historically certified, then selling it. That is not a rung a capitalised buyer pays a premium for. The credit is 20% of qualified rehabilitation expenditures the developer actually spends, so its value comes from the $2-10M rehab and not from the certification. Inside the rung, discovery (does it qualify?) is maybe 30-50% of the effort. The rest is stabilisation, holding costs, taxes and liability on a vacant shell, and getting through land-bank compliance. The physical step (rehab) is the whole value-creating act, and it sits with the buyer. Syndicators such as US Bancorp CDC buy credits from developers, not certified shells.
scored.step_up: The pitch claims 10-50x ($2-10k becomes $100-300k), but that is the credit value spread across the whole project, not the land price. The credit exists to close the gap between rehab cost and post-rehab value, and in weak markets like Detroit, St. Louis and Cleveland that gap often uses up the whole credit. A developer therefore pays little extra for a certified shell. Realistic uplift is maybe 1.5-5x on a tiny base ($5k becomes $10-25k), i.e. a few thousand to tens of thousands of dollars per asset. I found no comparable sales separating certified from uncertified shells; this is a judgement.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is genuinely 40-70% for screened buildings in or next to districts, so the relaxed C3 does not penalise it. But proving is cheap and fast. NPS allows 30 days for Part 1 review after the state preservation office's own 30-day review (NPS/state guidance). A buildings-only Part 1 written by a consultant typically costs about $5-20k. That is my estimate, and the search found no fee data. For a building already in a listed district, contributing status is often already written down. The $30-80k / 6-18 month figure applies only to a full individual National Register nomination. So the step is below the $50k / multi-year bar, and ML's gain on cost per proven asset is small next to holding, stabilisation and compliance costs.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: scanned state survey forms, Sanborn maps and old nomination PDFs. But the outcome is often already legible. National Register district nominations list contributing and non-contributing resources, many states publish GIS layers of survey and eligibility determinations, and local historic district maps are public. The illegible-signal edge only holds for not-yet-surveyed individually eligible buildings, a thin slice. Developers and preservation consultants already screen this by hand cheaply.
scored.right_bought: The price is fixed but the right comes with strings. Land banks (Detroit Land Bank Authority, Cuyahoga, St. Louis Land Reutilization Authority, Philadelphia) sell at schedule prices but tie the sale to end-use and rehab conditions. The Detroit Land Bank keeps an interest on title until it decides, in its sole discretion, that the rehab is done, and has repossessed 1,169 properties for noncompliance in three years. That is effectively a clawback of speculative flipping, and it makes the unrehabbed right hard to transfer. Tax-foreclosure sales outside land banks are mostly auctions, which price in hope value. So the cheap fixed price exists only where resale is restricted.
scored.buyer: Historic tax credit developers (and, indirectly, syndicators and tax-equity investors such as US Bancorp CDC, plus opportunity zone funds). They are capitalised but buy credits from developers, not certified shells. A developer can file Part 1 itself for a few thousand dollars, so certification adds little value for them to pay for.
scored.ladder: Certified-shell sales could lead to historic tax credit development, then syndication, then owning and operating the property. Each rung is a fragmented, local, low-margin real-estate business with heavy construction risk. There is a path to a mid-sized real-estate developer, not a trillion-dollar vertical chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value step-up is captured by the rehab, not by certification. The credit equals 20% of the developer's own spending, Part 1 is cheap (roughly $5-20k, about 60 days) and the developer can file it themselves, and land banks hold rehab-or-repossess interests on title that block flipping an unrehabbed certified shell. There is no expensive proving step that creates a large, sellable jump in value.
scored.one_line_reason: Certification is cheap, fast and doable by the buyer. The credit's value depends on the buyer's rehab spending, not on the shell. Land-bank reverter clauses block the flip, so the step-up is a few x on a tiny base and ML has little to improve.

scored.name: Chilean small-scale seaweed and mussel aquaculture concessions in designated AAA zones
scored.one_line: Apply for Subpesca/Sernapesca aquaculture concessions inside designated Áreas Apropiadas para la Acuicultura (AAA) at fixed fees. ML picks sites using scanned INFA environmental reports, satellite chlorophyll/SST and red-tide closure history. Run the technical project (CPS) and pilot culture to prove productivity and INFA compliance, then sell the operating concession to Chilean mussel and seaweed processors.
scored.unproven_right: A concesión de acuicultura for mussels or seaweed (not salmon, which is under moratorium). It is granted administratively in AAA zones with a fixed annual patente per hectare, and is transferable and mortgageable under the LGPA.
scored.proving_step: A technical-environmental baseline (CPS), the RCA where required, and one to two pilot growing seasons with documented yield and a clean INFA. Roughly $80-300k and 2-3 years. Perhaps 40-60% of sites prove productive. Failures come from red tide, low seed set, or grants that never complete; ML can lift the hit rate about 1.5-2x.
scored.proven_buyer: Integrated mussel exporters (St Andrews, Camanchaca and others in Chiloé) and alginate/carrageenan buyers. They pay going-concern prices for productive, compliant concessions.
scored.public_data: Subpesca concession registry and AAA maps. Sernapesca INFA reports (scanned PDFs). IFOP red-tide (HAB) monitoring bulletins. MODIS/Sentinel-3 ocean colour. SHOA charts.
scored.rough_step_up: Fees and application cost about $5-20k. A productive mussel concession trades at roughly $20-60k/ha, about $0.5-3M per site. That is ~50-200x on the right and ~3-8x on all-in. The ladder is moderate: processing, then branded export, then a seafood platform.
scored.frame: The rung would be a granted, proven-productive mussel or seaweed concession. Discovery (picking the site) is maybe 20-30% of the work inside that rung. Most of the work is regulatory: CPS, CIA/RCA, Subpesca, then Marina/SSFFAA, then Contraloría, often years of it. The rest is physical. You have to set longlines, collect seed and grow mussels for 12-18 months to show yield. That is running a farm, not a cheap drill hole. Buyers do exist, but they buy operating farms at modest multiples.
scored.step_up: I found no published per-hectare transfer prices. The candidate's own figures put the right (fees plus application) at about $5-20k and a productive site at $0.5-3M. The real cost basis is all-in, though: $80-300k plus years of farming capex. On that basis the uplift is about 3-8x, not 10^3. It is a going-concern valuation of a low-margin commodity farm. Mussel prices in Chile are depressed, and plenty of idle granted concessions already exist, which caps what a buyer will pay.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $80-300k and 2-3 years per site (candidate estimate), and the regulatory path often runs longer. Industry reporting says even a simple technical-project modification takes 9-12 months instead of 1-2 (Ex-Ante 2023). Base success is claimed at 40-60%. Expense alone would qualify under the relaxed C3, but the lift is doubtful. Productive mussel waters (Reloncaví, Chiloé interior seas) are long mapped, and red-tide closures are published by zone. ML over chlorophyll/SST gives maybe 1.1-1.3x, not 1.5-2x. The main failure modes are grants that never complete and Ley Lafkenche/ECMPO suspensions, and ML cannot predict those. Per Ex-Ante 2024, more than a third of pending concessions are suspended, about 75% of them in Los Lagos.
scored.data: Partly illegible: INFA reports are scanned PDFs and IFOP bulletins are scattered. But the outcome is largely written down already in legible form. Sernapesca keeps harvest and production declarations by concession (SIAC), and INFA results (aerobic/anaerobic status) go into the regulator's records. Red-tide closure areas are published. Incumbents in Chiloé know these waters well. The concession registry and AAA maps are open GIS layers.
scored.right_bought: It is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. New concessions are administrative applications at fixed fees inside AAA zones. Since there is no auction, the state does not capture hope value, and granted concessions are transferable and mortgageable under the LGPA. But Subpesca has declared many AAA areas in Los Lagos/Aysén "no disponibles", and ECMPO claims freeze new applications over millions of hectares (about 3.8M ha pending). The real cheap path is buying idle granted concessions from small holders. Those sellers know their own production history, and the caducidad-for-non-operation rules push them to sell or lose the concession, not to give it away mispriced. Weak information asymmetry.
scored.buyer: Integrated mussel exporters such as St Andrews, Camanchaca, Blumar mussel units, Orizon and Chiloé processors, plus alginate/carrageenan buyers. They are capitalised, but they are buying commodity farms in a market with idle capacity.
scored.ladder: Moderate: farm, then processing plant, then branded export, then a seafood platform. The Chilean mussel export industry is roughly $250-300M/yr, so the ceiling is a mid-sized seafood company, nowhere near the trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving means actually running an aquaculture farm for 1-2 seasons through a multi-year, Lafkenche-suspendable permit process. The payoff is a 3-8x going-concern multiple on a commodity farm, not a 10^3-10^4 step-up. On top of that, productivity is already legible in Sernapesca harvest and INFA records, and incumbents know the productive waters well.
scored.one_line_reason: Physical farming and regulatory delay dominate the rung, the step-up is only about 3-8x all-in, the outcome is already in Sernapesca records, and site-selection ML adds little where the productive waters are long known. The relaxed C3 does not rescue it.

scored.name: State submerged-land leases for subsea cable landings and seawater-cooled compute
scored.one_line: Company applies for sovereign submerged land easements at schedule rents from state land commissions (e.g. CA SLC and coastal states that lease at administrative rates) for nearshore cable-landing or cooling-intake corridors. It proves the corridor with a marine geophysical and benthic survey and sells it to a cable consortium or coastal data-centre developer.
scored.unproven_right: State submerged lands lease or easement application at a fixed or formula rent per linear foot or acre
scored.proving_step: Multibeam, sub-bottom and benthic habitat surveys plus a permitting fatal-flaw review, about $300k-$1M. Maybe 40-60% of ML-picked corridors survive.
scored.proven_buyer: Subsea cable consortia (hyperscaler-led) and coastal data-centre developers
scored.public_data: Scanned state lands commission staff reports, NOAA bathymetry and sediment data, old outfall and pipeline permits, and the reasons in coastal commission files for denied projects
scored.rough_step_up: Roughly 10-100x on rent cost, but buyers are few and permitting is political, so this is a speculative edge case.
scored.frame: The rung would be "permitted nearshore cable-landing or cooling corridor". Proving it is mostly physical and regulatory work, not discovery: about $300k-1M of marine geophysical, benthic and archaeological survey, then a CEQA Mitigated Negative Declaration or EIR, Coastal Commission, Army Corps and NOAA consults, and a beach-manhole/landing-site deal onshore. Finding the corridor is perhaps 20-30% of the work. Hardly anyone buys a corridor alone: consortia buy a fully permitted landing (landing station plus beach manhole plus route), and specialists like RTI Infrastructure already develop those themselves.
scored.step_up: Rent is set by formula and is small. CA SLC regulation 2 CCR 2003 charges $0.05 per diameter-inch per lineal foot, or uses comparables. The San Leandro/Bandwidth fiber lease set $5.00 per linear foot, which comes to $35,520/yr for 7,104 ft. Other SLC fiber leases (AT&T Montana de Oro, GT Landing) run about $96k-115k/yr. A permitted corridor might command a few $M premium from a buyer, against roughly $0.5-2M spent on survey and permitting. That is a 2-10x step-up on capital at risk, not 10^3-10^4. The 'near-zero to huge' framing only holds against the rent line, which is not the cost of proving.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive (about $300k-1M in surveys plus 1-3 years of CEQA and coastal permitting), so the expense leg of the relaxed C3 passes.
