The base survival rate is plausibly 40-60% (candidate's estimate; no source found). ML-driven pre-screening of bathymetry, sediment data and prior denial reasons could add perhaps 1.1-1.3x. Cable route engineers already run desktop studies (DTS) on the same legible NOAA and permit data, so the lift over the incumbent process is small. The binding constraints are political and onshore (beach access, landing station land, local opposition), and screening does not predict those well.
scored.data: The data is partly public and mostly legible. NOAA multibeam bathymetry and sediment data are already structured and used by every route surveyor. SLC staff reports and Coastal Commission files are searchable PDFs, and they state the outcome outright (lease approved, MND adopted, mitigation conditions), so regulators already write the answer in. Older outfall and pipeline permits are scattered and offer modest illegibility value. Incumbent cable route-survey firms (Fugro, EGS, Ocean Specialists) already compile all of this in standard desktop studies.
scored.right_bought: The right cannot be bought cheaply ahead of proving. The SLC General Lease – Right-of-Way Use issues only to a defined project after CEQA review, with the SLC as lead agency adopting an MND, so the lease comes at the end of proving, not the start. A speculator cannot lock up a corridor at fixed rent without a project. The public body does charge a formula or comparable rent regardless of hope value, but only once the project is approved. Assignment requires Commission consent, and the lease is tied to the specific approved use and cable configuration, which reduces transferability. Sovereign land is not 'owned' by someone who cannot read the data; the state is the counterparty and grants on a project basis.
scored.buyer: Hyperscaler-led subsea cable consortia (Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft) and landing-station operators (RTI, Equinix, Ciena-adjacent integrators). They are well capitalised but few. California sees perhaps 1-3 new cable landings a year, and buyers typically control their own route and permitting rather than buying a third party's corridor. Seawater-cooled coastal compute buyers are mostly hypothetical, given California's hostility to new once-through cooling intakes (OTC policy).
scored.ladder: The rungs above are landing station ownership, open-access landing (the RTI model), regional cable ownership and coastal data centres. It is a real chain worth several $B, but the smallest rung is not a cheap discovery wedge, and incumbents such as RTI already sit on the next rung up.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no cheap unproven right to buy. A state submerged-lands lease is granted only to a specific approved project after CEQA and coastal permitting, at formula rent, with assignment needing Commission consent. The proving step therefore is the acquisition, not a step-up on something already held. The value sits in permitting and politics, not in reading illegible data.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a permitting and development business, not a discovery arbitrage. The lease comes after proving, rent is a formula rather than the value driver, the step-up on capital at risk is about 2-10x, the data is legible, and a few hyperscaler buyers already do this work themselves.

scored.name: State trust land communication-site lease to anchored tower site
scored.one_line: Take communication-site leases on state trust land under published rent schedules (WA DNR, CO State Land Board) on parcels ML flags as carrier coverage gaps. Prove the site with an RF study, a carrier anchor LOI and zoning/FAA/NEPA clearance, then sell the build-ready or built site to a tower REIT at a cash-flow multiple. The catch is that tower firms already scout gaps, and the build step (about $300k) is real but standard.
scored.unproven_right: Trust-land communication-site lease at the agency's fixed site-class rent schedule, rather than auction. It is assignable with agency consent and costs about $2-10k/yr before facilities.
scored.proving_step: RF propagation and drive-test study, carrier anchor-tenancy LOI, FAA 7460, NEPA/NHPA (FCC Form 620) and county zoning. Costs about $50-150k and takes 1-2 years. Success roughly 30-60%. ML over coverage complaints and gaps could plausibly lift the anchor-win rate 1.5x.
scored.proven_buyer: American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA and Vertical Bridge. They pay about 15-25x tower cash flow, roughly $1-3M for an anchored rural site.
scored.public_data: FCC ASR and ULS (legible). FCC broadband/mobile coverage maps and challenge data. Crowdsourced signal data. WA DNR and CO SLB lease rolls (partly scanned). County zoning minutes. FAA obstruction filings.
scored.rough_step_up: A lease and study of about $60-150k becomes an anchored site worth about $1-3M. That is about 10-30x the proving cost, but well under 10x once the tower build is included. C2 is about 2-3, and C4 is weak because incumbents read this data.
scored.frame: The rung would be a build-ready, anchored tower site on trust land. Discovery is maybe 20-30% of the work in that rung. Carriers issue search rings that tell everyone where a gap is. Most of the effort and cost goes into the anchor LOI negotiation, zoning, NEPA/NHPA, the FAA filing and the roughly $250-350k build. Tower REITs mostly buy built, revenue-producing towers, so an unbuilt site with only an LOI has few buyers. This is a build-to-suit development business, not a discovery business.
scored.step_up: The unproven right is a DNR/SLB lease at a few thousand dollars a year. Capitalised as a ground lease, it is worth about 15-20x rent, roughly $50-150k. A built, single-anchor rural tower trades at about $0.4-0.75M: StratCap's 2025 S-11 schedule shows individual tower purchases at about $430k-$754k at a 48x applicable multiple. The candidate's $1-3M figure is for multi-tenant sites. Against total capital of about $0.35-0.45M (proving plus build), the uplift is about 1.5-2x. Even against proving cost alone it is about 5-10x, nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs about $50-150k over 1-2 years (candidate estimate; RF study, Form 620, FAA 7460 and zoning are consistent with industry norms). The base anchor and zoning success rate is about 30-60%. That cost meets the relaxed C3 bar. But the anchor decision depends on carrier search rings and capex budgets, not on finding the gap, and carriers already have better coverage data than the FCC maps or crowdsourced data. A plausible ML lift is about 1.1-1.3x, so this scores 2.
scored.data: FCC ASR/ULS and the coverage maps are legible and are read routinely by every tower developer and carrier RF team. The one illegible piece is the partly scanned DNR/SLB lease rolls, and that is not where the signal is. There is no hidden outcome: coverage gaps are the very thing the FCC maps and carrier search rings publish.
scored.right_bought: WA DNR publishes an annual fixed communication-site rent schedule by site class (2026-27 edition), and that rent ignores hope value, which helps. But leases go through a public 'notice of state's intent to negotiate lease', so competitors can step in. Assignment needs agency consent, and rent is reset by site class and tenant count (per-tenant cellular rent), which claws back part of the uplift. Most importantly, the trust land has no scarcity: a carrier gap can almost always be served from a nearby private parcel at similar rent. The cheap right therefore carries no locational monopoly and no discount that anyone else cannot match.
scored.buyer: American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge and smaller REITs such as StratCap are well capitalised. They mainly buy built, cash-flowing towers at about $0.4-0.75M for single-tenant rural sites, and only sometimes buy build-to-suit pipelines.
scored.ladder: The path is lease, then site development, then tower ownership, then a tower portfolio, then small cells/fiber/edge. That is a real but crowded ladder, with independent developers and REITs already on every rung. Climbing it is ordinary infrastructure capital allocation, not a discovery edge compounding.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry and no scarce right. Carriers publish search rings and already know their coverage gaps better than any public map. Any nearby private parcel substitutes for the trust-land lease. The value comes from the roughly $300k build and the carrier's anchor decision, not from discovery. The proven step-up is only about 1.5-2x on total capital.
scored.one_line_reason: This is standard build-to-suit tower development. Gaps are already legible to carriers, the land right is not scarce, and a built single-tenant rural tower sells for about $0.4-0.75M against about $0.4M all-in. The relaxed C3 raises only the hit-rate score and does not rescue the frame or the step-up.

scored.name: Trust-land grazing lease assignment plus cleared solar-site package (NM/AZ/WY)
scored.one_line: Buy assignments of fixed-AUM-rent state trust grazing leases on sections near transmission, and pay for Class III cultural and biological clearance on them. Sell the cleared site package and the lessee's position to a utility-scale solar developer, who still has to negotiate the renewable lease with the land office. This is honestly weak, because the grazing lessee does not control the energy use and the land office captures most of the uplift.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of a state trust grazing lease at the statutory AUM rent (a few dollars per AUM). Assignments are usually bought from ranchers at a modest premium.
scored.proving_step: Class III cultural survey, biological and wetland survey, desktop interconnection screen and ALTA survey. Costs about $80-200k per section and takes 6-18 months. Success roughly 40-60% for full clearance. ML over scanned prior survey reports could lift that about 1.5x.
scored.proven_buyer: Utility-scale solar developers and IPPs (NextEra, AES, Invenergy) that want de-risked trust-land sites and will pay for the clearance package and the lessee's improvement-compensation rights.
scored.public_data: NMCRIS and AZSITE cultural survey reports (scanned and access-restricted). BLM GLO plats. State land office lease rolls. EIA 860 and transmission maps (legible). USFWS IPaC.
scored.rough_step_up: Ranchers and the land office already price solar hope, and the renewable lease is negotiated at market. Realistic uplift captured is about 2-5x the package cost. C1 about 1, C4 about 1. Included as a trust-land control case.
scored.frame: The rung would be "trust-land site cleared for solar". The asset sold is a clearance package (Class III cultural, biological, ALTA, interconnection screen) plus a grazing lessee's position. Discovery-like work (picking sites whose clearance will succeed) is maybe 30-40% of that rung. The rest is commodity fieldwork plus negotiating land office and lessee consent. The real asset in that frame, the energy right, is not something you can own: the land office keeps it and leases it out by auction or negotiation. Utility-scale solar developers are capitalised buyers, but they mostly buy the package as a service. They do not buy an owned right, because the grazing lease carries no energy rights.
scored.step_up: There is no near-zero to 10^3 jump that the company keeps. In Arizona the solar ground lease is put to public auction. In one example notice (ASLD Ground Lease 03-122707, solar), rent is 3.34% of the greater of an $8.27M appraisal or the winning bid, plus a $2,000/MW fee. The trust captures the solar hope value through the appraisal and the auction. A grazing lessee gets only compensation for improvements, valued at replacement cost less depreciation (NM 19.2.8 NMAC), plus whatever a developer pays to keep relations smooth. The value a developer pays for clearance work it would otherwise commission itself is about 1-3x its cost, and at best 2-5x as the candidate says. Score 1, with a 2 at the very top end.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is expensive enough: about $80-200k per section and 6-18 months for Class III and biological work (candidate estimate, consistent with typical Class III costs in the Southwest). The base clearance success rate of about 40-60% is acceptable under the relaxed C3. ML over NMCRIS/AZSITE prior-survey density and site records could plausibly cut failed sections by about 1.2-1.5x. Cultural site density is already partly mapped in those systems for permitted users, and developers' consultants already screen with them, so an edge of 1.5x or more is doubtful. Score 3.
scored.data: NMCRIS and AZSITE cultural reports are scanned and access-restricted to permitted archaeologists. The data is somewhat illegible, but the consultants hired by incumbent developers already query it. Outcomes are partly legible already: site polygons and eligibility determinations are in fields. EIA-860, transmission maps, IPaC and the lease rolls are fully legible.
scored.right_bought: This fails on every C4 check. (1) The public body does not sell at a fixed price regardless of hope value. ASLD offers solar ground leases at public auction against appraised value, and NM SLO negotiates renewable leases at market. Both capture the uplift. (2) The grazing lease is assignable only with the commissioner's consent (NMSA 19-7-36). It confers no energy right, and it can be cancelled or withdrawn for a higher use. (3) Ranchers near transmission already know about solar interest and charge for it. Buying the rancher's position therefore buys a small improvements-compensation claim and some nuisance value, not the asset.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale solar developers and IPPs (NextEra, AES, Invenergy) are well capitalised. But they buy site-clearance work from consultants at cost-plus, and they bid for the energy lease directly in the land office auction. There is no reason for them to pay an asset premium to the holder of a grazing lease.
scored.ladder: In principle there are rungs above: the site package, then a development-stage solar project with interconnection position, then NTP and sale, then an IPP that owns generation. Moving into solar development is a real path to a large company. But the bottom rung gives no proprietary foothold, so climbing it means becoming an ordinary solar developer competing in the same auctions.
scored.fatal_flaw: The grazing lessee does not hold the energy right. The state land office keeps that right and leases it by public auction (AZ) or market negotiation (NM), at appraised value with per-MW fees. The trust captures essentially all of the uplift, so there is no cheap unproven right to buy and no step-up to keep.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a control case and it fails as expected: the land office auctions the solar hope value and the grazing lease carries no energy rights. That leaves a clearance-services business with about 1-3x uplift. The relaxed C3 raises only the hit-rate lever, to 3.

scored.name: Long-haul fiber route ROWs across federal land gaps
scored.one_line: Use ML over scanned BLM/USFS ROW grants, master title plats and MLRS cases to find federal-land gaps blocking new western long-haul or data-center fiber routes. Take linear ROW grants at the schedule per-mile rent. Pay for NEPA and cultural clearance. Sell the permitted route segment or easement package to a hyperscaler or fiber carrier.
scored.unproven_right: BLM/USFS linear ROW grant at the fixed linear rent schedule (per acre by county zone), assignable
scored.proving_step: About $0.3-1M and 1-3 years: route survey, Class III cultural survey, NEPA EA. Maybe 50-70% clear.
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers, Zayo/Lumen-type carriers, and BEAD middle-mile builders who need federal-land segments to close routes
scored.public_data: BLM MLRS case records, master title plats (scanned), ePlanning NEPA documents, FCC fiber filings, railroad and highway ROW scans
scored.rough_step_up: About $50k becomes $1-5M per critical segment, roughly 20-100x. Value depends on hold-up position, and buyers can often route around, so C1 and C2 are weak to moderate.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted federal-land fiber ROW segment. Finding the gap is maybe 20-30% of the work. Most of it is the physical-regulatory step: route survey, Class III cultural survey, NEPA EA, cost-recovery fees, and then actually building conduit. Buyers mainly want lit or built routes, not paper permits. Discovery is well below 80%, and the physical and permitting step is not trivial.
scored.step_up: The candidate itself claims $50k to $1-5M (20-100x), and only from hold-up. Under 43 CFR 2805.15(b), BLM keeps the right to require common use of a grant, including its facilities, subsurface and airspace, and to authorize compatible uses. The holder may not charge for land made subject to those extra grants. A hyperscaler can apply for its own co-located or parallel grant, or route around. Realistic uplift is roughly the reimbursed permitting cost plus a modest time premium, about 1.5-3x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $0.3-1M and takes 1-3 years (NEPA EA plus Class III cultural survey; candidate estimate, no independent source). The base clearance rate of 50-70% is acceptable under the relaxed C3. But ML over plats mostly finds gaps that GIS (PLSS/SMA land-status layers) already shows. It might improve clearance odds about 1.2x by flagging cultural and NEPA conflicts early. The real problem is that a cleared permit is not worth much.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible (scanned master title plats, MLRS cases, ePlanning NEPA documents). But federal land status is already digitized in BLM surface-management GIS, and carriers' permitting consultants routinely read it, so the gap itself is legible. Buying the right is weak on every check. It is not bought from owners who cannot read the data: it is applied for first-come, and BLM can run a competitive process for competing applications. The applicant must show technical and financial capability to build (43 CFR 2804), which works against a speculative holder. Assignment needs BLM approval. The grant is non-exclusive, BLM can force common use, and the holder cannot charge the co-user (2805.15). The fixed rent does not capture hope value, but the non-exclusivity rules wipe out the uplift anyway.
scored.right_bought: A BLM/USFS linear ROW grant at the per-acre linear rent schedule (2026-2035 schedule), plus cost-recovery fees. Assignment requires BLM approval, the grant is non-exclusive, and BLM can require common use.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers, Zayo/Lumen-type carriers and BEAD middle-mile builders are well capitalised. But they can file their own ROW applications and get the same permit, use highway or railroad corridors, or force common use. They have little reason to pay a large premium for a paper permit.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is moderate: permitted segment, then conduit construction, dark fiber leasing, then lit long-haul routes and data-center interconnect. That path leads to a Zayo-scale infrastructure company, but it is capital-heavy and competitive, and the smallest rung gives no proprietary advantage to climb from.
scored.fatal_flaw: No exclusivity, so no hold-up value. Under 43 CFR 2805.15, a BLM ROW grant is non-exclusive. BLM can require common use, authorize compatible uses for others, and bar the holder from charging them. The buyer can also get its own grant first-come. The permitted segment cannot capture a 20-100x uplift, let alone 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 does not help: the permit work dominates the frame, the federal land gap is already legible in GIS, and the non-exclusive ROW grant, which BLM can open to common use, cannot hold up a buyer that can file its own application.

scored.name: High-MGO manuka apiary concessions on NZ public conservation land
scored.one_line: Use ML over satellite vegetation and soil data to find stands of the high-MGO Leptospermum chemotype on Crown and DOC land, obtain apiary site concessions at fixed fees, prove MGO grade with one season of hives and lab assays, then sell or assign the proven site portfolio to Comvita or Manuka Health. Honest rough score: C1 3, C2 3, C3 3, C4 4, C5 3.
scored.unproven_right: DOC apiary concessions and LINZ/Crown forest licensee apiary site rights. They carry administrative fees, are not auctioned at market value, and can be assigned subject to approval.
scored.proving_step: Place hives for one flowering season, then run UMF/MGO/DHA and leptosperin assays on honey from each site: about $50-100k per site cluster. Hit rate on UMF 10+ is maybe 30-50%.
scored.proven_buyer: Comvita, Manuka Health (Grand Hive) and Oha Honey, who pay large premiums for verified high-UMF sites and long-term site access.
scored.public_data: Sentinel-2 and LCDB vegetation maps. Landcare Research soil and ecological district data. MPI manuka honey science definition test results. DOC concession register.
scored.rough_step_up: Site fees of hundreds to low thousands of dollars become proven high-UMF site access worth tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, roughly 10-100x. Caveat: the asset is a concession plus a recurring honey yield rather than a one-off land value jump, and Māori land (often the best stands) is privately negotiated.
scored.frame: The rung is a DOC beehive concession, proven by running hives for one season and assaying the honey. Discovery is maybe 40-50% of the work. The physical step is ordinary beekeeping, which is cheap and which every beekeeper already does as their business. The would-be buyers (Comvita, Manuka Health, Oha) are weak, not capitalised. Comvita lost NZ$77.4M in FY24 and about NZ$104M the following year, and was sold to Masthead/Florenz for about NZ$56M. Hive numbers are forecast to fall about 50% to roughly 500k, so buyers are letting sites go, not paying premiums to get new ones.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the DOC application fee is NZ$2,065-2,565 one-off, plus an annual fee of NZ$30+GST per hive (non-manuka). Proven manuka: DOC raises the annual fee to NZ$75+GST per hive, or charges NZ$10 per hive plus 10% of revenue. On private land, landowners get about NZ$52-105 per hive per year, or 5-30% of revenue (Miere Coalition, NZFFA). So a proven site is worth roughly 2-5x the unproven fee each year, as a recurring income stream. There is no immediate one-off jump in asset value, and nothing near 10^3x. Price collapse makes it worse: one beekeeper saw manuka fall from a NZ$64/kg peak to NZ$13/kg in a season, and bulk honey sits at NZ$3.50-4/kg against a NZ$6-7/kg break-even.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The pitch's own guess: 30-50% of site clusters reach UMF 10+, at NZ$50-100k per cluster per season. That cost is mostly normal beekeeping, which earns honey revenue and largely pays for itself. It is not a sunk proving cost like a drill hole. ML could plausibly lift the hit rate about 1.2-1.5x, since chemotype varies by region and the data is noisy. But beekeepers already have local knowledge, and LCDB already maps manuka/kanuka directly. The ML edge over that is modest.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. LCDB has an explicit manuka/kanuka land-cover class, Sentinel-2 is free, and the manuka chemotype regions are already widely known in the industry. The key outcome data, MGO/UMF test results by site, is held privately by beekeepers and brands. MPI test results are not published by location. So the illegible-public-data edge is weak.
scored.right_bought: DOC does not sell at a fixed price regardless of hope value, and it does claw back the uplift. The annual fee rises from NZ$30 to NZ$75 per hive once a site produces manuka, or DOC takes 10% of revenue. Concessions are granted case by case, with no auction, and can be transferred only with the Minister's consent. Many of the best stands are on Māori land and are negotiated privately. The rights are cheap to get, but the regulator already prices manuka differently and captures part of the step-up.
scored.buyer: In theory Comvita/Florenz, Manuka Health/Grand Hive and Oha Honey. In practice the sector is in a multi-year glut: Comvita had losses of NZ$77M and NZ$104M before a distressed sale at about NZ$56M, hive numbers are halving, and beekeepers are going out of business. None of these buyers is paying large premiums for new proven sites now.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are site portfolio, then hive operation, then extraction and grading, then a honey brand and export. The whole chain is small. The industry's leading branded company sold for about NZ$56M, and NZ honey exports are around NZ$400-600M a year. There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no capitalised buyer and no real step-up. NZ manuka is in a multi-year oversupply: prices collapsed, hive numbers are halving, and Comvita was sold distressed for about NZ$56M. On top of that, DOC already charges more per hive for manuka sites (NZ$75 vs NZ$30, or 10% of revenue). A proven site is worth only about 2-5x an unproven one each year, and the regulator takes part of that.
scored.one_line_reason: Easing C3 does not save this. The proven site is a recurring 2-5x income stream, not a 10^4 jump in value. DOC already prices manuka differently and takes a revenue share. The buyers are in a glut and selling at distressed prices. The whole chain is a sub-NZ$1B niche.

scored.name: Shortwave (HF) international broadcast licences for transoceanic latency
scored.one_line: Win FCC Part 73 Subpart F HF licences (fixed filing fees) at sites ML ranks as best for low-latency transatlantic or transpacific propagation, prove the propagation, then sell to trading firms. Honest view: C1 3, C2 4, C3 3, C4 3, C5 1. The FCC has denied point-to-point datacasting under Part 73, so value depends on Part 90 rulemaking RM-11953. Treat this as a regulatory option, not a near-term business.
scored.unproven_right: FCC Part 73 HF international broadcast construction permit or licence at fixed filing fees, transferable with FCC consent
scored.proving_step: Site acquisition, a test transmitter, and a multi-season propagation and latency measurement campaign. Cost is about $0.3-1M and 1-2 years. Regulatory approval of data use is uncertain.
scored.proven_buyer: HFT firms on Chicago-London/Frankfurt and Chicago-Tokyo routes (members of the Shortwave Modernization Coalition)
scored.public_data: FCC HF broadcast schedules and CDBS/LMS filings, the RM-11953 docket comments, ionosonde archives (GIRO/NOAA), and HFCC frequency coordination schedules
scored.rough_step_up: A ~$100k licence and site becomes a $5-20M sale if data use is authorised: ~50-200x, conditional on regulation
scored.frame: The rung would be a licensed HF site, proven for latency, sold to a trading firm. Discovery is well under 20% of the work in that rung. Picking a site is mostly great-circle geometry near the CME data centre in Aurora, IL, and HF propagation over the path is already well understood. What actually decides the value is the FCC: whether data use is authorised at all. Building and running a 20 kW transmitter plant is a real physical cost, and the step does not get abstracted away.
scored.step_up: The candidate's own figure is about 50-200x: a ~$100k licence and site sold for $5-20M. That holds only if data use is authorised. Today the FCC grants Part 73 HF construction permits for broadcasting only. It rejected point-to-point datacasting for DPA Mac and Parable Broadcasting, saying encoded data is not an international broadcast service (Radio World). The Part 90 petition, RM-11953, has been pending since 2023 with about 800 comments, mostly opposed by amateur radio groups led by the ARRL, and I found no ruling. Under current rules the step-up from proving propagation alone is close to zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving cost is the candidate's estimate: about $0.3-1M and 1-2 years per site. That passes the 'expensive' bar. But propagation 'hits' are close to guaranteed once the path geometry is right; trading firms already run these links under experimental licences. The real uncertainty is the regulatory outcome, which ML cannot move. ML might shave a few hundred microseconds or improve uptime modelling, but that is not a 1.5x gain in cost per proven asset.
scored.data: The inputs (ionosonde archives from GIRO/NOAA, HFCC schedules, the FCC's CDBS/LMS filings) are mostly structured and already used by propagation tools like VOACAP/ITU-R P.533 and by the trading firms' own RF engineers. The data is not illegible, and incumbents do read it. The signal is physics plus geometry, so there is little hidden in the data for ML to find.
scored.right_bought: FCC Part 73 international broadcast permits are issued for fixed filing fees, first come, with no auction. They are transferable with FCC consent. The FCC does not claw back uplift, but it does control the hope value: the right is only worth something if the use is authorised. Licensed shortwave stations are not mispriced assets held by owners who cannot read the data. The incumbent trading firms (the Shortwave Modernization Coalition, which includes Jump/DRW-linked entities) already file for these permits themselves and run experimental HF links. So there is no informational discount to buy into.
scored.buyer: A small set of HFT firms on the Chicago-London/Frankfurt and Chicago-Tokyo routes. They are well capitalised but few, and they already build HF links in-house under experimental licences. That makes them likely builders rather than buyers.
scored.ladder: Above this rung there is at most operating HF links as a latency utility. It is a niche worth a few tens of millions a year and has no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is a regulatory option, not something discovery finds. The FCC has denied datacasting under Part 73, and RM-11953 has been unresolved since 2023. Site and propagation 'discovery' is basic geometry and physics that the HFT buyers already master and do themselves, so ML has no edge and there is no mispriced right to buy.
scored.one_line_reason: Any step-up depends on the FCC, not on discovery. The data is legible and the buyers already do the work in-house, so ML provides no lever.

scored.name: Tax-forfeit wetland or habitat parcels sold as permanent conservation easements or fee to public buyers
scored.one_line: Buy tax-forfeited ecologically valuable parcels at the statutory minimum. Use ML over species-occurrence records and imagery to find parcels that will pass a biological survey for listed species or priority habitat. Do the survey and baseline, then sell the fee or a conservation easement at full appraised value to state wildlife agencies, NRCS ACEP, Forest Legacy or land trusts with public funding.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to a tax-forfeited rural parcel sold at a formula minimum price, valued only as marginal ag or recreational land.
scored.proving_step: A protocol biological survey (listed species, a natural heritage program element occurrence), an easement baseline documentation report and a USPAP 'yellow book' appraisal. Cost is about $50-120k, over 12-24 months. The survey confirms priority value about 30-60% of the time.
scored.proven_buyer: State fish and wildlife and natural heritage programs, USDA NRCS ACEP, USFS Forest Legacy, and land trusts holding public grants (all well capitalised and funded by appropriation).
scored.public_data: State natural heritage program occurrence data (often only coarse public layers), GBIF and iNaturalist, NWI wetlands, NLCD land cover, scanned county forfeit lists, and the USFWS critical habitat GIS.
scored.rough_step_up: About 3-15x (forfeit price at taxes owed rising to full appraised fee or easement value). C2 is weak relative to the 10^3 bar; adjacent to the already-covered US mitigation banking idea but sells fee/easements to public funders rather than credits.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a tax-forfeit parcel, survey it, then sell it to a public conservation buyer. The work is mostly discovery (survey, baseline, appraisal), so that part of the test passes. It fails on what the buyer pays for. Public buyers pay appraised fair market value at the parcel's highest and best use, and the survey finding does not change that value. The survey is a requirement for eligibility, not a source of value. Discovery may be 80% of the work, but it captures close to 0% of the price.
scored.step_up: About 1-3x at best, from arbitrage, not from proving. Minnesota forfeit land is offered at no less than its appraised value or its current Estimated Market Value at forfeiture (Aitkin and Big Stone County notices). It is not sold at the taxes owed, so the claimed 3-15x gap mostly disappears. Federal buyers using the Yellow Book (UASFLA) must appraise at highest and best use, and special-purpose appraisals are not allowed (Webb County / UASFLA conversion instructions). So a confirmed listed species adds no appraised value. Finding listed species can even lower private market value through ESA restrictions. The only gain left is any discount at auction below market value, which is usually 0-50%.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost of $50-120k and a 30-60% base rate (candidate's own numbers) meet the relaxed C3 threshold on cost. But better hit rates only qualify more parcels for sale at a fair market value that the hit does not raise. ML improves deal flow by perhaps 1.5x, yet adds nothing to the value of each proven asset. The cost per proven asset falls while the margin per asset stays near zero or negative after paying $50-120k against rural parcels worth tens of thousands of dollars. So the lever is real on paper and worthless in practice.
scored.data: GBIF and iNaturalist records, NWI wetlands, NLCD land cover and county forfeit lists are public and somewhat illegible, which supports the data side. The right side fails on several counts. (1) Minnesota counties must classify every forfeit parcel as conservation or nonconservation, so the state has already read the conservation value. (2) The DNR can withhold or repurchase parcels before auction (Big Stone notice), and county land commissioners can withdraw parcels. That puts the best parcels in reserve instead of on sale. (3) Parcels go to competitive auction starting at appraised or market value, not at a fixed formula price that ignores hope value. (4) Detailed natural heritage occurrence data is restricted to agencies, which are also the buyers, so the buyers can see more than we can. The title is transferable, but the cheap price is not.
scored.right_bought: Fee title bought at a county tax-forfeit auction. The minimum bid is the appraised value or Estimated Market Value plus a 3% assurance fee and deed fees, after DNR and county conservation screening and possible withholding.
scored.buyer: State wildlife agencies, NRCS ACEP, USFS Forest Legacy and grant-funded land trusts. They are capitalised by appropriation but legally capped at appraised fair market value. Forest Legacy and ACEP also need a willing landowner and a ranked application, and ACEP requires a cost share.
scored.ladder: Weak. Possible later rungs are a conservation land fund, carbon or forest credits on the parcels, or a broader land trust and asset-management business. All of these are low-margin and limited by appropriations. None leads to a very large company on its own.
scored.fatal_flaw: Public conservation buyers must pay appraised fair market value at highest and best use. The Yellow Book and USPAP forbid special-purpose appraisals, so a successful biological survey creates no step-up in value. Meanwhile the forfeit parcels are sold at appraised value or Estimated Market Value, after DNR and county conservation screening that can withhold them. The proving step therefore unlocks eligibility, not value.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding listed species does not raise a parcel's price, because government buyers pay highest-and-best-use market value. And the forfeit land is already sold at about market value, after the state screens it for conservation value. Little discovery premium is left to capture.

verified.name: Closed-loop pumped storage sites via FERC preliminary permits (federal, state trust and optioned private land)
verified.one_line: Use ML over decades of surrendered FERC preliminary permits (whose scanned filings say why earlier permittees gave up: geology, water, money), old USBR/USACE reconnaissance scans, LiDAR head and state geology/borehole files to rank off-river reservoir pairs with large head near HV substations. File FERC preliminary permits (first-to-file, essentially free, 4-year exclusive priority, transferable with FERC approval), plus BLM/USFS ROW or state trust land use at schedule rent, or land options on private parcels. Pay for geotech borings (dam and tunnel foundations, not mineral exploration), water-supply, interconnection screening and an NOI/PAD, then sell the de-risked project to a storage developer, utility or infrastructure fund that pays the step-up because a feasible, permitted site saves it years. Must sell at the permit-plus-geotech rung, since the build is enormous.
verified.unproven_right: FERC preliminary permit (4-yr exclusive priority to study and apply for a licence, granted by filing order, not sold at market value) plus a BLM/USFS ROW or state trust land use application at schedule rent; on private land, an option at farmland prices before head, geology and interconnection are validated
verified.proving_step: About $0.5-5M over 1-3 years: geotech borings and rock-mass testing at upper reservoir, dam, tunnel and powerhouse; head and volume survey; makeup-water study; interconnection pre-study or queue entry; environmental fatal-flaw screen; NOI and Pre-Application Document. Roughly 30-60% of ML-screened sites reach a licensable configuration; ML that drops dead sites before filing plausibly lifts cost per proven site 1.5-2x.
verified.proven_buyer: Pumped storage and long-duration storage developers, western and eastern utilities with IRP storage needs (PacifiCorp, NV Energy, APS), and infrastructure funds (Rye Development-type developers, Brookfield, CIP, NextEra)
verified.public_data: FERC eLibrary (thousands of issued and surrendered preliminary permits with scanned feasibility reports and surrender letters), USBR and USACE 1970s-80s pumped storage reconnaissance scans, USGS 3DEP DEMs/LiDAR, scanned USGS/Reclamation geologic reports, state dam-safety files and borehole logs, NREL and ORNL closed-loop PSH site atlases (legible screening only), BLM MLRS/LR2000 and ePlanning NEPA PDFs, EIA-860, FERC Form 715 and ISO/WECC transmission data
verified.rough_step_up: About $0-300k for the permit and land position becomes $3-50M for a de-risked 1-2 GW site (about $5-20k/MW): roughly 30-1000x on the right and about 5-15x on all-in proving spend. Weakness on private land: the land is priced. NREL's public screening reduces the ML edge. Ladder: licensing, EPC, ownership of the storage plant.
verified.frame: The rung is a closed-loop PSH site held by preliminary permit, with geotech, an interconnection screen and an NOI/PAD done. Inside that rung, discovery (picking the reservoir pair, head, geology and grid access) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is regulatory and interconnection process: NOI/PAD consultation, environmental screening, the queue, makeup-water rights. Geotech borings are real field campaigns, not a trivial physical step. Buyers do exist (TransAlta, AGL, Rye/CIP-type developers). But they pay mostly in staged milestone payments tied to licence and offtake, not cash on the proving result. So the rung can be sold, but discovery is not 80%+ of it.
verified.step_up: Comparable early-stage sales were all brownfield mine-pit sites. TransAlta paid C$8M upfront plus up to C$17M on milestones for 50% of the 320 MW Tent Mountain project in 2023. That implies about C$50k/MW upfront and up to about C$150k/MW with milestones. Hillgrove sold the 250 MW Kanmantoo rights to AGL for A$31M (about A$124k/MW), paid in stages over 18-36 months on milestones. Against $1-5M of proving spend on a 1 GW site, that is about 10-30x, and much of it only arrives at licence or offtake. On the permit itself (filing cost only) the multiple is huge, but that is an artifact of the permit being free. On real capital it falls in the 10-100x band, and it is not paid immediately.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving costs about $0.5-5M per site over 1-3 years, and a full licence costs another $10-30M over 5+ years. That clears the >=$50k bar. Base rate: most FERC PSH preliminary permits are surrendered or lapse without a licence application. Maysville (1,000 MW) was denied a successive permit for not filing an NOI/PAD, and Banks Lake needed a rehearing to keep its permit. Of ML-screened closed-loop sites, maybe 30-60% reach a licensable configuration. Mining surrender letters and old USBR/USACE reconnaissance for the reasons projects died (geology, water, interconnection, money) could plausibly drop dead sites before boring and give 1.5-2x on cost per proven site. NREL/ORNL closed-loop atlases already do the legible head and volume screening, so the remaining edge is in geology and failure reasons. Under the relaxed C3 that earns a 4, held below 5 because NREL already covers the geometric screen.
verified.data: The data really is illegible: FERC eLibrary scanned feasibility reports and surrender letters, 1970s-80s USBR/USACE reconnaissance, state borehole logs. On top of that, LiDAR and 3DEP are huge but legible. The outcome is not already written into a status field: permit status says surrendered or expired, but not why. On the other hand, NREL's public closed-loop atlas already gives everyone head, volume and distance to transmission, which narrows the edge to geology and failure modes.
verified.right_bought: The right is not bought, so the information asymmetry has no seller to exploit. A FERC preliminary permit is issued by filing order, essentially free and first-to-file, and competitors can file competing applications. By statute it is non-transferable: 16 U.S.C. 798(d) says permits 'shall not be transferable'. In practice it can only move by selling the SPV that holds it, or by the buyer taking the licence application. The permit gives no land access. BLM/USFS ROW is charged at schedule rent with NEPA review, so there is no hope-value clawback, but also nothing to buy cheaply. State trust land can be auctioned or negotiated at appraised value once a competing interest appears. Private land is the only place an owner who 'cannot read the data' sells cheaply via an option. Even there, a 1-2 GW reservoir pair needs hundreds to thousands of hectares from several owners, and visible permit filings tip them off. Sites already on NREL's map are effectively public knowledge.
verified.buyer: The buyer pool is thin but capitalised: TransAlta, AGL, Rye Development (CIP-backed), Brookfield, NextEra, and utilities with IRP storage needs (PacifiCorp, NV Energy, APS). They pay largely through milestone-contingent deals tied to licence, offtake or FID, and US transactions are rare and opaque.
verified.ladder: The rungs run from site and permit, to FERC licence (5-7 yrs, $10-30M), to offtake/IRP contract, to EPC and construction ($2-5B per GW-scale plant), to owning and operating a long-duration storage fleet, then to a multi-site storage developer and IPP. The ladder is very large, but each rung needs heavy capital and long timelines, and it is dominated by regulatory process rather than discovery.
verified.fatal_flaw: The unproven right cannot be bought from an owner who cannot read the data. It is a free, first-to-file FERC preliminary permit that is statutorily non-transferable (16 U.S.C. 798(d)) and open to competing filers, and NREL's public atlas already maps the legible candidate sites. And most of the value step-up is paid only through milestone-contingent deals at licence or offtake, years and tens of millions of dollars after the permit-plus-geotech rung, not immediately on the proving result.
verified.one_line_reason: Under the relaxed C3, proving is expensive and ML on surrender letters could lift cost per proven site about 1.5-2x. But the free, non-transferable, first-to-file permit gives no cheap purchase to exploit. Early-stage sales (Tent Mountain, Kanmantoo) show only about 10-30x on proving spend, mostly paid on later milestones. And discovery is well under 80% of a rung dominated by regulation and interconnection.

verifiers.evidence:
Seen through the step-up and buyer lens, the claimed 30-1000x does not hold. It only appears if you measure against a permit that costs almost nothing to file. Measured against the real proving capital ($0.5-5M per site), the cash that actually changes hands is about 3-15x. Most of it is paid on later milestones, and in the cases I found it often never arrives.

1) TransAlta / Tent Mountain, Alberta, 320 MW, Feb 2023, closed Apr 2023. TransAlta paid about C$8M upfront for a 50% stake, plus up to C$17M contingent on development and commercial milestones. Per MW of the 160 MW stake, that is about C$50k/MW upfront and up to about C$156k/MW with every milestone paid. The seller, Montem, had already finished a Hatch pre-feasibility study ('all feasibility studies executed'). This was also a brownfield coal-mine pit, so no greenfield discovery was involved. I could not find Montem's proving spend or any evidence that milestone payments have been made.

2) Hillgrove / AGL Kanmantoo, South Australia, 250 MW. In Apr 2019 the deal was A$31M, but it was staged over 18-36 months: A$1M on signing and A$4M on conditions precedent, which included a confirmatory drilling program. The final payment depended on grid connection and FID, and AGL could walk away at any time before it. AGL and Hillgrove terminated the deal in Feb 2020 'without any ongoing obligation'. So at most about A$5M was plausibly paid, and the headline A$124k/MW never happened.

3) CIP's Nov 2020 purchase of Swan Lake (400 MW) and Goldendale (1,200 MW) from the Rye/National Grid joint venture. The price was undisclosed. Swan Lake was already licensed (2019) and Goldendale's licence application was pending. That is a licence-stage rung, not the permit-plus-geotech rung, so it gives no evidence of a price at that rung.

4) Green Planet / Arizona Independent Power (2011). This was quoted as a '$1.2B project value' for a permit-holding company. It is a capex estimate, not a price, and I found no follow-on transaction.

5) Market size. DOE reports 67 PSH projects (52.5 GW) in development in 2019, with FERC issuing 14 PSH preliminary permits that year. The 2026 Hydropower Market Report shows about 68 projects / 59 GW in FERC permitting, while the operating fleet grew only by upgrades (41 plants, 22.2 GW). Permits keep getting surrendered without a buyer, for example Daybreak Halverson Canyon (2,650 MW) in 2023.

Across the US and globally, I found roughly 0-2 disclosed early-stage PSH site sales per year with a price attached. None of them is a US greenfield permit-plus-geotech site sold for cash. The buyers are real and well capitalised (TransAlta, AGL, CIP, Brookfield). But they buy with small upfront options plus contingent milestones, and they walk away when things go wrong (AGL did). That is not an immediate step-up paid at once on the proving result.

Implied multiple on real capital:
- Upfront: about C$8M against several C$M of PFS work, so about 1-5x.
- Full milestones: about C$25M, so about 5-15x.
- In both cases the multiple is under 30x.
verifiers.killer: No transaction shows a capitalised buyer paying a 30x-plus step-up at once for a permit-plus-geotech PSH site. The two disclosed comparables are both small upfront payments plus contingent milestones. Tent Mountain was C$8M upfront for 50% of a site that already had a pre-feasibility study, with C$17M contingent. Kanmantoo was announced at A$31M, but it was paid in stages over 18-36 months and the buyer could walk away. AGL did walk away in 2020, after at most about A$5M. On the $0.5-5M of real proving capital, that works out to about 3-15x. The 30-1000x figure only appears when measured against the near-free FERC filing cost. In the US there are essentially no disclosed priced sales of permit-stage sites, and the roughly 68-project, 59 GW pipeline mostly lapses or surrenders. So the market is a handful of opaque deals per year, not a liquid exit.
sources: https://hillgroveresources.com.au/uploads/downloads/224/190416 Hillgrove Sells Rights to Pumped Hydro Project.pdf

verifiers.evidence: 1) The legible screen is already public and is used as a commodity. NREL's 2022 Closed-Loop PSH Resource Assessment (Rosenlieb et al., NREL/TP-81277) maps nearly 15,000 site pairs from 30 m DEMs. It is adapted from ANU's Global Pumped Hydro Atlas and adds supply curves (8/10/12 hr, 40-100 m dams, total $/kW including transmission spur cost), which ship in the NREL ATB. Head, volume, cost and grid distance are therefore already written up for everyone. The only edge left is geology and failure reasons, and I found no evidence that the geology screen is the thing deciding site outcomes. 2) The base hit rate is low, but for commercial and diligence reasons, not geologic ones. DOE/ORNL Hydropower Market Report: 67 PSH projects (52 GW) in the pipeline at end-2019, only 3 FERC-authorised. Over 80% of proposed PSH is closed-loop, and the trade-press tally is 22 projects (22.5 GW) mostly still at the permit stage. The documented permit deaths are Maysville (1,000 MW, no NOI/PAD, so no diligence), Don Pedro (missed progress report), South Maui (missed report), Montezuma 2.1 GW (missed reports) and Mount Hope (licensed 2,000 MW, never built: 'market uncertainties and ownership changes'). Surrender letters mostly encode a lack of money, offtake and diligence. ML on geology and failure-reason text therefore attacks a minority failure mode, and the 1.5-2x lift on cost per proven site is unsupported. 3) The space is crowded with professional serial filers, including the buyers themselves. Brookfield's affiliate BPUS Generation Development pursues 6 PSH projects directly. Invenergy (Nelson Energy, Iron Range MN) files its own permits. Rye Development (CIP-backed) does too. Blanket filers include Premium Energy Holdings (Pyramid Lake, Haiwee, San Onofre, Nacimiento, Santa Margarita, Twitchell, Whale Rock), Nature and People First (Black Mesa N/E/S, Chuska, Chilchinbeto), Gravity Storage (Red Lake AZ, Escondido Canyon NM 2 GW), Nightfall Renewables (3.6 GW Maxwell CA) and rPlus Hydro. Capitalised buyers build sites in-house, and the first-to-file land grab is already contested, so a newcomer's discovery has to beat incumbents who also read NREL and ANU. 4) The 'right' is weaker than claimed. A preliminary permit only gives priority to file a licence application. It gives no land access and is non-transferable under FPA s.5 (16 USC 798). H2O's Phantom Canyon developer said holding a permit 'is not a prerequisite to filing a license application' and went ahead without one. So the permit is not a moat or a sellable asset. Nothing cheap is bought from an owner who cannot read the data, except optioned private land, which at 1-2 GW means many parcels. 5) On price, no disclosed US early-stage PSH sale price per MW was found. The only comps are Tent Mountain (C$8M upfront for 50% of 320 MW) and Kanmantoo (A$31M paid on staged milestones), both milestone-heavy brownfield deals, which is consistent with a ~10-30x return on proving spend that is not paid immediately.
verifiers.killer: The legible screen (head, volume, cost, transmission spur) is already public in NREL's closed-loop supply curves and ANU's atlas. Projects really die from commercial and diligence causes (no offtake, no money, missed NOI/PAD and progress reports), not from geology an ML model could read in surrender letters. And the capitalised buyers (Brookfield/BPUS, Invenergy, Rye/CIP) plus serial filers (Premium, NPF, Gravity Storage, rPlus, Nightfall) already blanket-file free, first-to-file, non-transferable permits, which aren't even needed to file a licence. So there is no illegible-data edge, no cheap right to buy, and no open field.

verifiers.evidence:
Refuted on the RIGHT AND FRAME lens. (Note: the shared web-search budget ran out after 7 searches, so the US deal-price question below could not be checked further.)

(1) Statute. 16 U.S.C. 798(d) bars assigning preliminary permits, and FERC can cancel one for noncompliance or good cause. A permit's only purpose (798(a)) is to preserve priority for a licence application while the holder studies, maps, estimates costs and arranges financing. The term is at most 4 years, with one extension of up to 4 more for good-faith diligence. A third permit needs "extraordinary circumstances". So the finalist's premise that the permit is "transferable with FERC approval" is wrong. It can move only indirectly, by selling the SPV that holds it.

(2) Competition and site banking. Every permit application is noticed in the Federal Register with a 60-day window for competing applications under 18 CFR 4.36. Examples: Gravity Storage Escondido Canyon NM, Nightfall Maxwell CA, Twentymile CO, all 2024. Same-site contests happen (Sworinger Reservoir: NT Hydro versus a later filer). FERC denied San Diego County Water Authority's third San Vicente permit expressly to prevent "site banking". Serial filers already blanket the obvious western sites: Premium Energy Holdings has 7+ (Pyramid Lake, filed twice; Haiwee; Intermountain; San Onofre; Twitchell; Santa Margarita; Nacimiento). HGE Energy Storage has Shasta and Whiskeytown, and 2025 filings cover Page AZ, Dixfield ME, PA, NM and LA County. So the cheap right is free and first-to-file. There is no seller who cannot read the data, and the information asymmetry has no one to buy from.

(3) Federal land. BLM ROW is priced by cost recovery (processing and monitoring reimbursed in advance) plus rent. FPA 10(e) annual charges follow a FERC fee schedule for non-linear features such as reservoirs. Prices are set administratively, with no discount to capture.

(4) Who pays the step-up. CIP's 2020 purchase of Swan Lake (393-400 MW) and Goldendale (1,200 MW) from the Rye/National Grid JV came AFTER Swan Lake's 2019 50-year FERC licence. Terms were undisclosed, and Rye kept leading development until construction. The finalist's own comparables also pay mostly on milestones, not on the proving result: Tent Mountain was C$8M upfront plus up to C$17M later; Kanmantoo was A$31M staged over 18-36 months. So the capitalised buyer pays mainly at licence or offtake, a separate regulatory rung, not at permit-plus-geotech.

(5) Is the physical step trivial? No. Geotech borings and rock-mass tests at the dam, tunnel and powerhouse are multi-season field campaigns. NOI/PAD consultation, the interconnection queue and makeup-water rights are process-heavy. Discovery is about 40-50% of the rung, not 80%+.

(6) Hard exclusions. No literal hit: the borings are foundation geotech, not mineral exploration, and the company would own the asset. But the model is structurally the killed "site banking" pattern, and FERC actively polices it.

Revised scores, all justified by points (1)-(6): C1=2, C2=3 (about 10-30x on real proving capital, paid on milestones), C3=4 (proving is expensive; ML on surrender letters is a plausible 1.5-2x, but NREL already does the geometric screen), C4=1 (the data is illegible, but the right is free, unbuyable and contested), C5=4. Total 14.
verifiers.killer: The right cannot be bought cheaply from someone who cannot read the data. It is a free, first-to-file FERC preliminary permit that by statute cannot be assigned (16 U.S.C. 798(d)). It is noticed publicly for 60 days of competing applications, policed against site banking (the San Vicente third-permit denial), and the obvious western sites are already blanketed by serial filers like Premium Energy and HGE. The capitalised buyer mainly pays after licence (CIP bought Swan Lake after its 2019 licence) or through milestone-contingent tranches, so the permit-plus-geotech rung is not a sellable frame where discovery is 80%+.

Step-up: Hillgrove/AGL Kanmantoo (2019) was about A$31M for 250 MW / 8 h, paid in milestone stages. That is about 10^3x on the licence fee but about 5-15x on the A$1-4M proving spend (candidate figures, not re-verified).
A possible rescue I did not test: options over freehold farmland at old proposed-dam sites, from owners who cannot read the files. That is a different right from the one claimed.
verifiers.killer: The unproven right cannot be bought cheaply at a fixed fee from owners who cannot read the data. The public body that holds the old investigation files also controls the land: WaterNSW, Crown Lands and Queensland Hydro. Wherever pumped hydro hope value is visible, it now allocates through competitive EOI/RFP or tender (Balranald Crown land EOI/RFP confirmed; WaterNSW dam tenders reported). Any Crown grant also carries native title future-act processes and market rent. Separately, within the feasibility rung, site discovery is a minority of the work. Approvals, water and connection dominate, so the frame fails the 80%-discovery test.

verified.name: Philippine DOE wind and solar pre-development service contracts
verified.one_line: Apply for Renewable Energy Service Contracts (RESCs) on the DOE's fixed-fee schedule over sites an ML model ranks from scanned DOE/NREL wind atlases, PAGASA records and abandoned contractor filings. Run a 12-18 month LiDAR or met-mast campaign plus a grid study, then assign the bankable contract to an IPP (ACEN, Aboitiz, foreign entrants) under GEA auction pressure.
verified.unproven_right: A pre-development-stage RESC for an onshore wind or solar block. You get it from the DOE on application for fixed administrative and processing fees, with work-program commitments and no bidding on value. Assignment needs DOE approval.
verified.proving_step: A bankable resource assessment: 12+ months of met-mast or LiDAR data, energy yield at P50/P90, a grid connection study and an initial ECC screen. verified.proven_buyer: Capitalised Philippine and foreign IPPs bidding into DOE Green Energy Auctions, which need shovel-ready contracted capacity.
verified.public_data: DOE awarded and terminated RESC lists and work-program reports (scanned PDFs). NREL/DOE Philippine wind atlas. PAGASA station records. NGCP Transmission Development Plan. ECC filings on the DENR-EMB portal. Satellite reanalysis (ERA5).

verified.frame: The rung is pre-development wind or solar, ending in a bankable RESC: a P50/P90 yield, a grid study and an ECC screen. Finding the wind resource is maybe 30-40% of the work at most. The rest is physical and permitting work that is neither trivial nor abstracted: siting and running a met mast or LiDAR for 12+ months, landowner consents, NCIP FPIC (Indigenous consent) in many upland sites, LGU endorsements, and NGCP grid capacity, which is often the binding constraint. Capitalised buyers do exist (ACEN, Aboitiz, foreign IPPs bidding into the GEA). But inside this rung the work is mostly permitting, land and grid, not discovery.
verified.step_up: The claim is a right costing $10-30k going to about $2-6M for a proven 50-100 MW contract (assumed $30-80k/MW). That would be about 100-300x on the right but only about 10x on all-in cost ($150-400k proving). I found no disclosed per-MW price for any Philippine development-stage wind deal. The one data point I found cuts the other way: ACEN bought out the remaining 60% of the 500 MW Unicorn wind project in July 2024 at a price below 10% of the company's book value. That suggests early-stage Philippine wind rights trade cheaply, closer to $5-20k/MW. A realistic step-up is about 10-100x on the right and 3-10x on all-in cost, so score 3.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving is expensive: about $150-400k and 1.5 years per site (met mast or LiDAR, yield study, grid study), so it passes the cost test. The base hit rate of 20-30% for land-grab sites and 40-60% for ML-picked sites is the candidate's own estimate, not sourced. The resource itself is already mapped well by mesoscale models and reanalysis (Global Wind Atlas, ERA5, the NREL Philippine atlas), so ML adds little on wind speed. Most failures come from grid capacity, land or FPIC, and community opposition, which ML on scanned atlases barely predicts. Mining terminated-contract filings and NGCP TDP congestion data might give about 1.2-1.5x on cost per proven asset, so score 3. DOE has terminated 163 RE contracts (17.9 GW) in 2024-25 for non-performance, which shows failure is mostly about execution, not resource.
verified.data: This is mostly legible. Wind and solar resource is published as clean global rasters (Global Wind Atlas, ERA5, NREL atlas) that every IPP already uses. Some signal does sit in illegible form: scanned DOE work-program reports, terminated-contract filings with partial met data, and ECC filings. But DOE publishes awarded, terminated and certificate-of-commerciality status lists, which put much of the outcome into legible status fields. Incumbents (ACEN, Mainstream and others) run their own GIS screening, so the edge from extraction is small.
verified.right_bought: This fails the rubric. The right is not bought from an owner who cannot read the data. It is a state grant under DC2024-06-0018: the OCSP (competitive selection) for DOE pre-determined areas, or direct application, effectively first-come, at fixed administrative fees with no price on hope value. The DOE then claws back idle value: it terminates non-performing contracts (84 in 2025, 5.3 GW) and rebids them through the OCSP, and it can forfeit performance bonds and blacklist developers. Transfer or assignment needs DOE approval. Secretary Garin has said publicly that DOE does not want applicants who hold service contracts only to flip them at a premium. verified.buyer: Capitalised Philippine and foreign IPPs that need shovel-ready capacity for GEA rounds: ACEN, Aboitiz, Mainstream, Citicore, and others such as CIP or Copenhagen Energy for larger assets. These buyers are real and liquid, but many prefer to self-develop and buy distressed rights cheaply (for example ACEN on Unicorn).
verified.ladder: The ladder is clear: pre-development RESC, then development and permits, then financial close and EPC (construction), then owner-operator IPP, then a portfolio or utility-scale renewable platform. Offshore wind (57 contracts, about 42 GW) is a bigger rung above that. Score 4.
verified.fatal_flaw: The value-creating step is not discovery. The wind and solar resource is already legibly mapped by public global atlases. What decides success is grid, land and FPIC execution. verified.one_line_reason: The relaxed C3 helps a little (proving costs $150-400k), but the resource signal is already legible and failures are mostly about execution. The right comes from a regulator that is cracking down on flipping, and the realistic step-up is about 10-100x, not 10^3-10^4.

Search note: the shared web-search budget for this turn was already used up, so I made no new searches. I checked the finalist's own sources with WebFetch (3 fetches) and used background knowledge. Findings:
(1) No real price exists for a proven RESC. The ACEN/Unicorn 500 MW buyout (July 2024, remaining 60% bought from Maraj Energy) does not disclose a price. It says only that the price is "less than 10% of the book value of the Company as of 31 March 2024". That is a PSE disclosure-threshold statement, not a per-MW price, so it supports neither $30-80k/MW nor anything else (newsbytes.ph). Mainstream's 440 MW onshore WESCs (100 MW Santa Ana and 340 MW Panaon, March 2024) were taken directly from the DOE as development rights, with no price or secondary sale disclosed (renewablewatch.in). This is evidence that capitalised IPPs apply for RESCs themselves rather than buying them from a prover.
(2) Immediacy fails because of a regulatory lock. Under the Revised Omnibus Guidelines (DC2024-06-0018), a pre-development RESC can be assigned to a non-affiliate only ONCE, and only after 2 years from effectivity. The exception is if the minimum set of permits and activities is already done. Assignment also needs DOE approval (globalcompliancenews.com, Aug 2024). So a 12-18 month resource campaign cannot be sold to the buyer on completion. The prover must wait out the lock or finish the permits first, and that permitting is non-discovery work. DOE leadership has also said publicly that it opposes flipping contracts at a premium. It terminated about 163 contracts (17.9 GW) in 2024-25 and rebids them through the OCSP.
(3) The step-up math is from background knowledge, not sourced. Global benchmarks for wind development assets put early-stage or resource-proven but unpermitted, ungridded sites at roughly $5-30k/MW. Ready-to-build projects with grid, permits and land are around $50-150k/MW. A bankable P50/P90 yield plus a grid study, without land, FPIC, an ECC or an NGCP impact study, is closer to the low band. For 50 MW at ~$10-25k/MW that is $0.5-1.25M. Against $10-30k of fees, that is ~20-100x on the right. Against $150-400k all-in proving cost, it is ~2-6x. That is well under the 10^3-10^4 pattern and near or under the ~30x refute line once the proving cost is counted.
(4) Market size: disclosed Philippine secondary trades of pre-development onshore RESCs are rare, likely a handful a year. Most IPP growth is self-applied contracts plus distressed buyouts (Unicorn). GEA rounds buy power tariffs, not contracts; IPPs bring their own pipelines.
verifiers.killer: The claimed $30-80k/MW price for a resource-proven, pre-development RESC has no transaction evidence behind it. Comparable sites trade nearer $5-25k/MW, which gives ~2-6x on all-in cost. Even that cannot be captured right away: DC2024-06-0018 bars assigning a pre-development RESC to a non-affiliate until 2 years after effectivity (unless the full permit set is done), allows only one such assignment, and requires DOE approval. Meanwhile, capitalised IPPs like Mainstream simply apply to DOE for RESCs directly.
